本[ほん]を読[よ]みます。
ご飯[はん]を食[た]べます。
音[おん]楽[がく]を聞[き]きます。
手[て]紙[がみ]を書[か]きます。

cloze_variants.nudge: 水 isn't drinking anything — it's what gets drunk.
本 doesn't read; it gets read.
ご飯 is on the receiving end of 食べます.
音楽 isn't listening — you're listening to it.
手紙 is what comes out of 書きます, not who writes it.

items.explanation_markdown:
Imagine it is early morning. You have just woken up, you stumble into the kitchen, and you pour yourself some coffee. If you want to describe this routine, you already know the word for coffee (コーヒー) and the verb for drinking (飲[の]む). 

But in Japanese, you cannot just shove a noun and a verb together and hope your listener figures it out. You need a way to tell them, "Hey, this coffee? It is the thing taking the hit. It is the target of my action."

In English, we rely entirely on the order of the words to know who is doing what. "I drink coffee" makes perfect sense, but "Coffee drink I" sounds like nonsense. Japanese, however, handles this completely differently. Instead of relying on a strict order, Japanese uses tiny grammatical tags attached to the ends of words to announce their job in the sentence.

Enter the particle を.

## How the object marker works

Think of を as a target reticle. It is a particle—a little word that attaches directly to the end of a noun—and its entire job is to point at an action and say, "The action happens to THIS."

Whenever you eat something, drink something, watch something, or buy something, the thing receiving that action gets the を particle.

```jp
コーヒーを飲[の]む。
パンを食[た]べる。
本[ほん]を読[よ]む。
```
*I drink coffee.*
*I eat bread.*
*I read a book.*

Typing and pronunciation note: When you are typing on a keyboard, you will type this character as "wo". However, in modern spoken Japanese, the "w" sound is almost entirely dropped. You will hear native speakers pronounce it exactly like the vowel "o" (お). It is a special character that exists almost exclusively to serve as this grammar particle.

## Building bigger sentences

Because particles like を act as permanent nametags for your words, it gives Japanese incredible flexibility. Let's bring back the topic marker は (the particle that means "as for X...") and see how they play together.

```jp
私[わたし]はお茶[ちゃ]を飲[の]む。
彼[かの]女[じょ]は映[えい]画[が]を見[み]る。
```
*I drink tea.*
*She watches a movie.*

Notice the natural rhythm of a standard Japanese sentence: Topic は Object を Verb. The topic sets the stage at the beginning, the object receives the action in the middle, and the verb rigidly anchors the very end of the sentence.

But here is where the particle system shines. Because the particles are attached to the nouns, you can actually shuffle the order of the information before the verb, and the sentence still means the exact same thing.

```jp
私[わたし]は肉[にく]を食[た]べる。
肉[にく]を私[わたし]は食[た]べる。
```
*I eat meat.*
*As for the meat, I eat it.*

Both sentences mean you are eating meat. The second one just places a bit more emphasis on the meat by putting it first. Because を is glued to 肉[にく], and は is glued to 私[わたし], your listener never gets confused about who is eating and what is being eaten.

## Asking what someone is doing

You will use を constantly when asking people about their plans or their habits. If you want to ask "what" someone is doing, you combine the question word 何[なに] (what) with the を particle.

```jp
何[なに]を買[か]う？
明日[あした]、パンを買[か]う。
```
*What will you buy?*
*Tomorrow, I will buy bread.*

```jp
毎[まい]日[にち]、何[なに]を見[み]る？
映[えい]画[が]を見[み]る。
```
*What do you watch every day?*
*I watch movies.*

> Notice how we didn't use the topic marker は for "you" or "I" in these examples? If you are looking right at your friend and asking a question, they already know you are talking to them. Japanese loves efficiency—if the topic is obvious from the context, you just drop it entirely and jump straight to the object and the verb.

## Rules and exceptions

There is one massive, unbreakable rule for を: it only ever works with action verbs.

You use it for eating, reading, buying, seeing, and listening. You absolutely **never** use it with the copula です (the word that works like *is/am/are*). 

If you want to say "It is water," you say `水です`. If you try to say `水をです`, you are basically saying "I am doing an action to the water... is." It is grammatical gibberish. Save を strictly for when a noun is actively having something done to it.

## Casual speech

Here is a messy truth about conversational Japanese that textbooks often hide until much later: when you are chatting casually with your friends, the を particle frequently vanishes into thin air.

When the context is totally clear, native speakers speak quickly and drop the object marker to save a syllable.

```jp
お酒[さけ]飲[の]む？
これ食[た]べる。
```
*Want to drink alcohol?*
*I'll eat this.*

Technically, these are `お酒を飲む？` and `これを食べる。`. While you are still building your muscle memory and getting used to how Japanese sentences are structured, you should practice using を every time. But do not be surprised when you hear your Japanese friends skipping it in casual situations.

## Contrast: は vs を

Because Japanese lets you omit so much information, it is completely normal for beginners to get confused about when to use the topic marker は and when to use the object marker を. 

Let's look at a sentence with both, and then see what happens if we mix them up.

```jp
猫[ねこ]は魚[さかな]を食[た]べる。
```
*The cat eats fish.*

Here, the cat (猫[ねこ]) is the topic. We are talking about the cat. The fish (魚[さかな]) is the target of the eating. The universe is in harmony.

But what if you panic and swap the particles?

```jp
魚[さかな]は猫[ねこ]を食[た]べる。
```
*The fish eats the cat.*

Now the fish is the topic (the one doing the action), and the cat is the one taking the hit! 

This is why particles are so vital. は sets the stage and introduces the main actor. を paints the target on the thing receiving the action. 

を is your absolute best friend for describing what you do to the world around you. You drink water, you read books, you meet friends. But what happens when something does an action *to* you? Or what if you want to emphasize exactly *who* is doing the action, rather than just treating them as a general topic? Hold onto that thought—it becomes incredibly important when we introduce the subject marker が a little later on.
caution_notes: を is only ever used with action verbs, never with the copula です.
In casual conversation, native speakers frequently drop the を particle entirely if the context is obvious.

example_sentences.furigana: 猫[ねこ]がいます。
誰[だれ]が来[らい]ますか。
お金[かね]がありません。
私[わたし]は犬[いぬ]が好[す]きです。
時[じ]間[かん]がありません。

cloze_variants.nudge: Nothing has been introduced yet — 猫 is brand-new here.
You can't ask 誰 about something already known — this is the unknown piece.
ありません has to say what is missing, and お金 is that thing.
私 already took the first slot — 犬 fills the second one.
The sentence points straight at what's absent.

items.explanation_markdown:
You're sitting in a quiet room and something moves in the corner. You want to say it out loud — "a cat!" — but not as the topic of a conversation, just pointing at the plain fact that a cat is *there*. This is the moment が was built for.

が is the subject marker: the little word that tags **who or what is actually doing the verb or being the thing**. Where は steps back and says "as for this, here's my comment," が leans in and points: *this one, right here, is the one.*

```jp
猫[ねこ]がいる。
```

*There's a cat.*

Notice there's no "as for" flavor here. You're not commenting on the cat as an already-known topic — you're announcing it. が does that announcing work.

## How it works

The structure is as simple as it looks: **Noun + が + Predicate**. The noun before が is the subject — the thing that exists, acts, or is described by whatever comes after.

The clearest place to feel が is with question words. When you ask *who* or *what* is doing something, you almost always reach for が, because you're asking the listener to fill in the unknown subject.

```jp
誰[だれ]がいる。
```

*Who's there?*

You can't make 誰[だれ] a topic — you can't comment on something you don't know yet. So は is off the table, and が steps in naturally. This is the single most reliable が instinct you can build: **question-word subjects take が.**

And the answer comes back with が too, because the answer is the newly-identified subject:

```jp
彼[かれ]がいる。
```

*He's there.*

が works the same way for existence and possession. When you're stating that something simply *exists* or that you *have* it, the thing that exists is marked with が.

```jp
お金[かね]がある。
```

*There's money. / I have money.*

Same shape every time: the thing being pointed at, then が, then the predicate. You don't conjugate が or change it — it's one fixed syllable doing one job.

## Rules and exceptions

The trap almost every learner falls into is reaching for が when they mean a general topic. If you're talking *about* yourself as the subject of an ongoing conversation, は is usually what you want. が is for the *new*, the *specific*, the *answer to a question* — the piece of information that wasn't already on the table.

> When a question word like 誰[だれ] or 何[なに] is the subject, use が, never は. "As for who?" is not a sentence.

There's a mirror rule that surprises people: the *answer* to a が question also takes が, but if you then shift to talking about that person generally, you switch back to は. The particle tracks what's new versus what's settled, not the grammar of the word itself.

> が marks the subject, but not every subject wears が. Once something becomes the known topic of the conversation, it often trades が for は.

## Casual speech

が itself doesn't contract — it's already a single clean syllable, so there's nothing to shorten. But in fast, casual speech, people often just *drop* it entirely when the meaning is obvious.

```jp
今[いま]、猫[ねこ]がいる。
猫[ねこ]いる。
```

*Right now, there's a cat. / A cat, there is.*

The first line is the full, neutral form. The second is what a friend might actually say pointing across the room — が gone, meaning intact. This dropping is casual only; in careful or polite speech, keep the が in.

## Contrast

Here's where が earns its keep against は, the topic marker you already know. Swap one for the other and the *feeling* of the sentence changes completely.

```jp
彼[かれ]がいる。
彼[かれ]は来[く]る。
```

*HE's the one who's here. / As for him, he'll come.*

The first line answers "who's here?" — が spotlights 彼[かれ] as the new, specific subject. The second uses は to set 彼[かれ] up as the topic and then comments about him. が points a finger; は sets a stage.

And against を, the direct object marker: を marks *what the action lands on*, while が marks *who does the action*. In a fuller sentence they'd sit on opposite sides of the verb — the doer in が, the done-to in を. For now, just hold the split: が is the actor, を is the target.

That's the whole core: が points at the subject, especially when it's new information or an answer to *who* or *what*. Hold onto this feeling — it comes back the moment we meet の and start linking nouns together.
caution_notes: When a question word like 誰 or 何 is the subject, use が — never は.
が marks new or specific subjects; once something becomes the known topic, it usually switches to は.
In casual speech が is often dropped entirely, but keep it in polite or careful sentences.

example_sentences.furigana: 私[わたし]の本[ほん]です。
日本[にほん]語[ご]の先[せん]生[せい]です。
友[とも]達[だち]の車[くるま]です。
学[がっ]校[こう]の近[ちか]くです。
これは母[はは]の傘[かさ]です。

items.explanation_markdown:
You are sitting at a table with a classmate, and you notice a book left behind. You want to ask who it belongs to, or perhaps declare that it belongs to you. In English, you would use an apostrophe-s ('s) or the word "of". 

In Japanese, you handle this with a single, incredibly useful particle: の.

## How it works

The particle の is a linker. Its primary job is to connect two nouns together, turning them into one single noun block. The most common way you will use this is to show possession.

The rule is strict: the owner or describing noun always comes first, followed by の, and then the thing being owned or described.

```jp
これは誰[だれ]の本[ほん]ですか。
```
*Whose book is this?*

```jp
それは私[わたし]の本[ほん]です。
```
*That is my book.*

Just like in English, you can chain these connections together as much as you need to. You just keep inserting の between the nouns.

```jp
私[わたし]の友[とも]達[だち]の猫[ねこ]は魚[さかな]を食[た]べます。
```
*My friend's cat eats fish.*

## Dropping the obvious noun

Sometimes, repeating the noun feels clunky. If someone points to a coffee and asks whose it is, you do not need to reply "It is his coffee." You can just say "It is his."

Japanese does the exact same thing. You can drop the final noun completely, leaving の hanging at the end of the phrase, as long as the context makes it obvious what you are talking about.

```jp
このコーヒーは誰[だれ]のですか。
```
*Whose coffee is this?*

```jp
彼[かれ]のです。
```
*It is his.*

> When you drop the noun like this, の acts like "mine", "yours", "his", or "hers". Just remember that the item you are dropping must be clearly understood from the conversation.

## More than just ownership

Because Japanese rarely lets you smash two nouns directly together, you will use の for much more than just possession. It is the universal glue for any situation where one noun describes another.

If you want to say "Japanese teacher" or "school photographs", you cannot just say `日本語先生` or `学校写真`. You have to bridge them with の.

```jp
日本[にほん]語[ご]の先[せん]生[せい]は明日[あした]来[らい]ます。
```
*The Japanese teacher is coming tomorrow.*

```jp
学[がっ]校[こう]の写[しゃ]真[しん]を見[み]ます。
```
*I will look at photos of the school.*

## Don't mix up the order

The biggest trap for English speakers is reversing the order when translating phrases that use the word "of". In English, you say "the window of the room". The main thing (the window) comes first.

In Japanese, the main thing you are talking about always comes last. 

If you say `部屋の窓`, you are talking about the room's window. If you accidentally say `窓の部屋`, you are talking about a room made of windows. Always put the modifier first.

## The difference a particle makes

Since you already know は (the topic marker), let's look at how replacing it with の completely changes your sentence. 

```jp
私[わたし]は友[とも]達[だち]です。
```
*I am a friend.*

```jp
私[わたし]の友[とも]達[だち]です。
```
*(They are) my friend.*

The first sentence uses は to make "I" the topic of the whole sentence. The second sentence uses の to link "I" and "friend" into a single concept before the sentence even finishes.

Now you can talk about all the things that belong to you or your friends. Hold onto this ability to link words together—it will be crucial when we learn how to talk about going *to* a specific location, like a friend's house, using に next.
caution_notes: Always put the modifier first—Japanese doesn't let you reverse the order like the English 'of'.
You cannot drop the linking particle の when combining nouns, even for compound ideas like 'Japanese teacher'.
It is safe to drop the second noun (leaving just の) only when the context makes it obvious what item you are talking about.

example_sentences.furigana: 食[た]べるのが好[す]きです。
読[よ]むのが速[はや]いです。

example_sentences.japanese: どうして行かないんですか。
example_sentences.furigana: どうして行[い]かないんですか。
頭[あたま]が痛[いた]いんです。

items.explanation_markdown:
You're at a friend's house and notice them putting on their coat. If you just ask 帰[かえ]りますか, it translates to "Will you go home?"—but it sounds a bit cold, like you're reading a survey question. You aren't just asking a random fact; you are seeing their coat and asking for an explanation based on that context. How do you ask "Oh, are you heading home?" with natural curiosity?

You use the explanatory んです.

```jp
帰[かえ]るんですか。
```
*Are you going home?*

### How it works

To build this, you take a verb in its plain, dictionary form (like 帰[かえ]る instead of 帰[かえ]ります) and add んです.

```jp
明日[あした]行[い]くんです。
```
*The thing is, I'm going tomorrow.*

To ask a question, you just add the question particle か to the end.

```jp
何[なに]を買[か]うんですか。
```
*What is it that you are buying?*

Why does this exist? Japanese has a tool called a *nominalizer*—a little word that turns an entire verb phrase into a noun-like thing you can talk about. Here, that word is の. When you add の to a verb, you turn "I go" into "The situation is that I go." 

In spoken Japanese, の often gets squished into ん, and we cap it off with です to make it polite. (In formal writing, you'll still see the unsquished version: のです).

### Casual speech

If you are talking to a friend and dropping です, this pattern changes slightly. The ん untangles back into a clear の, and you just raise your pitch at the end to make it a question.

```jp
今[いま]食[た]べるの？
```
*Are you eating now?*

```jp
どうして飲[の]まないの？
```
*Why aren't you drinking?*

> When answering casually, using a flat の at the end of a statement (行[い]くの。) can sound very soft or traditionally feminine. Men often use んだ instead, but when you're just starting out, simply replying with the plain verb (行[い]く。) is your safest bet.

### Reading the room

Because this pattern is all about explanations and shared context, it comes with a catch: you shouldn't use it for everything.

If you walk into a room and announce out of nowhere, 明日[あした]行[い]くんです (The thing is, I'm going tomorrow), people will wait for the rest of your story. It sounds like you are making an excuse or explaining a problem. Save it for when someone asks you why, or when you are reacting to something you both can see.

### Contrast: Invitations vs. Explanations

Let's look at how this fits with what you already know. You learned that adding ませんか to a verb stem makes a polite invitation. It looks similar to asking a negative んです question, but the meaning is totally different.

```jp
コーヒー、飲[の]みませんか。
```
*Won't you drink some coffee?*

```jp
コーヒー、飲[の]まないんですか。
```
*Are you not drinking coffee?*

The first invites them to drink. The second notes that they don't have a cup, and asks for the reason why.

Mastering んです is the key to sounding like you're actually participating in a conversation rather than just reading textbook sentences at people. Hold onto this feeling of modifying the ends of verbs—it becomes incredibly important when we look at ongoing actions with ている later on!
caution_notes: Using んです on every single sentence sounds like you are constantly making excuses; save it for when you need to explain something or react to shared context.
In casual speech, declarative statements ending in a flat の can sound traditionally feminine, so answering simply with the plain verb is often safer.

example_sentences.furigana: 学[がっ]校[こう]に行[い]きます。
七[なな]時[じ]に起[お]きます。
友[とも]達[だち]に会[あ]います。
椅[い]子[す]に座[すわ]ります。
日本[にほん]に住[す]んでいます。

items.explanation_markdown:
You are making weekend plans. You want to tell your friend you are heading to the park, and you want to ask what time they usually wake up. To say *where* you are going or *when* an event happens, you need a way to pinpoint that information. In Japanese, we use the particle に.

## How it works

Think of に as a dart. You throw it, and it lands on a specific, fixed target. That target can be a place on a map, a specific time on a clock, or even a person.

First, let's throw the dart at a map. When you use motion verbs like 行[い]く (to go) or 帰[かえ]る (to return home), に attaches to the place to mark your exact destination.

```jp
私[わたし]は学[がっ]校[こう]に行[い]きます。
```
*I go to school.*

```jp
彼[かれ]は家[いえ]に帰[かえ]ります。
```
*He returns home.*

Next, throw the dart at a calendar or a clock. に attaches to specific times to say exactly *when* an action happens.

```jp
何[なに]時[じ]に起[お]きますか。
```
*What time do you wake up?*

```jp
日[にち]曜[よう]日[ひ]に公[こう]園[えん]に行[い]きます。
```
*I will go to the park on Sunday.*

Finally, you can throw the dart at a person. When an action is directed at someone—like meeting them or asking them a question—に marks that person as your target.

```jp
友[とも]達[だち]に会[あ]います。
```
*I meet a friend.*

```jp
先[せん]生[せい]に聞[き]きます。
```
*I ask the teacher.*

## Rules and exceptions

Here is where に gets tricky, and it trips everyone up the first week—that's normal! You cannot just put に after *every* time word.

Remember how に is a dart hitting a fixed target? Some time words are relative. "Tomorrow" (明日[あした]) changes depending on when you say it. "Today" (今日[きょう]) is a floating concept, not a fixed number on a clock or calendar. Because they aren't fixed points, they reject the に dart.

> Relative time words like 今日[きょう] (today), 明日[あした] (tomorrow), and いつ (when) never take に.

So, you just leave them bare in the sentence:

```jp
明日[あした]、学[がっ]校[こう]に行[い]きます。
```
*I will go to school tomorrow.*

## Casual speech

In casual, everyday conversation, Japanese speakers often drop particles completely if the meaning is obvious. The destination に is one of the first to disappear when you are talking to friends.

```jp
明日[あした]、公[こう]園[えん]行[い]く？
```
*Are you going to the park tomorrow?*

## に vs を

You learned を (the direct object particle) for the thing you physically act upon. Compare these two sentences:

```jp
水[みず]を飲[の]みます。
```
*I drink water.*

```jp
友[とも]達[だち]に会[あ]います。
```
*I meet a friend.*

In the first sentence, water is the object you are directly consuming. In the second, your friend is the *target* you are directing your "meeting" action toward. You aren't "consuming" your friend! That is why interaction verbs like 会[あ]う (to meet) and 聞[き]く (to ask/listen) take the target particle に, not the direct object を.

Whether it's a place, a time, or a person, に is your trusty dart for hitting the target. Hold onto this concept of a destination—soon you will meet へ, a particle that lives in the same space but cares more about the journey than the exact landing spot.
caution_notes: Relative time words like 'today' or 'tomorrow' do not take the に particle because they are not fixed points in time.
Interaction verbs like 会う (to meet) and 聞く (to ask) take the target particle に, not the direct object particle を.

example_sentences.furigana: 東[とう]京[きょう]へ行[い]きます。
家[いえ]へ帰[かえ]ります。
学[がっ]校[こう]へ来[らい]ました。

example_sentences.english: I want to go to the sea.
example_sentences.furigana: 海[うみ]へ行[い]きたいです。

items.explanation_markdown:
You pack your bag and step out the door. The weather is beautiful, and you're heading toward the park. How do you describe that trajectory—the physical direction you are moving in?

```jp
私[わたし]は公[こう]園[えん]へ行[い]きます。
```
*I am heading to the park.*

## How it works

To mark the direction you are traveling, attach the particle へ directly to your destination noun. It works almost exclusively with movement verbs like `行く` (to go), `来る` (to come), and `帰る` (to return).

> When reading, this character is written as へ (he), but when used as a particle, it is always pronounced "e" (like the "e" in "elephant"). You already saw this quirk when the character は became the topic particle "wa".

The structure is always the place you are heading toward, followed by へ, followed by the movement.

```jp
先[せん]生[せい]が学[がっ]校[こう]へ来[らい]ます。
```
*The teacher comes to the school.*

```jp
明日[あした]、海[うみ]へ行[い]きます。
```
*Tomorrow, we will head to the sea.*

```jp
彼[かれ]は家[いえ]へ帰[かえ]ります。
```
*He is returning home.*

## Rules and exceptions

Because へ is an arrow pointing outward, it only makes sense when there is actual physical movement involved. You cannot use it to describe where an action takes place if you are staying still. For example, you cannot say `部屋へ本を読みます` to mean reading a book inside a room.

Additionally, while the particle に can attach to a time word to mark when something happens, へ is strictly spatial. You cannot attach it to a time word to say something like `何時へ行きますか` (toward what time are you going?).

## Contrast: The arrow vs. the thumbtack

If you're thinking, "Wait, didn't I already learn に for going to a place?", you are absolutely right. 

```jp
公[こう]園[えん]に行[い]きます。
```
*I go to the park.*

```jp
公[こう]園[えん]へ行[い]きます。
```
*I head toward the park.*

In modern, everyday spoken Japanese, these two sentences are practically interchangeable. Most of the time, nobody will bat an eye if you use に instead of へ when talking about your destination.

The difference is nuance. に acts like a thumbtack on a map—it focuses strictly on the final endpoint. へ acts like an arrow—it highlights the direction of travel and the journey itself. Because it draws attention to the path, へ can sometimes sound a bit more sweeping or poetic. It is also common in formal announcements (like a train heading toward a specific station).

Remember: へ points the arrow, and に marks the spot. Hold onto this spatial logic, because you will soon meet で—a particle that builds the stage for where actions actually happen once you arrive.
caution_notes: The particle へ is always pronounced 'e' (like in elephant), not 'he'.
Use へ exclusively with movement verbs (like 行く, 来る, 帰る); it cannot be used for stationary actions.
Unlike に, you cannot attach the direction particle へ to a time word.

items.meaning: at / by / with (place of action, means)

example_sentences.furigana: 図[と]書[しょ]館[かん]で勉[べん]強[きょう]します。
バスで行[い]きます。
箸[はし]で食[た]べます。

example_sentences.english: I read a book at home.
example_sentences.furigana: 家[いえ]で本[ほん]を読[よ]みます。
駅[えき]で待[ま]ちます。

items.explanation_markdown:
You've got your weekend plans sorted. You know what you want to do and what you want to eat. But if a friend asks exactly where all this is happening, or how you plan to get there, you're going to need the particle で.

で attaches directly to the end of a noun. It operates like a tag that tells your listener about the background details of your action.

## Setting the stage

When you do an active verb—like reading, eating, or watching a movie—you need a stage for that action to happen on. You mark that location with で. Think of it as answering "where is this event taking place?"

```jp
週[しゅう]末[まつ]、図[と]書[しょ]館[かん]で本[ほん]を読[よ]む。
```
*On the weekend, I read books at the library.*

```jp
家[いえ]で映[えい]画[が]を見[み]る。
```
*I watch movies at home.*

```jp
これ、どこで買[か]う？
```
*Where do you buy this?*

## Marking the tool

The second job of で is marking the means or method of an action. It tells us what tool you used to get the job done. In English, this usually translates to "by" or "with".

```jp
バスで学[がっ]校[こう]に行[い]く。
```
*I go to school by bus.*

```jp
箸[はし]で魚[さかな]を食[た]べる。
```
*I eat fish with chopsticks.*

## The "at" trap: で vs. に

This one trips everyone up the first week—that's completely normal. In English, we use "at" or "in" for almost everything location-related. Japanese splits the job between で and the particle に you learned earlier.

に acts like a dart hitting a dartboard. It marks a destination you are moving toward, but it doesn't describe a stage where a full activity takes place. If you are traveling toward a place, use に (or へ). If you are actively doing something once you get there, use で.

```jp
公[こう]園[えん]に行[い]く。
```
*I go to the park.*

```jp
公[こう]園[えん]で遊[あそ]ぶ。
```
*I play at the park.*

> Be careful: if you try to say `公園に遊ぶ`, a Japanese speaker will be very confused. You can't "play toward" a park!

So で handles the "where" and the "by what means". But what if you want to say you watched a movie *with* a friend? Don't use で here. Tools take で, but companions take a different particle entirely. Hold onto that thought—it becomes important when we meet と later.
caution_notes: Use で for the location where an action takes place, not に.
Don't use で to say you are doing something with a person; it is strictly for tools and means.

example_sentences.furigana: パンと卵[たまご]を買[か]います。
友[とも]達[だち]と行[い]きます。

example_sentences.english: There are a dog and a cat.
example_sentences.furigana: 犬[いぬ]と猫[ねこ]がいます。
先[せん]生[せい]と話[はな]します。

items.explanation_markdown:
You're sitting at a cozy diner in Tokyo, and you want to order a nice breakfast. You know the words for coffee, bread, and eggs. You could just point and say the words one by one, hoping the waiter understands you want them all.

But that feels a bit choppy, like a robot reading a grocery list. You want to sound like a human, smoothly connecting your thoughts. In English, you'd just use the word "and." It's one of the first words we master as children, endlessly chaining our thoughts together.

In Japanese, the most common equivalent is the particle と. It is small, it is incredibly common, and it is going to immediately make your sentences sound far more natural. But there is a catch. The Japanese と has a very specific personality, and it handles a second job that might surprise you.

## Connecting the dots

Let's start with its most basic job. When you want to bundle two physical things together, you place と right between them. It acts exactly like a plus sign (+) in mathematics, sitting squarely between two nouns.

```jp
パンと卵[たまご]
```
*Bread and eggs.*

It doesn't change the words around it, and it doesn't require any special conjugation. You simply drop it in. This means you can string more than two things together if your list is getting long. You just keep inserting a new と after every single noun, like links in a chain.

```jp
肉[にく]と魚[さかな]と卵[たまご]を買[か]います。
```
*I will buy meat, fish, and eggs.*

Look closely at how that sentence flows. The particle と bundles all three of those food items together into one giant noun phrase. Then, the direct object particle を steps in. It marks that entire bundle as the single target of the verb "to buy". You don't need a separate を for the meat and the fish; the と linked them up so they could share it.

When you are pointing at a menu or trying to explain what you need, combining demonstrative words (like "this" and "that") with と is incredibly powerful.

```jp
これとそれを使[つか]います。
```
*I will use this one and that one.*

This instantly elevates your ability to communicate your choices. You aren't just pointing and grunting anymore; you are building a proper grammatical structure that tells the listener exactly what you intend to do with multiple items.

## "With" someone

Now we arrive at the feature that often surprises English speakers. In English, the concepts of "and" and "with" feel fundamentally different. We think of "and" as a way to list things, and "with" as a way to show accompaniment.

But Japanese looks at the underlying logic. If you say "my friend and I will go," you are describing a situation where two people are traveling together. That is functionally identical to saying "I will go with my friend."

Because of this shared logic, the particle と handles both jobs perfectly.

```jp
私[わたし]は友[とも]達[だち]と公[こう]園[えん]へ行[い]きます。
```
*I will go to the park with a friend.*

When you attach と directly to a person or an animal, and then follow it up with an action, it naturally translates to "together with." You do not need to hunt for a separate vocabulary word for "with". The particle itself carries all the weight.

```jp
毎[まい]日[にち]、お父[ちち]さんとお茶[ちゃ]を飲[の]みます。
```
*Every day, I drink tea with my father.*

This pattern is incredibly versatile. Whether you are studying with a classmate, living with a sibling, or just walking with your dog, と is the particle you need. If you want to be completely unambiguous and emphasize the "togetherness" of the action, you can pair it with the vocabulary word 一[いっ]緒[しょ]に (together).

```jp
彼[かの]女[じょ]と一[いっ]緒[しょ]に映[えい]画[が]を見[み]ます。
```
*I will watch a movie together with my girlfriend.*

You will hear this specific combination constantly in daily Japanese conversation. It adds a nice sense of warmth and cooperation to the sentence.

## The boundaries of と

This is the part of the lesson where English speakers usually stumble, because our English brains try to trick us. Because we use the English word "and" for absolutely everything, we assume we can sprinkle と everywhere too. But Japanese grammar is much stricter about categorizing words.

> The golden rule of と is that it can only connect nouns. You can never use it to link verbs, adjectives, or entire sentences.

Let's say you are describing your weekend plans. You want to say, "I will eat and sleep." It is extremely tempting to take the verbs for eat and sleep and just stick と between them. But if you say `食べると寝る`, a native Japanese speaker will look at you with total confusion. In their mind, you just tried to use a physical plus sign to combine two actions. It feels structurally broken. This particle is strictly reserved for bridging things, people, places, or ideas. You will learn completely different grammar patterns for linking actions or describing a sequence of events later in your journey.

The second major boundary is that と is strictly exhaustive. When you use it, you are presenting a complete, closed list.

```jp
犬[いぬ]と猫[ねこ]
```
*A dog and a cat.*

When you say this phrase, you are stating that there is a dog and a cat, and *absolutely nothing else*. If you were at a pet store and there were also birds and fish present, using と here means you are actively excluding them from your statement. It paints a closed box with only the mentioned items inside. If the listener opens the box, they expect to find exactly a dog and a cat, no more, no less.

## と versus で (The two "withs")

Because English uses the single word "with" in two completely different ways, you have to run a quick mental check when translating your thoughts into Japanese. Think about the difference between the sentences "I ate with a friend" and "I ate with chopsticks."

In the first sentence, the friend is a companion sharing the experience. In the second sentence, the chopsticks are merely a tool you are wielding to accomplish the task. You already know the particle で, which marks the tool, means, or method you use.

```jp
お金[かね]で本[ほん]を買[か]います。
```
*I buy books with money.*

Here, money is the tool you are using to facilitate the purchase. If you accidentally used と in this situation and said `お金と本を買います`, you would completely change the meaning. You would be telling the shopkeeper, "I will buy money and books." They might wonder how exactly one goes about purchasing money.

When you want to mark a living companion who is joining you in the action, you must always use と.

```jp
友[とも]達[だち]と本[ほん]を買[か]います。
```
*I will buy books with a friend.*

Before you speak, ask yourself: Are you using this object to accomplish a task? Use で. Is this person or animal keeping you company? Use と.

## と versus に (Targets vs Partners)

You have also learned the particle に, which acts as a target or a direction for your action. Sometimes, swapping に for と completely changes the social dynamic of what is happening in the sentence.

Let's imagine you are confused at a train station and you need to ask someone for directions.

```jp
駅[えき]員[いん]に聞[き]きます。
```
*I will ask the station staff.*

In this sentence, に acts like an arrow pointing your question directly at the station staff. They are the clear target of your action. But watch what happens if you accidentally swap that particle for と.

```jp
駅[えき]員[いん]と聞[き]きます。
```
*I will listen with the station staff.*

Suddenly, the entire scenario has shifted. You and the station staff are now partners, standing side-by-side, listening to someone else speak! The particle に directs the action *at* someone, while と pulls them alongside you to experience it together.

This exact same shift happens with verbs involving meeting people.

```jp
先[せん]生[せい]に会[あ]います。
```
*I will meet the teacher.*

```jp
先[せん]生[せい]と会[あ]います。
```
*I will meet with the teacher.*

Both of these sentences are perfectly natural Japanese, and they are often used interchangeably in casual speech. However, using に feels a bit more one-sided—you are going to the teacher, perhaps because they called you into their office. Using と implies mutual coordination. It feels like you both checked your calendars, agreed on a time, and chose to meet up as equals.

## Casual speech notes

Unlike some of the heavier grammar patterns you will encounter later, the particle と itself doesn't contract or change shape in casual speech. It remains perfectly intact whether you are speaking formally to a boss or casually to a close friend. 

What *does* change is how often it gets dropped entirely. In very fast, casual Japanese, speakers will sometimes just list nouns with a slight pause between them instead of explicitly using と (saying "pan, tamago" instead of "pan to tamago"). But as a learner, you should always keep it in your toolkit to ensure you are understood clearly.

## Wrapping up

The particle と is the foundational glue you need to start building more complex, descriptive sentences, as long as you remember to only stick nouns together. Whenever you need to list your favorite foods, or talk about who is joining you for a weekend trip, this is the tool you will reach for.

Just remember that it always creates a closed, complete list. If you want to say things like "meat, fish, and things like that" without sounding like you're reciting a strict legal inventory, you'll need a slightly softer particle. Hold onto that thought—we will meet the open-ended particle や in a future lesson to solve exactly that problem.
caution_notes: と can only connect nouns, never verbs or sentences.
Lists made with と are exhaustive; they imply nothing else is included.

example_sentences.japanese: 野菜や果物を食べます。
example_sentences.english: I eat vegetables, fruit, and so on.
example_sentences.furigana: 野[や]菜[さい]や果物[くだもの]を食[た]べます。
本[ほん]や雑[ざっ]誌[し]を読[よ]みます。

example_sentences.english: I like dogs, cats, and such.
example_sentences.furigana: 犬[いぬ]や猫[ねこ]が好[す]きです。

items.explanation_markdown:
You just walked into a massive, sprawling shopping mall. The store shelves are overflowing with hundreds of different sections, and you spend an entire afternoon just browsing. Later that evening, a friend asks you what you looked at.

If you try to list every single thing you saw, you are going to be talking for a long, long time. You don't want to recount the entire floor plan of the building. You just want to give them a sampler platter of your day: "I looked at books and magazines, things like that."

When you first start learning a language, you often feel a bit like a lawyer. You have to be overly precise because your grammatical toolbox is still small. If someone asks what you did or what you saw, you try to list every single thing to be completely accurate. Alternatively, you leave things out and feel a slight twinge of guilt, as if you are hiding the truth.

But native speakers do not talk like lawyers in their everyday lives. They speak in broad, relaxed strokes. They give a few key details, a couple of prominent examples, and then they let the listener's imagination fill in the rest of the gaps.

You already know how to use the particle `と` to say "and." But `と` has a massive catch: it creates a closed, airtight loop. If you say you looked at books `と` magazines, you are telling your friend that you looked at exactly those two things, and absolutely nothing else in the entire store. If you actually looked at photographs as well, using `と` makes your statement technically untrue.

When you want to give a few examples without claiming it is the whole exhaustive list, you need a different grammatical tool. Enter the particle `や`.

## How the open list works

The particle `や` sits right between two nouns, in the exact same physical spot where `と` would normally go. But instead of locking the list down and throwing away the key, `や` props the door wide open. It tells your listener, "Here are a couple of examples of what is going on, but please do not hold me to this being everything."

```jp
本[ほん]や雑[ざっ]誌[し]を読[よ]みます。
```
*I read books, magazines, and things like that.*

By using `や` instead of `と`, you leave a little ghost space at the end of your sentence. The listener inherently knows that there might also be newspapers, manga, or internet articles involved in your reading habits, even though you did not bother to explicitly name them.

Sometimes, you want to make that "ghost space" a little more obvious. You can do this by sticking the word `など` at the very end of your list, right after the final noun. The word `など` translates roughly to "etcetera," "and so on," or "and the like."

```jp
朝[あさ]ご飯[はん]にパンや果物[くだもの]などを食[た]べます。
```
*I eat bread, fruit, and the like for breakfast.*

Adding `など` does not dramatically change the core meaning of the sentence—the `や` already did the heavy lifting of making the list open-ended—but it rounds out the phrasing beautifully. It acts like a little verbal wave of the hand, confirming out loud that the list trails off into other unspoken items. You will hear native speakers use this combination constantly.

Grammatically, when you use `Noun A + や + Noun B`, Japanese treats that entire clustered chunk as one single, giant mega-noun. The grammatical machinery that comes afterward—like the object marker `を` or the subject marker `が`—does not care how many items are packed inside that basket. It just attaches to the very end of the cluster (or to `など`, if you used it) and treats the whole thing exactly the same way it would treat a single, solitary word.

## The rules of the sampler platter

Japanese grammar is notoriously strict about keeping different kinds of words in their own separate lanes. English is quite lazy by comparison. In English, the word "and" is a universal Swiss Army knife. We use it to connect nouns ("cats and dogs"), adjectives ("big and red"), and verbs ("I ate and slept").

Japanese absolutely does not work this way. The most important rule you must remember for `や` is that it **only connects nouns**.

You cannot use it to connect adjectives, and you absolutely cannot use it to connect verbs. If you want to say that you wake up and eat, you have to use an entirely different grammatical machine. Using `起きるや食べる` is a fast track to sounding completely broken. A native speaker will hear the `や` and immediately expect another noun; when a verb comes out instead, their brain will skip a beat. Keep this particle strictly confined to people, places, and things.

> You might be tempted to string together four, five, or six nouns with `や`, just like you might freely do in English ("I bought apples and bananas and oranges and grapes"). Resist this urge. In Japanese, chaining more than two or three items with `や` sounds extremely clunky, robotic, and overwhelming. Give two strong examples and let the particle do the rest of the unspoken work.

Let's look at another scenario, this time using locations instead of objects. You are planning your weekend out in the city and chatting with a coworker about your plans.

```jp
明日[あした]、海[うみ]や公[こう]園[えん]へ行[い]きます。
```
*Tomorrow, I will go to the sea, a park, and so on.*

This paints a picture of a relaxed, flexible, and open itinerary. If you end up going to a movie theater or a coffee shop as well, you haven't broken any promises or lied about your weekend, because the `や` kept your schedule completely open to additions.

## The closed box vs. the open basket

Because you now have two different ways to say "and" with nouns, let's put them right next to each other so you can truly feel the difference. This is what language teachers call a minimal pair: two sentences that are completely identical except for the one single piece of grammar we are swapping out.

First, let's look at the particle you already know, the exhaustive (closed list) `と`.

```jp
今日[きょう]、肉[にく]と魚[さかな]を買[か]います。
```
*Today, I will buy meat and fish.*

Think of `と` as a closed box. Imagine you are running an errand for a very strict chef. If you give them this sentence, you are stating as an absolute fact that your entire grocery purchase will consist of meat and fish, and absolutely zero other items. There is no room for interpretation. If you also buy vegetables, you have violated the boundaries of the `と` box.

Now, swap in our new pattern, `や`.

```jp
今日[きょう]、肉[にく]や魚[さかな]などを買[か]います。
```
*Today, I will buy meat, fish, and so on.*

This is the open basket. If you are just describing your general grocery shopping plans to a friend, this is the one you want to use. It means that meat and fish are the headliners of your shopping trip, but you are probably also going to pick up some water, maybe some vegetables, or whatever else catches your eye. You are simply painting a general picture of your errands.

If you are ever trying to decide which one to use in a live conversation, take a split second to ask yourself: "Am I giving an exact, restricted inventory, or am I just giving a few examples?" If it is a strict inventory, use `と`. If it is just a sampler platter, reach for `や`.

## Casual speech and structural glue

In casual Japanese, especially when you are speaking quickly with close friends, you probably already know that speakers love to drop grammatical particles. Target markers like `に`, object markers like `を`, and subject markers like `が` frequently vanish into thin air when the context makes it obvious what is happening.

However, `や` is structural glue. It holds the core meaning of the nouns together, so it does not get dropped.

Imagine you are hanging out with a friend, and they ask what you usually drink on a hot day.

```jp
水[みず]やお茶[ちゃ]飲[の]む。
```
*I drink water, tea, and so on. (Casual)*

Notice how the object marker `を` is completely gone, which is incredibly common in casual speech, but the `や` remains untouched. It is essential for letting your friend know that water and tea are just a few options among many.

## Connecting people

Finally, keep in mind that this open basket is not just for objects and places. `や` works beautifully with people, too. Imagine you are at a large school event and you are describing the massive crowd gathering in the courtyard.

```jp
学[がっ]校[こう]で先[せん]生[せい]や学[がく]生[せい]に会[あ]います。
```
*I meet teachers, students, and others at school.*

You might also meet parents, station staff, or police officers on your commute, but teachers and students are the primary groups you are choosing to highlight. The target particle `に` clips right onto the end of the `先生や学生` block without skipping a beat.

Hold onto this concept of making open-ended lists. Right now, you are building these lists with `や`. Soon, you will meet the particle `も` (also / too), which you can use to explicitly stack even more additions onto these kinds of open-ended scenarios. Until then, enjoy the freedom of not having to list every single noun in your vocabulary!
caution_notes: The particle や can only connect nouns; never use it to connect adjectives or verbs.
Chaining more than two or three nouns with や sounds unnatural—stick to a few strong examples and let the particle imply the rest.

example_sentences.furigana: 私[わたし]も学[がく]生[せい]です。
これもください。
彼[かれ]も来[らい]ます。

cloze_variants.nudge: Someone just said they're a student, and 私 joins them.
You've already ordered something; これ gets added to it.
Others are already coming, and 彼 joins that group.
You were already drinking something else; 水 joins the list.
There's already another animal here, and 猫 adds to it.

items.explanation_markdown:
You are out grabbing drinks with a friend at a local cafe. They step up to the counter, look at the menu, and order a coffee. You are next in line, and honestly, a coffee sounds perfect to you right now too. 

In English, you have a few easy ways to express this shared feeling. You might say, "I'll have a coffee too," or simply agree with a quick, "Me too." 

In Japanese, expressing this is incredibly straightforward. You use the particle も to add that precise "also" or "too" nuance to your sentence. It is one of the most common and useful tools you will learn, because it instantly makes your speech sound connected to the people around you.

```jp
友[とも]達[だち]はコーヒーを飲[の]みます。
私[わたし]もコーヒーを飲[の]みます。
```
*My friend will drink coffee.*
*I will also drink coffee.*

## How it works

Whenever you want to show that a new person, place, or thing shares a trait or performs the exact same action as something that was already mentioned, you bring in も. You attach it right after the noun you want to elevate.

But here is the most important mechanical rule to remember: this particle completely devours the basic marker particles. You already know は (the topic marker), が (the subject marker), and を (the object marker). When も steps onto the stage, those basic markers vanish.

If you want to say "I am a student too," you do not stack the particles together. You never say `私はも` or `私もは`. The new particle just steps in and takes over the job completely.

```jp
私[わたし]は学[がく]生[せい]です。
彼[かれ]も学[がく]生[せい]です。
```
*I am a student.*
*He is also a student.*

Why does Japanese do this? Think of basic particles like は and が as structural scaffolding. They hold the sentence up. But も is a spotlight. When you shine that spotlight on a noun, everyone already knows it is the main subject based on context, so the language prioritizes the "also" feeling over the rigid grammatical scaffolding.

This devouring rule works exactly the same way when you are dealing with the objects of a sentence. Imagine you are at a store. You decide to buy a book, but then you see a movie on the shelf next to it that you also want. You are performing the exact same action on a second object.

Instead of using the object marker を for the movie, you simply swap it out.

```jp
本[ほん]を買[か]います。
映[えい]画[が]も買[か]います。
```
*I will buy a book.*
*I will buy a movie too.*

It is wonderfully efficient. The listener already knows what action is happening, and by simply dropping in も, you seamlessly add another item to the list of things being bought.

## Rules and exceptions

> **Watch out:** English gives you a lot of freedom to float the word "also" around a sentence. You can say "I also drink water," or "I drink water also." Japanese is strictly rigid in its structure. The particle も must physically attach directly to the noun it is talking about.

There is another fantastic feature of this particle that trips up learners at first, but makes perfect sense once you see it in action. When you use it in a negative sentence, the meaning naturally shifts to "neither" or "not either."

Because Japanese verbs carry the negative meaning at the very end of the sentence, the particle itself does not need to change. You just swap out the topic or object marker exactly as you did before, and the negative verb takes care of the rest.

```jp
今日[きょう]は肉[にく]を食[た]べません。
魚[さかな]も食[た]べません。
```
*I will not eat meat today.*
*I will not eat fish either.*

This is often a huge relief for English speakers. In English, we have to learn entirely new vocabulary words to handle negatives—"also" turns into "neither", and "too" turns into "either". Japanese does not make you memorize a new set of negative grouping words. It trusts you to use the exact same building blocks and just flip the verb to negative at the end.

## Contrast: も vs. と

Since you are learning how to group things together, it is very common to wonder how this new particle compares to the particle と, which you already know means "and."

While they seem somewhat similar when translated, they serve very different purposes in a Japanese conversation. The particle と groups multiple things together into one tidy, closed package. It implies you are looking at the whole group at once.

On the other hand, も adds new information to an established pattern. It is a follow-up. You establish a fact first, and then you use it to say, "Hey, this other thing fits that fact as well."

Let's look at the difference when talking about animals at the park.

```jp
犬[いぬ]と猫[ねこ]を見[み]ます。
```
*I see a dog and a cat.*

In that sentence, you are observing both animals in one single thought. Now look at how the feeling changes when we split it up.

```jp
犬[いぬ]を見[み]ます。
猫[ねこ]も見[み]ます。
```
*I see a dog.*
*I see a cat too.*

Here, you noticed the dog first. That was your established action. Then, you noticed the cat, and you wanted to emphasize that the cat shares the exact same action as the dog. It feels much more conversational and layered.

When you are first starting to speak Japanese, you might feel like you are just firing off isolated, robotic sentences. Learning this particle is your first big step toward sounding like a natural participant in a conversation. It allows you to piggyback on what other people are saying and build a bridge between speakers.

For now, spend your time practicing swapping out those basic markers when you want to say "too." Keep this versatile little word in your back pocket. Later on in your studies, you will see how it can stack with other directional particles like から (from) to mean things like "even from," but you already have the core pattern down perfectly.
caution_notes: Remember that も completely replaces the basic marker particles は, が, and を, rather than stacking with them.
Unlike English where 'also' can float around the sentence, the particle も must physically attach directly to the noun it modifies.

example_sentences.furigana: 九[きゅう]時[じ]から働[はたら]きます。
駅[えき]から歩[ある]きます。
日本[にほん]から来[らい]ました。
朝[あさ]から雨[あめ]です。

items.explanation_markdown:
You're at a welcome party for new students and someone asks where you traveled from, or a friend wants to know when your new schedule starts. How do you mark the starting point of your journey or your time?

## How it works

To express "from" a place or a time, Japanese uses the particle から (a little word that attaches to nouns to show their grammatical role). It works like a thumbtack on a map or a calendar, pinning down the exact starting point of whatever action you are talking about.

You just attach it directly to the end of the noun. Remember that Japanese particles always come *after* the word they modify. So "from here" becomes "here from" (ここから).

```jp
どこから来[らい]ましたか。
```
*Where did you come from?*

```jp
家[いえ]から歩[ある]きます。
```
*I will walk from home.*

It works exactly the same way for time. If an action starts at a specific moment, just attach から to that block of time.

```jp
今日[きょう]から学[がっ]校[こう]に行[い]きます。
```
*I will go to school from today.*

```jp
何[なん]時[じ]からコーヒーを飲[の]みますか。
```
*From what time will you drink coffee?*

## Rules and exceptions

Word order with particles trips everyone up the first week — that is completely normal. Unlike English, you never put the "from" before the word. A guess like `から家` means nothing in Japanese because the particle must always be attached to the back of the noun.

> Because から marks a starting line, it feels very natural with verbs involving movement (like 行[い]く or 来[く]る) or continuous actions that have a clear beginning.

## Contrast

You already know a few ways to mark locations and times, and it is easy to get them mixed up. Let's look at に and から. 

Think of に as an arrow pointing at your destination. から is the starting block you push off from. Swap them, and the entire direction of your sentence reverses.

```jp
日本[にほん]に行[い]きます。
```
*I will go to Japan.*

```jp
日本[にほん]から来[らい]ました。
```
*I came from Japan.*

The same logic applies to time. The particle に pinpoints an exact moment something happens, while から just tells you when the block of time begins.

```jp
朝[あさ]に本[ほん]を読[よ]みます。
```
*I will read a book in the morning.*

```jp
朝[あさ]から本[ほん]を読[よ]みます。
```
*I will read a book from the morning.*

Now you can pin down exactly where and when things start. Hold onto this starting point — soon we will meet the particle まで (until), which lets you cap the other end of the timeline!
caution_notes: Japanese particles always attach to the end of the noun, so Noun + から translates to 'from Noun', never the other way around.
While に pinpoints an exact destination or time, から only marks the starting point where the action originates.

example_sentences.furigana: 五[ご]時[じ]まで働[はたら]きます。

example_sentences.english: I walk as far as the station.
example_sentences.furigana: 駅[えき]まで歩[ある]きます。

example_sentences.japanese: ここから学校まで近いです。
example_sentences.english: It's near from here to school.
example_sentences.furigana: ここから学[がっ]校[こう]まで近[ちか]いです。
夜[よる]まで勉[べん]強[きょう]しました。

items.explanation_markdown:
You're waiting for a friend at a coffee shop. They text you that they're running late, and you want to reply, "I'll wait until noon." You know the words for "noon" and "wait," but you need a way to draw a line in the time.

Enter まで. It acts like a boundary marker, setting the exact point where an action stops.

```jp
昼[ひる]まで待[ま]ちます。
```
*I will wait until noon.*

## Drawing the line

まで attaches directly to the end of a noun. You can think of it as meaning *until* when you're talking about time, or *as far as* when you're talking about physical space.

If you're explaining how far you plan to walk with someone, you just attach it to the location:

```jp
駅[えき]まで歩[ある]きます。
```
*I will walk as far as the station.*

Notice how the rule is exactly the same for both time and place? Japanese loves this kind of consistency. You take the limit (noon, the station), tag it with まで, and follow it up with your verb.

## The dynamic duo: から and まで

You already know that から marks a starting point (*from*). Because から sets the start and まで sets the end, they show up together constantly to express "from X to Y."

```jp
朝[あさ]から晩[ばん]まで遊[あそ]びます。
```
*I will play from morning until evening.*

This combo works perfectly for physical distances, too. You just bracket your start and end points.

```jp
家[いえ]から学[がっ]校[こう]まで歩[ある]きます。
```
*I will walk from the house to school.*

> When using まで with time, the action needs to be something continuous that fills the time up to the limit, like sleeping, playing, or waiting.

## Setting limits: まで against へ

You learned earlier that へ indicates the direction you are heading. So, how is that different from using まで with a place? Let's look at them side by side.

```jp
海[うみ]へ行[い]きます。
```
*I will go toward the sea.*

```jp
海[うみ]まで行[い]きます。
```
*I will go as far as the sea.*

When you use へ, you're just pointing your compass. The sea is your destination, but it's mostly a statement of where you are headed.

When you use まで, you are emphasizing the *extent* of the journey. You're saying, "My trip continues up to the sea, and that is where the travel stops." It highlights the physical distance it takes to get there.

This particle is all about setting clear boundaries. Hold onto this concept of marking a limit—it becomes incredibly handy when we want to ask questions about those limits using `か` later on!
caution_notes: When using まで with time, the action must be continuous, filling the space up to that limit.

example_sentences.japanese: 寒いから、コートを着ます。
example_sentences.english: Because it's cold, I'll wear a coat.
example_sentences.furigana: 寒[さむ]いから、コートを着[ちゃく]ます。

example_sentences.japanese: 忙しいから、行きません。
example_sentences.english: I won't go because I'm busy.
example_sentences.furigana: 忙[いそが]しいから、行[い]きません。

example_sentences.english: I won't buy it because it's expensive.
example_sentences.furigana: 高[たか]いから、買[か]いません。

example_sentences.english: Because it's raining, I'll stay home.
example_sentences.furigana: 雨[あめ]だから、家[いえ]にいます。

items.explanation_markdown:
You're at a friend's place for dinner, and the food is genuinely great. Your friend asks why you're going back for a third helping — and you want to say *because it's delicious*. But hold on: you don't have adjectives like "delicious" yet in your toolkit, so let's pick a reason you *can* say. Your friend asks why you're not drinking the beer, and the honest answer is: *because I'm a student* (and, let's say, too young). That "because" is から.

から is the workhorse "because" of Japanese. You take your reason, say it as a full sentence, and stick から on the end. That's the whole trick — no rearranging, no special verb form. The reason comes first, then から, then (often) the result.

## How it works

The structure is refreshingly flat: **a full clause + から**. Whatever sentence states your reason, you just append から to it.

Because the clause in front is a complete sentence, it can end in a verb, an adjective, a noun + です, whatever — から doesn't care. Here's a noun-predicate reason (someone *is* something):

```jp
私[わたし]は学[がく]生[せい]ですから。
```

*Because I'm a student.*

Notice から sitting right after です. That's the polite pattern, sometimes listed as ですから — but it's really just です (the word that works like *is/am/are*) plus から glued on. Nothing new to memorize.

You can put the reason and the result in one breath. Reason first, から, then the consequence:

```jp
今日[きょう]は忙[いそが]しいですから、昼[ひる]ご飯[はん]は肉[にく]です。
```

*Because I'm busy today, lunch is meat.*

Here the reason ends in the い-adjective 忙[いそが]しい ("busy"). から attaches straight to it — again, no reshaping the word. The comma after から is just breathing room; it's optional.

You can also flip the order. Say the result, then tack the reason on afterward as its own sentence ending in から:

```jp
昼[ひる]ご飯[はん]は肉[にく]です。忙[いそが]しいですから。
```

*Lunch is meat. Because I'm busy.*

This after-the-fact version is extremely common in speech — you blurt the point, then justify it. Both orders mean the same thing.

## Rules and exceptions

The big thing to internalize: から attaches to a **whole clause**, not to a noun by itself. English lets you say "because of the rain," gluing "because" onto a noun. Japanese から can't do that alone — it needs a real predicate in front. So you say 寒[さむ]いですから ("because it's cold"), not 寒[さむ]さから for "because of the cold."

You have a choice of politeness on the clause before から. Both of these are fine:

```jp
今日[きょう]は寒[さむ]いですから。
今日[きょう]は寒[さむ]いから。
```

*Because it's cold today.* (polite / plain)

The first keeps です for a polite tone; the second is the plain form. Here's the useful rule of thumb: match the clause before から to the formality of the sentence you're in. In a polite conversation, ...ですから feels smoother; among friends, the plain ...から is normal.

> から carries a slightly *subjective*, personal-reason flavor — it's *your* reason, sometimes with a hint of insistence. That's fine in most speech, but be aware that leaning on it hard ("...から！") can sound like you're pushing your excuse. When you want a softer, more neutral "because," Japanese has another tool (see the closing note).

One more trap: don't confuse this reason-から with the から that means "from" (a starting point). Same three sounds, totally different job. The "from" one attaches to nouns (a place, a time); the "because" one attaches to a clause. Context and what's in front of it tell them apart.

## Casual speech

In casual Japanese, you mostly just drop the です and keep the plain clause + から:

```jp
今日[きょう]は忙[いそが]しいから。
```

*Because I'm busy today.*

You'll also hear だから standing alone at the start of a reply — literally "because (it) is" — used like "that's why" or, with attitude, "like I said." And a blunt だから何[なに]？ means "so what?" These are set phrases built from the same だ + から; you don't need to produce them yet, just recognize them.

## Contrast

You haven't learned any sibling patterns yet, so there's nothing to swap から against inside your current toolkit — which actually makes this the cleanest possible time to lock in one idea: **から = reason, and it lives at the end of the reason clause.** Reason, then から, then result. Get that shape into your ear now.

The only contrast worth flagging is the internal one from the rules section — reason-から (clause + から) versus from-から (noun + から). Keep them mentally in separate drawers.

Because you have this now, a whole category of sentences opens up: any time you can state a fact, you can turn it into a reason. Lock in the shape — reason clause, then から — because the very next "because" you meet, ので, lives in exactly the same space but sounds softer and more matter-of-fact. When you learn it, you'll define it against today's から.
caution_notes: から attaches to a whole clause with a real predicate, never to a bare noun the way English 'because of' can.
Match the politeness of the clause before から to the sentence around it: ...ですから in polite speech, plain ...から among friends.
Don't confuse reason-から (clause + から) with the から that means 'from' (noun + から); they look identical but attach to different things.

items.explanation_markdown:
You're at your friend's place and their little sister is asleep on the couch. Someone turns the music up and you want to gently explain *why* everyone should keep it down — not bark an order, just point at the reason. In Japanese, the soft way to lay a reason on the table is ので.

You already have から for "because." ので lives in the same room, but it wears softer shoes. It presents the reason as a plain fact of the situation rather than as your personal push, which makes it perfect for explanations, apologies, and polite requests.

```jp
赤[あか]ちゃんですので、こちらはどうですか。
```

*It's a baby, so how about over here?*

## How it works

The core move is dead simple: take a clause in its **plain form** (the dictionary-style, non-polite form of a verb, adjective, or です), and stick ので on the end. The whole thing means "because [clause]."

With a plain verb, you just attach it directly.

```jp
明日[あした]、病[びょう]院[いん]ので、今日[きょう]は家[いえ]にいます。
```

*Because I have the hospital tomorrow, today I'm staying home.*

With an い-adjective, same deal — the adjective is already plain, so ので slots right on.

```jp
これは安[やす]いので、これにします。
```

*This one's cheap, so I'll go with this one.*

Here's the one spot that trips everyone up the first week — that's normal. With **nouns and な-adjectives**, the plain form of です is だ, but before ので that だ becomes **な**, not だ. So it's `noun + な + ので`, never `noun + だ + ので`.

```jp
彼[かれ]は医[い]者[しゃ]なので、こちらがいいです。
```

*He's a doctor, so this way is better.*

```jp
父[ちち]は今[いま]、病[びょう]気[き]なので、私[わたし]が行[い]きます。
```

*My father is sick right now, so I'll go.*

Notice 病[びょう]気[き] (a noun/な-type word here) takes な before ので. Say it out loud a few times — 医[い]者[しゃ]なので, 病[びょう]気[き]なので — and let the な feel automatic.

## Rules and exceptions

The big constraint: ので points at the reason, and the reason clause comes **first**. You don't lead with the result. The shape is always `[reason]ので、[result]`.

> ので attaches to the **plain** form even when your main sentence is polite. So you get 病[びょう]気[き]なので、行[い]きます — plain before ので, polite です/ます at the very end. Mixing plain-then-polite like this is correct and normal.

Because ので frames things as objective fact, it clashes with strong personal commands and blunt opinions. If you're barking an order or insisting on your own will, ので feels too soft and から fits better. For explanations and polite requests, ので is your friend.

One more: don't drop the な with noun sentences. 学[がく]生[せい]ので is a classic beginner slip; it must be 学[がく]生[せい]なので.

## Casual speech

In fast, casual speech ので often squeezes down to んで. It means exactly the same thing — it just sounds more relaxed and spoken.

```jp
今日[きょう]は病[びょう]気[き]なんで、うちにいます。
```

*I'm sick today, so I'm staying home. (casual)*

You'll hear んで constantly in conversation, especially tacked onto a light apology or excuse. It's not rude, just informal — keep the full ので for writing and polite situations.

## Contrast

Here's the pairing that matters. You know から; both から and ので mean "because." The difference is attitude.

- から pushes: it's *your* reason, and it can carry a bit of "so there." It happily sits under commands and strong opinions.
- ので lays a fact down gently: it's just how the situation is. It softens requests and apologies.

Swap them in a request and you can feel it:

```jp
安[やす]いので、これにします。
```

*It's cheap, so I'll go with this one. (calm, matter-of-fact)*

```jp
安[やす]いから、これにします。
```

*It's cheap, so I'll go with this one. (a touch more "because I say so")*

Same information, different temperature. When you want to sound considerate — to a teacher, a station worker, anyone you're being polite with — reach for ので.

That's the whole trick: ので is から's gentler twin, plain form in front, な glued onto nouns. Hold onto this reason-first shape — it's the same instinct you'll lean on soon when we start ordering events in time with てから ("after doing").
caution_notes: With nouns and な-adjectives, use な before ので (医者なので), never だ — 学生ので is wrong.
The reason clause with ので comes first, and ので attaches to the plain form even when the sentence ends politely.
ので frames the reason as objective fact, so prefer から under strong commands or blunt opinions.
In casual speech ので often contracts to んで with the same meaning.

先[せん]生[せい]に聞[き]きます。

items.explanation_markdown:
Imagine you are studying at the library. You have a difficult book open in front of you, and nothing is making sense. You spot the teacher sitting at a desk across the room. You want to walk over and ask a question.

You already know the noun for teacher, and you know the verb 聞[き]く, which means to listen or to ask. But if you just throw those two words into the air next to each other, the relationship between them is completely muddy. Are you asking the teacher? Are they asking you? Are you both listening to a strange noise in the library?

In Japanese, verbs often need a clear target. When an action involves another person—especially when you are communicating with them or directing a physical action toward them—you need a way to draw a firm line from yourself to that person. You need a grammatical arrow.

## How it works

To point your action at someone, you attach the particle に directly to the noun of the person receiving the action. The basic structure is incredibly consistent: **Person + に + Verb**.

You can think of this に as a targeting laser. It marks the recipient, or what grammar books usually call the "indirect object". Whenever you are doing something *to* someone—speaking to them, writing to them, or calling them on the phone—に is the little piece of grammatical machinery that connects the person to the action.

```jp
駅[えき]員[いん]に聞[き]く
```
*I will ask the station staff.*

```jp
友[とも]達[だち]に電[でん]話[わ]する
```
*I will call a friend.*

In both of these scenarios, the action is moving away from the speaker and landing squarely on the recipient. You are tossing the conversational ball, and the に tells the listener exactly who is supposed to catch it. It acts beautifully as the English equivalent of "to".

This does not just apply to speaking. It applies to any action where something is being transferred from you to another person. If you read a story, the person on the receiving end takes に.

```jp
子[こ]供[ども]に本[ほん]を読[よ]む
```
*I will read a book to the child.*

## Rules and exceptions

The "arrow" intuition works perfectly for communication verbs. However, Japanese verbs do not always line up perfectly with English prepositions. This is where you have to start feeling the shape of the Japanese language itself, rather than just translating word-for-word in your head.

The biggest trap for new learners is the verb 会[あ]う (to meet). In English, the verb "meet" takes a direct object. You just "meet a friend"—there is no "to" or "at" involved. Because of this English habit, it is incredibly tempting for learners to leave the particle out entirely or try to guess a different one.

> In Japanese, you do not just "meet" someone; you direct your meeting *at* them. The verb 会[あ]う essentially demands に to mark the person you are encountering.

```jp
今日[きょう]、彼[かの]女[じょ]に会[あ]う
```
*I will meet my girlfriend today.*

Another sharp edge to watch out for is that に only marks the destination of the action. It does not dictate what is being transferred or where the action is physically taking place. If you are at a hospital and you are asking a doctor a question, the doctor gets the に because they are the target of the question.

## Casual speech

When you listen to native speakers chatting informally, you will notice that particles sometimes get swallowed or dropped entirely to save breath. Topic markers often vanish into thin air.

However, に is a structural load-bearing particle. While other markers frequently disappear in casual Japanese, dropping に when marking a recipient is much rarer. If you drop it, the listener might completely lose track of who is doing what to whom.

You might hear the sound soften or blend very quickly into the surrounding vowels in fast, casual speech, but the grammatical beat is almost always there. When you are speaking casually with a friend, keep your に firmly attached to the recipient.

```jp
お母[はは]さんに電[でん]話[わ]する
```
*I will call mom.*

## Contrast: Directing vs. sharing

You already know the particle と, which connects nouns exhaustively and can mean "with" when doing an action alongside someone. Because English uses "with" and "to" somewhat interchangeably in certain social contexts ("I talked to him" vs. "I talked with him"), it is very easy to mix up に and と.

When you use に, you are emphasizing a one-way transfer. You are the one initiating the action, and the other person is the passive receiver. When you use と, you are emphasizing a shared, two-way action. You and the other person are engaged in it together as equals.

```jp
男[おとこ]の人[ひと]に話[はな]す
```
*I will speak to the man.*

```jp
男[おとこ]の人[ひと]と話[はな]す
```
*I will speak with the man.*

Swapping one for the other completely changes the dynamic of the interaction. Using に feels like you are giving a report, delivering news, or directing information at him. Using と feels like a mutual back-and-forth conversation. Both are grammatically correct, but they paint very different pictures of the room.

## Contrast: Destination vs. origin

You also already know the particle から, which marks a starting point or origin ("from"). Since に marks the destination, these two particles live on opposite ends of the same conceptual road. Using them with the exact same verb highlights exactly how powerful particles are in Japanese.

```jp
父[ちち]から聞[き]く
```
*I will hear it from my father.*

```jp
父[ちち]に聞[き]く
```
*I will ask my father.*

Notice how the verb 聞[き]く radically shifts its English translation depending entirely on the particle. When the arrow points away from your father (から), he is the source, so you are "hearing" information originating from him. When the arrow points toward him (に), he is the destination, so you are "asking" him a question.

## Contrast: Target vs. location

You also know the particle で, which marks the location where an action happens or the tool you use to complete an action. When you are learning to use に, it is important not to confuse the target of your action with the location of your action.

Imagine you are sitting at a coffee shop, and you decide to call your older brother. The coffee shop is the location where the action occurs, so it takes で. Your brother is the target receiving the phone call, so he takes に.

```jp
喫[きっ]茶[さ]店[みせ]でお兄[あに]さんに電[でん]話[わ]する
```
*I will call my older brother at the coffee shop.*

The particles act as strict job titles for the nouns in the sentence. No matter what order you put the words in, the に ensures your older brother is always the one whose phone is ringing. The で ensures the coffee shop is always the place you are sitting while you make the call.

Hold onto this concept of に acting as a one-way targeting laser. You will soon learn sentence-ending tags like よ, which add strong assertion and emphasis to your statements (like saying "I'm telling *you*!"). When you start emphasizing your sentences later, knowing exactly who you are pointing your verbs at will make your Japanese feel incredibly sharp and intentional.
caution_notes: The verb 会う (to meet) requires に to mark the person you are meeting, unlike the English verb which takes a direct object.
The particle に only marks the destination or recipient of an action, not what is being transferred.
Do not drop に in casual speech when marking a recipient, as it can cause the listener to lose track of who is receiving the action.
