items.explanation_markdown:
You are sitting at a restaurant with a coworker. They are staring intently at the menu, entirely unable to decide, and you want to ask what they are going to eat. 

In English, turning a simple statement of fact into a question requires you to scramble the entire sentence. "You eat" gets dismantled, flipped around, and rebuilt into "What will you eat?" 

One of the biggest reliefs of Japanese grammar is that you never have to do that. You do not rearrange the sentence structure at all. Instead, you simply pull a single syllable from your grammatical toolkit and snap it onto the very end of the sentence. 

That little syllable is か.

```jp
何[なに]を食[た]べますか。
```
*What will you eat?*

## How it works

Think of か as a spoken question mark. Historically, the Japanese writing system did not use any punctuation at all. There were no commas, no periods, and certainly no question marks. Because everything was written in a continuous, unbroken stream of characters, the language needed a dedicated word to signal that a sentence was an inquiry rather than a fact.

To use it, take a complete, polite statement—ending in either the polite verb suffix ます or the copula です (the word that works like *is/am/are*)—and simply add か to the very end. The particle takes care of all the grammatical heavy lifting.

```jp
明日[あした]、本[ほん]を読[よ]みますか。
```
*Will you read a book tomorrow?*

```jp
あの人[ひと]は学[がく]生[せい]ですか。
```
*Is that person a student?*

One of the best things about this particle is how cleanly it stacks with the rest of the language. When you want to ask a specific question, the question word simply slots into the exact space where the answer would normally live. 

Let's say you want to talk about returning from a location. First, look at a standard statement using the starting-point particle から.

```jp
図[と]書[しょ]館[かん]から帰[かえ]ります。
```
*I will return from the library.*

If you don't know where the person is returning from, you do not move any words to the front of the sentence. You simply swap the location (図[と]書[しょ]館[かん]) for the question word (どこ), leave the particle から exactly where it is, and lock the sentence with か.

```jp
どこから帰[かえ]りますか。
```
*Where will you return from?*

This modular logic works with any particle you already know, like the recipient marker に.

```jp
誰[だれ]に話[はな]しますか。
```
*Who will you speak to?*

## Rules and exceptions

Because this particle explicitly labels the sentence as a question, you generally do not need a written question mark in standard Japanese. A polite sentence ending in か typically finishes with a standard full stop (。).

> You will absolutely see question marks used on the internet, in manga, and in text messages to add visual emotion, but in clean, standard writing, the particle does all the work.

Another detail to watch is your intonation—the rising or falling pitch of your voice at the end of a sentence. In English, we rely heavily on a rising pitch to make a question sound like a question. In Japanese, because か is doing the mechanical work, your intonation does not need to spike aggressively. A slight, gentle rise is natural, but pitching your voice sky-high can sound overly dramatic.

## Casual speech

This is where the textbook rules break down in real life, and it trips up almost everyone in their first week of speaking.

The rule to "just add か" only applies when you are speaking politely, using です or ます. When you drop those polite endings to speak casually with friends, the rules change entirely. In casual speech, you **do not** add か to the end of a plain verb.

If you say `お茶を飲むか` (Will you drink tea?) instead of polite `お茶を飲みますか`, you will sound incredibly rough. It gives off the abrasive vibe of a tough guy in an action movie or someone aggressively grumbling to themselves.

Instead, modern casual Japanese drops the particle completely. You simply state the plain phrase and raise your intonation sharply at the end. Because the particle is gone, this is the one time standard Japanese actually relies on a written question mark to show that tone.

```jp
お茶[ちゃ]を飲[の]む？
```
*Will you drink tea?*

## Contrast: The power of one syllable

The power of a single syllable is immense in Japanese. Because the language relies so heavily on context, subjects like "I" and "you" are almost always dropped. 

When you state a fact without a question marker, the listener automatically assumes you are talking about yourself or an established truth. The moment you attach the particle, the focus pivots immediately to the listener. It is a minimal pair where swapping nothing for something changes the entire reality of the conversation.

```jp
今日[きょう]、肉[にく]を食[た]べます。
```
*I will eat meat today.*

```jp
今日[きょう]、肉[にく]を食[た]べますか。
```
*Will you eat meat today?*

Without か, you are declaring your own dinner plans. The moment you add it, you are now asking about theirs.

Hold onto this idea of sentence-ending particles changing the whole mood of a statement—it becomes incredibly important when we meet ね to ask for agreement later on.
caution_notes: In formal writing, a sentence ending in か typically finishes with a standard full stop (。) rather than a question mark.
Never attach か directly to a casual verb; instead, drop the particle entirely and just use a rising intonation.

example_sentences.furigana: いい天[てん]気[き]ですね。
暑[あつ]いですね。
おいしいですね。
そうですね。

items.explanation_markdown:
You are sitting in a coffee shop with a friend. You take a sip of your drink, and it is absolutely fantastic. You look across the table and want to share this feeling. If you simply state, "This coffee is delicious," you are just reporting raw data. You are stating a fact into the air. 

But human conversation is rarely just about exchanging data. Most of the time, we talk because we want to connect. You do not just want your friend to know the coffee is good; you want them to take a sip, nod, and agree with you. You want to share the space. 

To build that connection in Japanese, you do not need to change your vocabulary or learn a complex new verb form. You just need to reach for one little syllable and attach it to the very end of your sentence: the particle `ね`.

This single character is the heartbeat of natural Japanese conversation. It softens your statements, invites the listener in, and transforms a rigid textbook sentence into a living, breathing human interaction. When you master it, you stop sounding like a robot and start sounding like a person.

## How it works

The mechanics of this pattern are incredibly forgiving. Because `ね` is a sentence-ending particle (a tiny word that attaches to the very end of a complete thought to add emotional color), it does not force you to change any of the grammar that comes before it. 

Think of it like the caboose at the end of a train. You build your sentence exactly as you normally would, using the polite forms you already know, and then you just hook `ね` onto the back.

If you are ending a sentence with an adjective, it attaches right after the copula `です` (the word that works roughly like *is/am/are*).

```jp
このコーヒーはおいしいですね。
```
*This coffee is delicious, isn't it?*

It works exactly the same way when you are making a statement about the weather, or anything else you are observing together in the moment.

```jp
今日[きょう]の天[てん]気[き]は寒[さむ]いですね。
```
*Today's weather is cold, isn't it?*

It also attaches seamlessly to the end of your verb phrases. If you are looking at a menu and making an observation about a price, the structure remains perfectly intact.

```jp
その本[ほん]は高[たか]いですね。
```
*That book is expensive, isn't it?*

## The power of pitch

While the grammar is simple, the real magic of this pattern lives entirely in your voice. How you change your pitch—your intonation—when you say that final syllable completely changes what you are asking the listener to do. 

When your voice rises at the end of the sentence, tilting up just a bit on the `ね`, you are seeking confirmation. You are essentially asking, "Right?" or "Don't you agree?" You are holding out a conversational baton and waiting for the other person to take it. 

Imagine you are walking down the street with your friend, trying to figure out where you are. You spot a building you recognize, but you want to be sure.

```jp
図[と]書[しょ]館[かん]はあそこですね。
```
*The library is over there, right?*

Because your voice tilts up, your friend knows they need to answer you. But what if the roles are reversed? What if your friend makes a statement, and you want to show that you completely agree?

This is where the falling pitch comes in. If you keep your voice flat, or let it drop slightly on the `ね`, you are no longer asking a question. You are validating what the other person just said. You are nodding with your voice.

If your friend complains about the winter air, you do not need to repeat the whole sentence back to them. You can just catch their baton and agree.

```jp
寒[さむ]いですね。
```
*It really is cold, isn't it.*

This call-and-response rhythm—one person rising to ask for agreement, the other person falling to provide it—is the absolute core of how Japanese people build harmony in everyday life.

## Rules and exceptions

Because this pattern is all about building a shared reality, there is one major edge case that trips everyone up during their first month of speaking. It comes down to a simple rule: you cannot share a space if you are the only one standing in it.

Do not use this particle to ask for agreement on private information that only you could possibly know. 

If you are talking about your own internal feelings, your own name, or your own future actions, the listener has no way to agree with you. If you say `私は学生ですね` (I am a student, aren't I?), you sound like you have bumped your head and forgotten who you are. The listener cannot confirm your own life for you.

> Reserve this pattern for things both you and your listener can observe, experience, or figure out together. If it is entirely in your own head, leave the ending plain.

There is also a physical limit to how much harmony one conversation can take. Because it feels so friendly, new learners often fall into the trap of attaching it to every single sentence they speak. 

If you end five sentences in a row with it, you stop sounding like an empathetic adult and start sounding like a kindergarten teacher talking to toddlers. Use it when you genuinely want to check in with your listener, not just as a nervous verbal tic.

## Casual speech

When you are talking to close friends or family members, you drop the polite armor of `です` and `ます`. When you strip away that politeness, sentences can sometimes feel a bit blunt or sudden. This is exactly where sentence-ending particles do their heaviest lifting.

In casual speech, the particle stays exactly the same, but it attaches directly to the plain forms of your verbs and adjectives. It acts as a cushion, ensuring your statement still feels warm and inviting even without the polite packaging.

```jp
明日[あした]一[いっ]緒[しょ]に映[えい]画[が]館[かん]に行[い]くね。
```
*We are going to the cinema together tomorrow, right?*

In these very relaxed settings, you can also stretch the sound out into `ねえ`. This elongated version is incredibly common at the very beginning of a sentence. It works beautifully as an attention-grabber, physically drawing the listener's ear toward you before you ask your question. It translates roughly to "Hey..." or "Listen..."

```jp
ねえ、お母[はは]さんはどこですか。
```
*Hey, where is mom?*

## Contrast

You already know how to ask a question using the particle `か`. Since rising intonation on `ね` also asks a kind of question, it is completely normal to wonder how to choose between the two. 

The difference comes down to how much you think you already know. 

When you use `か`, you are standing in the dark. You genuinely do not have the information, and you need the listener to give it to you. You are starting from zero.

```jp
あの人[ひと]は医[い]者[しゃ]ですか。
```
*Is that person a doctor?*

When you use `ね`, you are holding a flashlight. You are pretty sure you already know the answer based on the context, but you are pointing your beam of light at it and asking the listener to look at it with you and confirm. You are starting from ninety percent.

```jp
あの人[ひと]は医[い]者[しゃ]ですね。
```
*That person is a doctor, right?*

Right now, you are practicing how to build consensus and share space with the people around you. But what if you have a piece of information that your listener definitely does not know, and you want to assert it with absolute confidence? Hold onto that thought—it becomes very important when we meet the emphasis tag `よ` later.
caution_notes: Do not use this pattern to ask for agreement on private information that only you could possibly know, like your own name or your own internal feelings.

example_sentences.furigana: これはおいしいよ。
もう遅[おそ]いよ。
危[あぶ]ないよ。

items.explanation_markdown:
Imagine you are at a local diner with a friend. You are both scanning the menu, trying to figure out what to order. Your friend sighs, frustrated because all the meat dishes look pretty expensive, and they are trying to save money.

But you notice something they missed—the fish dish at the very bottom of the page is actually incredibly cheap.

You want to point this out. You want to confidently hand them this new, helpful piece of information so they don't order something they can't afford. In English, you might say, "This one is cheap, you know!" or lean heavily on your tone of voice and say, "Hey, the fish is *cheap*!"

How do you capture that exact feeling of handing over a new fact in Japanese? You don't need to learn a complicated new verb or a formal phrase. You just need one tiny syllable.

In Japanese, to confidently give new information to someone, you use the sentence-final particle よ. It is one of the most common, expressive, and vital tools in the entire language, and mastering it completely transforms how natural you sound in everyday conversation.

## How it works

The particle よ attaches directly to the very end of your completed sentence. 

It is a "sentence-final particle"—a little word that sits at the absolute end of a phrase and tells the listener how to feel about the information. It does not change the grammatical structure of the sentence itself. If you take it away, the sentence still means the exact same thing on paper. 

Instead, it adds a powerful layer of speaker intent. Think of it as a verbal exclamation mark, or a spotlight you are shining on the sentence. It signals to the listener: "I have some information, and I believe you do not have it yet."

```jp
これ、安[やす]いですよ。
```
*This one is cheap, you know.*

In this diner scenario, you saw the price, but your friend didn't. You are handing them that fact.

```jp
私[わたし]は明日[あした]行[い]きますよ。
```
*I am going tomorrow, I'm telling you.*

Here, you are clarifying your own schedule to someone who wasn't sure what your plans were.

In English, when we want to emphasize a point or show that we are telling someone something new, we usually just change our tone of voice. We might say, "I *am* going tomorrow," emphasizing the word "am."

Japanese is a pitch-accent language. Every word has a specific high or low pitch pattern built into its pronunciation. If you try to loudly stress a random syllable in Japanese just to add emotion, you might accidentally change the meaning of the word entirely! Because they cannot just mess with the pitch of the words themselves, Japanese speakers use sentence-final particles like よ to carry all that emotional and communicative weight.

You can attach it right after the polite endings `です` and `ます`. It smoothly wraps up the sentence and delivers it firmly to the listener. Because it flags new information, it is heavily used when teaching someone something, answering a question with a definitive fact, or reminding someone of something they seem to have forgotten.

```jp
今日[きょう]は日[にち]曜[よう]日[ひ]ですよ。
```
*Today is Sunday, remember?*

If your friend is rushing to get ready for work and they genuinely forgot it's the weekend, this is exactly what you would say. You are correcting their misconception with a solid, undeniable fact.

## Rules and exceptions

Because よ literally communicates "I know this and you don't," it comes with a bit of a sharp edge. It is an incredibly useful tool, but if you overuse it, you can accidentally sound incredibly arrogant.

If you attach it to every single sentence in a conversation, you will start to sound like a bossy know-it-all lecturing the listener. You are essentially saying, "Listen to me, I am telling you this fact. And this fact. And this one."

Use it when you are genuinely sharing a new piece of information, correcting a misunderstanding, or providing a warning. Do not use it for things the listener obviously already knows.

> Be very careful using よ with your boss, your teacher, or anyone of higher status. Because it carries that "let me tell you how it is" energy, using it freely with superiors can easily come across as condescending.

The major exception to the "don't use it with superiors" rule is when you are warning them of immediate danger. In a warning, the new information is urgent and helpful, so the condescending nuance completely disappears.

```jp
先[せん]生[せい]、危[あぶ]ないですよ。
```
*Teacher, it's dangerous!*

If a car is rushing down the street and your teacher doesn't see it, you absolutely want to use よ to grab their attention and deliver the warning immediately.

## Casual speech

When you are talking with close friends or family, you drop the polite `です` and `ます` endings. Sentences become shorter and much more direct. 

In these casual conversations, よ becomes even more important for managing the tone of your voice.

A plain, casual sentence can sometimes sound blunt or cold. Attaching よ to the end of a casual verb or adjective adds personality. It shows you are actively engaging with your friend, rather than just stating raw facts into the void.

```jp
私[わたし]は毎[まい]日[にち]忙[いそが]しいよ。
```
*I am busy every day, you know.*

```jp
一[いっ]緒[しょ]に食[た]べるよ。
```
*We are eating together, I'm telling you.*

Notice how it attaches directly to the plain adjectives (`忙しい`) and the plain verbs (`食べる`). It flows perfectly in casual speech, keeping the conversation lively and assertive without needing the formal politeness of `です`.

## Contrast: The information gap

You have already learned the particle ね, which also lives at the very end of a sentence. Because both ね and よ occupy the exact same physical space in a sentence, learners constantly mix them up. 

But their functions are complete opposites. The difference entirely depends on who holds the information. This is called the "information gap."

Use ね when you believe both of you have the information, and you expect the listener to agree. It bridges the gap and brings you together. It translates roughly to "...right?" or "...isn't it?"

Use よ when you exclusively hold the information, and you are trying to cross the gap to give it to the listener. It translates roughly to "...you know" or "...I'm telling you."

Let's look at the exact same sentence, changed only by the final particle:

```jp
あの映[えい]画[が]、楽[たの]しいですね。
```
*That movie is fun, isn't it?*

In this situation, you and your friend just walked out of the movie theater together. You both watched it. You are looking for agreement on a shared experience.

```jp
あの映[えい]画[が]、楽[たの]しいですよ。
```
*That movie is fun, I'm telling you.*

In this situation, you watched the movie last week, but your friend has never seen it. They ask you if it's worth watching. You are handing them your review.

If you mix these up, the conversation gets weird fast. If you try to tell a friend about a brand new movie they haven't seen using ね, they will be very confused—how can they agree that it's fun if they have never experienced it? 

If you walk out of a movie you just saw together and use よ, your friend might think you are lecturing them about a movie they literally just watched sitting right next to you.

Always ask yourself: "Do we both know this, or am I teaching them something?"

You are officially ready to start sharing your knowledge, giving recommendations, and correcting misconceptions. Hold onto this feeling of pinpointing exactly what you want to emphasize—it will be incredibly useful when we start setting boundaries and limits with grammar like だけ (only) a little later on in your journey.
caution_notes: Avoid overusing よ with superiors or in every sentence, as the "I know something you don't" nuance can make you sound like a condescending know-it-all.

items.explanation_markdown:
You're describing your morning to a friend, and you want to say two things that happened in a row: you woke up, and then you ate breakfast. In English you'd just drop an "and" between them. In Japanese, you don't reach for a word that means "and" — you bend the first verb into a new shape called the て形[けい] (te-form), and that shape does the connecting for you.

Watch it link two actions into one smooth sentence:

```jp
起[お]きて、朝[あさ]ご飯[はん]を食[た]べます。
```

*I wake up and eat breakfast.*

The first verb 起[お]きる became 起[お]きて, and that little て is doing all the work of "and then." The second verb stays polite and normal (食[た]べます), carrying the tense for the whole sentence. That's the core idea: the て形[けい] is a connector that hands the tense and politeness off to whatever comes after it.

## How it works

The て形[けい] (the connective form — the shape a verb takes when it needs to hook onto something) is built from the plain dictionary form of the verb. How you build it depends on which group the verb belongs to.

**Ichidan verbs** (the "る-droppers", like 食[た]べる and 見[み]る) are the easy ones. Drop the る, add て. That's it.

```jp
食[た]べる → 食[た]べて
```

*to eat → eating / eat and…*

So 見[み]る becomes 見[み]て, 起[お]きる becomes 起[お]きて, 寝[ね]る becomes 寝[ね]て. One clean rule, no surprises.

**Godan verbs** are messier, because the ending sound changes depending on the last kana. This is the part everyone has to drill, so here's the whole map:

- く → いて (書[か]く → 書[か]いて)
- ぐ → いで (the voiced version keeps its voicing: で, not て)
- ぶ・む・ぬ → んで (飲[の]む → 飲[の]んで, 遊[あそ]ぶ → 遊[あそ]んで)
- す → して (話[はな]す → 話[はな]して)
- う・つ・る → って (買[か]う → 買[か]って, 待[ま]つ → 待[ま]って, 帰[かえ]る → 帰[かえ]って)

Here's the intuition, not just the chart: the sounds cluster by what's easy to say. The nasal-ish endings (ぶ・む・ぬ) all collapse into んで, and the "small tongue-tap" endings (う・つ・る) all collapse into って. You're not memorizing five random rules — you're memorizing three sound families.

```jp
書[か]いて
飲[の]んで
待[ま]って
```

*writing / drinking / waiting (all te-form)*

**The irregulars** are just two verbs, and you already know both. 来[く]る becomes 来[らい]て, and する becomes して. 行[い]く looks godan but breaks the く→いて rule — it goes to 行[い]って, not `行いて`. That one exception bites everyone, so tuck it away now.

Put it all together and you can chain a whole morning:

```jp
毎[まい]朝[あさ]起[お]きて、朝[あさ]ご飯[はん]を食[た]べます。
```

*Every morning I get up and eat breakfast.*

Notice again: only the *last* verb is 食[た]べます. Everything before it rides on the て形[けい], and the politeness plus the tense live entirely in that final verb.

## Rules and exceptions

The biggest thing to understand: **the て形[けい] carries no tense and no politeness by itself.** It's a hinge. Whether the sentence is polite or plain, present or past, is decided by the verb at the very end.

That means to talk about the past, you don't touch the て形[けい] at all — you only change the final verb.

```jp
起[お]きて、朝[あさ]ご飯[はん]を食[た]べました。
```

*I got up and ate breakfast.*

Same 起[お]きて as before. Only 食[た]べます turned into 食[た]べました, and suddenly the whole thing is in the past. The て form never conjugates for tense — resist the urge to invent a past te-form.

> 行[い]く → 行[い]って is the one you'll get wrong. By the く→いて rule you'd expect `行いて`, but it isn't. It's 行[い]って, patterning with the う・つ・る family instead.

One more constraint: don't use ます-form before the て. Learners fresh off the polite endings sometimes write `食べますて`. That's not a thing. The て attaches to the plain verb stem, never to ます.

## Casual speech

The te-form itself doesn't contract much, but it has one very common everyday job: it becomes a soft command or request on its own. Said with a rising, gentle tone, a bare て形[けい] means "do this, please" in casual speech.

```jp
起[お]きて。
```

*Get up. / Wake up. (casual, spoken to someone close)*

You'd say this to a family member who's oversleeping, not to your boss. It's warm and informal. The fuller polite request form is coming later, but this stripped-down version is what you'll actually hear at home.

## Contrast

You already know ます, ました, and ません — the polite endings that finish a sentence and lock in the tense. The te-form lives in a completely different spot: it never finishes a sentence (except the casual command above), it *connects* to more.

Compare a sentence that stops after one action with one that chains two:

```jp
毎[まい]朝[あさ]、朝[あさ]ご飯[はん]を食[た]べます。
```

*Every morning I eat breakfast.*

That's complete — ます closes it. Now put an action *before* it, and the earlier verb has to become て形[けい] to make room:

```jp
昨日[きのう]起[お]きて、コーヒーを飲[の]みました。
```

*Yesterday I got up and drank coffee.*

The final verb 飲[の]みました handles "yesterday" and the past tense for both actions. 起[お]きて just links in front of it. Swap the final verb's ending — to 飲[の]みます, 飲[の]みません — and you've changed the whole sentence's tense or polarity without ever retouching 起[お]きて. That's the division of labor: **te-form connects, the final verb decides.**

Hold onto this. Once you meet the plain past た形[かたち] soon, you'll notice the te-form and the ta-form are built from nearly the same sound rules — learn て cleanly now and た comes almost free.

That's the whole pattern: bend the earlier verb to て形[けい], let the last verb carry tense and politeness, and you can string your day together in one breath.
caution_notes: The te-form carries no tense or politeness itself — the final verb in the sentence decides both.
行く is irregular: it becomes 行って, not the expected 行いて.
Never attach て to a ます-form; it hooks onto the plain verb (食べて, not 食べますて).
For godan verbs, group the endings by sound: ぶ・む・ぬ → んで and う・つ・る → って.

items.explanation_markdown:
You are sitting in the doctor's office. The doctor turns to you and needs you to open your mouth so they can check your throat. How do they tell you to do that politely? They use the pattern てください (please do).

When you need someone to perform an action—whether you're ordering at a restaurant, giving directions to a taxi driver, or instructing a student—this is your go-to pattern.

## How it works

To make a polite request, take a verb in its て-form and attach ください. 

The て-form is a special verb shape used for connecting actions. ください is a polite word for "please" or "give me." Put them together, and you turn a plain action into a polite request.

```jp
口[くち]を開[あ]けてください。
```
*Please open your mouth.*

```jp
ここに名[な]前[まえ]を書[か]いてください。
```
*Please write your name here.*

```jp
明日[あした]、うちに来[らい]てください。
```
*Please come to my house tomorrow.*

If the verb's て-form ends in で (like 飲[の]む becoming 飲[の]んで), you simply attach ください to that. The structure works exactly the same way.

```jp
水[みず]を飲[の]んでください。
```
*Please drink water.*

## Rules and exceptions

Because ください translates to "please," a lot of learners assume it is the perfect, universally polite way to ask for anything. But Japanese politeness is tricky.

てください is fundamentally a *direction*. You are telling someone to do something. It is polite in its packaging, but it is still a command. 

It is perfect when you have the social right to direct someone (a doctor to a patient, a customer to a shop staff), when giving instructions, or when encouraging someone to do something beneficial for them (like offering food).

> **Careful:** Do not use てください to ask a boss or a superior for a favor. If you say `見てください` (Please look) to your manager, it comes across as bossy. 

## Casual speech

If ください is the polite wrapper, what happens when you are talking to a close friend or family member? You just chop it off entirely.

In casual speech, the request simply ends on the て or で. 

So, instead of the formal `ここでちょっと待ってください。` (Please wait here a little), you would just say `ここでちょっと待って。` It is short, punchy, and completely natural with people you are close to.

```jp
ここでちょっと待[ま]ってください。
```
*Please wait here a little.*

## Directing vs. Inviting

Let's look at how てください feels next to a pattern you already know: ませんか (won't you?). They both involve asking someone to do an action, but the feeling is very different.

```jp
一[いっ]緒[しょ]に来[らい]てください。
```
*Please come with me.*

When you use てください, you are giving an instruction. You expect them to follow your lead. 

```jp
一[いっ]緒[しょ]に来[らい]ませんか。
```
*Won't you come with me?*

When you use ませんか, you are offering an invitation. You are giving them the option to say yes or no. If you want to hang out with a friend, use ませんか. If you are guiding someone who needs to follow you, use てください.

Getting comfortable with the て-form is a huge milestone. Hold onto it—it becomes incredibly important when we learn how to say you are *allowed* to do something with てもいい very soon.
caution_notes: Even though it translates to 'please', てください is fundamentally a direction or command.
Avoid using てください to ask a boss or superior to do something, as it can sound bossy.

items.explanation_markdown:
You get a message from a friend asking what you are up to. You're in the middle of a meal. If you reply with 食[た]べます, it sounds like you're stating a daily habit or telling them you will eat later. To say "I *am eating* right now," you need the pattern ている.

## How it works
To show that an action is currently in progress, take the **て-form** of a verb (which you already know from making requests like てください) and add いる. In polite speech, this becomes います.

```jp
朝[あさ]ご飯[はん]を食[た]べています。
```
*I am eating breakfast.*

```jp
友[とも]達[だち]を待[ま]っています。
```
*I am waiting for a friend.*

This pattern is the Japanese equivalent of the English "-ing" ending. It frames the verb as an ongoing action.

```jp
今[いま]、雨[あめ]が降[ふ]っています。
```
*It is raining right now.*

## Rules and exceptions
For most verbs, the ている pattern means "is currently doing." But for a few specific verbs, it means a lasting state. Think of instantaneous actions, like "getting to know" someone. Once you cross that threshold, you remain in the state of knowing them. Because of this, knowing a person or a fact is almost always expressed with ている.

```jp
彼[かれ]を知[し]っています。
```
*I know him.*

> Watch out for the verb 分[わ]かる (to understand). It already describes a continuous state of mind all on its own, so we normally just use 分[わ]かります. Using `分かっている` usually sounds like an annoyed "I already know that!"

## Casual speech: dropping the "i"
When speaking casually with friends, native speakers naturally take shortcuts. It is incredibly common to drop the い entirely. Instead of saying ている, they just say てる.

```jp
テレビを見[み]てるの？
```
*Are you watching TV?*

*(Notice the explanatory の you learned earlier making an appearance here to ask for context!)*

## Contrast: Habit vs. Happening Now
It is very easy to default to standard dictionary or ます forms for everything you want to say, but they have distinct jobs. A standard verb talks about general truths, routines, or the future. The ている pattern snaps the focus to right now.

```jp
毎[まい]日[にち]、お茶[ちゃ]を飲[の]みます。
```
*I drink tea every day.*

```jp
今[いま]、お茶[ちゃ]を飲[の]んでいます。
```
*I am drinking tea right now.*

Hold onto this continuous state pattern—it becomes a crucial building block later when we talk about rules and things you *must not* do (てはいけない).
caution_notes: The verb 分かる (to understand) already describes a state, so it usually remains as 分かります rather than taking ている.
When speaking casually, it is extremely common to drop the い and say てる instead of ている.

items.explanation_markdown:
You're at a friend's place in Tokyo, and the tea on the table smells amazing. You want a cup, but it's not yours to just grab. In English you'd ask "can I have some?" — in Japanese you reach for てもいい, the pattern that asks *is it okay if I…?*

```jp
このお茶[ちゃ]を飲[の]んでもいいですか。
```

*Is it okay if I drink this tea?*

That's the whole job of てもいい: you describe an action, then ask whether doing it is permitted — or, without the question, you *grant* that permission to someone else. It's the polite handshake around "may I" and "you may."

## How it works

The build is simple because you already own the hard part. Take a verb, put it into its て-form (the same form you learned for てください and ている), then bolt on もいい.

```jp
食[た]べる → 食[た]べて → 食[た]べてもいい
```

*eat → eating(-form) → may eat*

The literal pieces are worth seeing once. も means *even*, and いい means *good*. So 食[た]べてもいい is *even if I eat, it's good* — "even doing this is fine," which is exactly how permission feels. That's your *why*: the も is what makes it *permission* rather than a command.

To make it polite, add です on the end. Both of these are correct; the first is plain, the second is the one you'll say to a stranger or a teacher.

```jp
ここに座[すわ]ってもいい。
ここに座[すわ]ってもいいですか。
```

*I may sit here. / Is it okay if I sit here?*

When you're the one *giving* permission, drop the question and just state it. A parent to a child, a host to a guest:

```jp
テレビを見[み]てもいいですよ。
```

*You may watch TV.*

There's also a more formal, more generous-sounding variant: てもかまいません, literally *even doing it, I don't mind*. Use it when you want to sound extra accommodating — a station attendant, say, telling you it's no trouble.

```jp
ここで待[ま]ってもかまいません。
```

*You may wait here (I don't mind at all).*

## Rules and exceptions

The most common early mistake is dropping the も. Learners hear that permission is "て + いい" and write `食べていい` thinking that's the neutral form. In casual speech that contraction does happen (more on that below), but in careful, polite Japanese the も carries the *permission* meaning — leave it out in a formal setting and it sounds unfinished. When in doubt, keep the も.

> てもいい asks about *your own* action or grants one to someone else. It does **not** work as a general "is X allowed here?" sign-style rule. For that broader "is it forbidden?" feeling you'll want a different pattern (coming very soon).

Another sharp edge: adding か makes it a genuine request for permission, and the answer matters. If you ask 飲[の]んでもいいですか and the host says だめ (no good), you don't drink. Without か, you're not asking — you're telling someone it's fine. Mixing those up can make you sound like you're granting yourself permission out loud, which is a little odd.

One more: because いい is an adjective, some learners try to bend it like `食べてもいかった` for the past. Don't chase that at N5 — stick to the present *may / it's okay* meaning, which covers almost every situation you'll meet.

## Casual speech

Among friends, two things happen. First, the polite です falls away. Second — and this is the big one — the も itself often contracts out, so てもいい becomes ていい in fast speech.

```jp
これ食[た]べてもいい。
これ食[た]べていい。
```

*Can I eat this? (both casual)*

Both are casual and both are fine between friends; the second, with the も gone, is the more relaxed of the two. The tone alone (a rising, questioning tone) does the work that か does in polite speech.

> Keep the も in anything written, formal, or spoken to someone above you. The dropped-も version is friends-and-family territory only.

## Contrast

You've met てください — *please do this* — and it lives right next door, because both attach to the て-form. But they point in opposite directions. てください *asks the other person to act*; てもいい asks whether *you* may act, or tells the other person they *may*.

```jp
窓[まど]を開[あ]けてください。
窓[まど]を開[あ]けてもいいですか。
```

*Please open the window. / Is it okay if I open the window?*

The first hands the job to your listener. The second keeps the action with you and just checks permission. Swap one for the other and you've flipped who's doing the opening — a real change in meaning, not just politeness.

It's also worth setting てもいい beside ませんか, the invitation you learned. ませんか pulls the other person into an activity with you — *won't you…?* — while てもいい is purely about whether an action is allowed.

```jp
一[いっ]緒[しょ]に行[い]きませんか。
一[いっ]緒[しょ]に行[い]ってもいいですか。
```

*Won't you go together (with me)? / Is it okay if I come along?*

The first is a warm invitation you extend; the second is you asking to be let in. Same activity, completely different social move.

Here's the one-line recap: て-form + もいい asks or grants permission — *may I / you may*. Hold onto the shape, because the moment you can say "you may," the natural next question is "and what may I *not* do?" — that's てはいけない, *must not*, waiting for you just around the corner.
caution_notes: In polite Japanese keep the も — dropping it (食べていい) is casual only and sounds unfinished in formal speech.
Add か to ask for permission; without か you are granting permission, not requesting it.
てもいい asks about your own action or grants one to someone else — it is not a general 'is X allowed here?' rule sign.
てください asks the other person to act; てもいい keeps the action with you or lets the listener act — don't swap them.

items.explanation_markdown:
You're standing in a quiet library, and your friend pulls out their phone to make a call. Before they even tap the screen, you want to stop them — not with a polite "please don't," but with the flat, no-exceptions "you can't do that here." That's the job of てはいけない.

This is the pattern for rules and prohibitions: the sign on the wall, the thing the teacher says, the line you don't cross. It's the mirror image of something you already know — てもいい, which grants permission. Where てもいい opens a door, てはいけない slams it shut.

```jp
ここで電[でん]話[わ]を使[つか]ってはいけません。
```

*You must not use the phone here.*

## How it works

The build is simple because you already own half of it. Take a verb, put it in its て-form (the same て-form you use for てください and てもいい), and attach はいけない. That's the whole machine.

```jp
食[た]べる → 食[た]べて → 食[た]べてはいけない
飲[の]む → 飲[の]んで → 飲[の]んではいけない
```

*eat → (te-form) → must not eat*
*drink → (te-form) → must not drink*

The polite version just swaps いけない for いけません. Same meaning, more formal register — the kind of thing you'd see on a posted notice or hear from station staff.

```jp
ここでお酒[さけ]を飲[の]んではいけません。
```

*You must not drink alcohol here.*

Why はいけない? Literally いけない is a word meaning "it won't do" or "it's no good." So the whole thing reads like "doing X won't do." That's a useful intuition: you're not commanding a person directly, you're declaring that a certain *action* is not acceptable. The は in the middle is the topic particle — it's marking "as for doing this thing" — which is exactly why it's pronounced *wa*, not *ha*.

```jp
夜[よる]にコーヒーを飲[の]んではいけない。
```

*You must not drink coffee at night.*

## Rules and exceptions

The て-form does the heavy lifting, so every irregular て-form you've already met carries straight over. 行[い]く becomes 行[い]って (not `行きて`), 話[はな]す becomes 話[はな]して, 待[ま]つ becomes 待[ま]って. If your て-form is right, the prohibition is right.

```jp
その部屋[へや]に入[はい]ってはいけません。
```

*You must not enter that room.*

One thing to watch: because いけない ends like a negative, learners sometimes try to negate it again to say "don't have to." That's a different pattern entirely, and stacking negatives here just produces something broken. Don't reach for `食べてはいけなくない` — it isn't a thing.

> てはいけない is genuinely strong. It's the register of laws, safety signs, and adults laying down rules to children. Saying it to your host at a dinner party — even about something small — lands like scolding. For softening someone's behavior gently, this is the wrong tool.

The subject is usually left unspoken, because a prohibition tends to apply to everyone or to "you." But you can name who's bound by the rule with は or が when you need to be clear about it.

```jp
子[こ]供[ども]はお酒[さけ]を飲[の]んではいけません。
```

*Children must not drink alcohol.*

## Casual speech

In real conversation, てはいけない contracts hard. The ては collapses into ちゃ, so 食[た]べてはいけない becomes 食[た]べちゃいけない. This is everywhere in casual speech — friends, family, anyone you'd already be speaking plainly with.

```jp
それを食[た]べちゃいけない。
```

*You can't eat that.*

The で-form verbs (the ones whose て-form is で, like 飲[の]む → 飲[の]んで) shift to じゃ instead: 飲[の]んではいけない → 飲[の]んじゃいけない. Same logic, just following the voicing of the sound before it.

```jp
今[いま]、帰[かえ]っちゃいけない。
```

*You can't go home right now.*

Even the ending often gets trimmed — people drop off after ちゃ and just let the tone or a trailing だめ carry the "no good" meaning. But for now, ちゃいけない is the reliable casual form to lock in.

## Contrast

Line てはいけない up against てもいい, the permission pattern you learned right before it. They share the て-form base and differ only in the tail, but they're opposites — and that's the cleanest way to feel the meaning.

```jp
ここで写[しゃ]真[しん]を見[み]てはいけません。
```

*You must not look at photos here.*

```jp
ここで写[しゃ]真[しん]を見[み]てもいいです。
```

*You may look at photos here.*

One tail says "no," the other says "yes." If you can build one, you can build the other — same verb, same て-form, just choose the door.

It's also worth separating this from てください, your request pattern. てください asks someone to *do* something as a favor; てはいけない tells them an action is *off-limits* as a rule. "Please close the door" and "you must not close the door" are not two shades of the same idea — one is a polite ask, the other is a prohibition.

So: て-form plus はいけない is your "off-limits" stamp, softening to ちゃいけない among friends. When you later want to say "please *don't*" as a gentle request rather than a hard rule, you'll meet ないでください — a much softer way to hold someone back, and the natural next step from here.
caution_notes: Build it from the て-form: 行く → 行って → 行ってはいけない, never 行きて.
The は in てはいけない is pronounced wa, not ha, because it's the topic particle.
てはいけない is strong — the register of rules and signs; it lands as scolding in casual polite situations.
In casual speech ては contracts to ちゃ (食べちゃいけない) and で-verbs use じゃ (飲んじゃいけない).

example_sentences.furigana: ご飯[はん]を食[た]べてから、出[で]かけます。

example_sentences.japanese: 宿題をしてから、遊びます。
example_sentences.furigana: 宿[しゅく]題[だい]をしてから、遊[あそ]びます。

items.explanation_markdown:
You just walked through the door. You are starving, but your hands are completely dirty from the train. You want to tell your family you are going to eat *after* you wash your hands.

```jp
手[て]を洗[あら]ってから、ご飯[はん]を食[た]べます。
```
*After washing my hands, I will eat.*

## How it works

You already know the て-form (the versatile form that lets you link verbs and make requests). To say you will do something *after* doing something else, just take the て-form of the first action and attach から.

The action in the てから half of the sentence always happens first. The second half of the sentence is what happens next.

```jp
うちに帰[かえ]ってから、寝[ね]ます。
ご飯[はん]を食[た]べてから、映[えい]画[が]を見[み]ます。
```
*After returning home, I will sleep.*
*After eating a meal, we will watch a movie.*

## Controlling time

Here is a convenient trick: the てから part of your sentence does not have a tense of its own. It just locks the two events into a sequence.

To change the sentence from future to past, you only need to change the very last verb in the sentence.

```jp
本[ほん]を読[よ]んでから、寝[ね]ました。
窓[まど]を閉[し]めてから、出[で]ました。
```
*After reading a book, I slept.*
*After closing the window, I left.*

## The "because" trap

This trips everyone up the first week, so it is completely normal if it feels weird at first. You previously learned that から means "because." So why does it suddenly mean "after"?

It is all about what the particle attaches to. If から follows a plain verb or a polite `ます`, it gives a reason ("because"). But if it attaches *specifically* to a て-form, the meaning transforms into a strict sequence ("after").

Look at how swapping just the verb form completely flips the meaning of the sentence:

```jp
映[えい]画[が]を見[み]るから、帰[かえ]ります。
映[えい]画[が]を見[み]てから、帰[かえ]ります。
```
*Because I will watch a movie, I will go home.*
*After watching a movie, I will go home.*

## Casual speech

When speaking casually with friends, the pattern works exactly the same way. You just drop the polite `ます` on the final verb at the very end of the sentence.

```jp
手[て]を洗[あら]ってから、ご飯[はん]を食[た]べる。
```
*After washing my hands, I will eat.*

> You can only use てから with verbs, because nouns do not have a て-form. If you want to say something like "after the movie," you will need a different pattern called 後[あと]で that we will tackle a little later. For now, master your sequences!
caution_notes: The てから phrase has no tense of its own; you only change the final verb to make the sentence past tense.
Attaching から to a dictionary-form or polite verb means 'because', but attaching it to a て-form means 'after'.

example_sentences.furigana: 今日[きょう]は行[い]かない。
肉[にく]を食[た]べない。
お金[かね]がない。
彼[かれ]は来[らい]なかった。

items.explanation_markdown:
You're relaxing in your friend's living room. It's late, and you have a long day tomorrow. They ask if you want coffee. If you say コーヒーを飲[の]みません, you sound perfectly polite, but maybe a little stiff for a late-night hangout. It sounds almost formal, like you're speaking to a waiter. How do you casually tell them "I won't drink it" without putting up that formal barrier? You need the plain negative: the ない form.

## Bending the verb

When you first learned to speak politely, you used ません to say you don't or won't do something. The ない form takes over that exact same job in casual speech. To make it, we just need to change the tail end of the verb.

Think of Japanese verbs as falling into a couple of main families. For the verbs that simply drop their final る sound when they conjugate (often called ru-verbs, like 食[た]べる and 見[み]る), the rule is effortless. You just chop off that final る and replace it with ない.

```jp
肉[にく]を食[た]べない。
テレビを見[み]ない。
```
*I don't eat meat.*
*I don't watch TV.*

Now, for the other major family of verbs (often called u-verbs), it requires a slight vowel shift. You take the final syllable of the dictionary form, shift its vowel from an "u" sound to an "a" sound, and then attach ない. 

For example, 飲[の]む ends in the syllable *mu*. Shift that to *ma*, and you get 飲[の]ま. Then add ない. 行[い]く ends in *ku*. Shift that to *ka*, and you get 行[い]か.

```jp
コーヒーを飲[の]まない。
今日[きょう]は学[がっ]校[こう]に行[い]かない。
```
*I won't drink coffee.*
*I won't go to school today.*

There is one special catch with this vowel shift. If your verb ends in the pure vowel う, like 買[か]う (to buy) or 会[あ]う (to meet), that final vowel shifts to a わ sound, not an あ sound. So 買[か]う becomes 買[か]わない.

```jp
新[あたら]しい靴[くつ]を買[か]わない。
友[とも]達[だち]に会[あ]わない。
```
*I won't buy new shoes.*
*I won't meet my friend.*

Finally, there are always irregulars that like to break the rules. The only one you need to worry about right now is 来[く]る (to come). It completely changes its pronunciation at the beginning of the word, becoming 来[らい]ない (こない).

```jp
彼[かれ]は来[らい]ない。
```
*He will not come.*

## Talking about the past

How do you talk about the past? When you want to say you *didn't* do something, you already know to use ませんでした.

The casual ない form handles the past a bit differently. To make the casual past negative, you take the ない ending, drop the final い, and add かった. So, ない becomes なかった. 

If you want to casually say you didn't play, you conjugate 遊[あそ]ぶ to 遊[あそ]ばない, and then change it to 遊[あそ]ばなかった.

```jp
昨日[きのう]は遊[あそ]ばなかった。
```
*I didn't play yesterday.*

> **Watch out:** Don't try to mix politeness levels in a single verb. A sentence is either entirely polite (using ません) or entirely casual (using ない). Never say `見ませんない` or `飲まないません`. Choose the single level that matches your relationship with the listener.

## Distance and closeness

The difference between ません and ない isn't a change in dictionary meaning—it's a change in social distance.

```jp
私[わたし]は行[い]きません。
僕[ぼく]は行[い]かない。
```
*I will not go. (Polite)*
*I won't go. (Casual)*

The ません ending puts a respectful, safe buffer between you and the listener. It's the default choice for your teachers, station staff (駅[えき]員[いん]), and people you just met. It shows you respect their boundaries.

The ない form deliberately removes that buffer. You use it with close friends, your immediate family like your siblings (兄[きょう]弟[だい]), and when you are just thinking out loud to yourself. In fact, if you insist on using polite forms with your best friend, it can actually sound cold, like you are intentionally pushing them away. Mastering these plain forms is crucial for building real, close relationships in Japanese.

Once you get comfortable using ない and なかった, you'll start to notice they both end in that trailing い sound. Hold onto that thought—because when you formally learn how い-adjectives (like 大[おお]きい and 小[ちい]さい) conjugate later, you'll find they behave exactly the same way. The language is beautifully consistent once you know what to look for.
caution_notes: Never try to mix politeness levels in a single verb—choose either the polite ません or the casual ない, but never combine them.

example_sentences.furigana: ここでたばこを吸[す]わないでください。

example_sentences.japanese: 心配しないでください。
example_sentences.furigana: 心[しん]配[ぱい]しないでください。
忘[わす]れないでください。

items.explanation_markdown:
You're at home with a terrible cold, wrapped in a blanket. Your well-meaning friend walks in and goes straight for the window to let in some freezing winter air. You need to stop them politely but quickly.

You already know how to ask someone to do something using てください. Here is how you ask them *not* to.

```jp
窓[まど]を開[あ]けないでください。
```
*Please don't open the window.*

## How it works

To make a negative request, you take the negative form of the verb (the *nai* form) and attach でください.

For a regular *ru*-verb, just drop the final る and add ない:

```jp
傘[かさ]を忘[わす]れないでください。
```
*Please don't forget your umbrella.*

For a *u*-verb, change the final *u* vowel sound to an *a* sound, then add ない. So 飲[の]む (to drink) becomes 飲[の]まない:

```jp
その水[みず]を飲[の]まないでください。
```
*Please don't drink that water.*

And for irregular verbs, you just have to remember their shapes. 心[しん]配[ぱい]する (to worry) becomes 心[しん]配[ぱい]しない:

```jp
心[しん]配[ぱい]しないでください。
```
*Please don't worry.*

## The missing joint

> A very common trap is forgetting the little で in the middle. It is never `飲まないください`. The で acts like a structural joint, basically meaning "in a state of not doing [verb], please exist."

Grammatically, this is still a polite request because of ください. But because you are directly telling someone what to do (or not do), it can feel a little heavy-handed if used with a boss or teacher. With friends, coworkers, or strangers on the street, it is perfectly fine.

## Casual speech

When you are talking to family or close friends, the full polite phrase often feels too stiff. In casual Japanese, you simply chop off the ください and end the sentence on で.

```jp
今日[きょう]は学[がっ]校[こう]に行[い]かないで。
```
*Don't go to school today.*

## Personal requests vs. Hard rules

You recently learned てはいけない (must not). They might seem like they do the same job, but they live in entirely different spaces.

てはいけない expresses a strict rule or prohibition. You use it to state a fact about what is forbidden.

```jp
ここに入[はい]ってはいけない。
```
*You must not enter here. (It is against the rules)*

ないでください is a personal favor. You are making a request of the person in front of you.

```jp
私[わたし]の部屋[へや]に入[はい]らないでください。
```
*Please don't enter my room. (I am asking you not to)*

Hold onto this negative *nai* form shape. Soon, we'll see how swapping out the でください for something else gives you the power to say what you *must* do.
caution_notes: Always include the particle で between the negative verb and ください; never attach ください directly to the nai-form.
While grammatically polite, this pattern is a direct command and can sound blunt if used with superiors.

example_sentences.furigana: 勉[べん]強[きょう]しなければなりません。

example_sentences.japanese: 薬を飲まなければなりません。
example_sentences.furigana: 薬[くすり]を飲[の]まなければなりません。

items.explanation_markdown:
You're at a friend's house. The food is delicious, and everyone is having a good time, but you look at the clock. It's late. How do you tell everyone that you really have to leave?

```jp
私[わたし]は帰[かえ]らなければなりません。
```
*I have to go home.*

## How it works

How does this tongue-twister actually work? It attaches to the negative stem of a verb—the same form you use for `ないでください`. Take `飲む` (to drink), change it to `飲まない` (don't drink), drop the `ない`, and stick `なければならない` right on the end.

Why is it so long? It's actually a logical combination of two ideas. `なければ` means "if you don't," and `ならない` means "it won't do" or "it is no good." Literally, "if you don't do it, it's no good." That is how Japanese expresses "must."

```jp
薬[くすり]を飲[の]まなければなりません。
```
*I have to take medicine.*

```jp
明日[あした]、学[がっ]校[こう]に行[い]かなければなりません。
```
*I have to go to school tomorrow.*

## Rules and exceptions

> Because `ならない` is just a verb sitting at the end of the phrase, its politeness needs to match your situation. Change it to `なりません` when speaking politely, but leave it as `ならない` with friends.

Japanese also has a nearly identical twin to this pattern: `なくてはいけない`. It follows the exact same rules and means the exact same thing (literally, "as for not doing it, it's bad"). You will hear both used interchangeably, so just pick the one that feels easier to say for now.

```jp
今日[きょう]、会[かい]社[しゃ]に行[い]かなくてはいけません。
```
*I have to go to the office today.*

## Casual speech

Saying `なければならない` every single time you need to do something takes entirely too much breath. In casual conversation, native speakers almost never say the whole thing out loud. Instead, they squish it down into a single, snappy word: `なきゃ`.

Just take the negative stem and add `なきゃ`. It immediately makes you sound natural and relaxed.

```jp
今[いま]、寝[ね]なきゃ。
```
*I have to sleep now.*

```jp
明日[あした]、本[ほん]を買[か]わなきゃ。
```
*I have to buy a book tomorrow.*

## Two sides of the rules

You already know how to lay down the law with `てはいけない` (must not). These two patterns are two sides of the strict-rule coin. One forces you to do something, and the other forces you *not* to. Notice how they look side by side.

```jp
お酒[さけ]を飲[の]んではいけません。
```
*You must not drink alcohol.*

```jp
薬[くすり]を飲[の]まなければなりません。
```
*I have to take medicine.*

Now you can clearly talk about your obligations. But what if you *don't* have to do something? Hold onto this negative stem—it will come in handy again when we look at `なくてもいい` to finally let yourself off the hook!
caution_notes: This pattern literally means "if you don't do it, it's no good," which is how Japanese expresses "must."
Because the pattern ends in a verb, you must conjugate the end to なります or ならない to match the politeness of your conversation.
In everyday casual speech, this long phrase is almost always contracted down to just なきゃ.

example_sentences.furigana: 来[らい]なくてもいいです。

example_sentences.japanese: お金を払わなくてもいいです。
example_sentences.furigana: お金[かね]を払[はら]わなくてもいいです。

example_sentences.japanese: 急がなくてもいいです。
example_sentences.furigana: 急[いそ]がなくてもいいです。

items.explanation_markdown:
Your friend starts walking really fast toward the cinema because they think the movie starts soon. You just checked the clock, and you know you have plenty of time. How do you tell them, "You don't have to hurry"?

```jp
急[いそ]がなくてもいいです。
```
*You don't have to hurry.*

## How it works

You already know how to say that something is permitted using `てもいい` (it's okay to do). To say that someone *doesn't have to* do something, we just apply that same idea to a negative action: "it is okay even if you don't do it."

To build it, take the negative `ない` form of a verb, drop the final `い`, and add `くてもいい`. For example, `食べる` (to eat) becomes `食べない`, which then becomes `食べなくてもいい` (don't have to eat). It behaves exactly like an *i-adjective* (a describing word ending in "i").

Let's look at it in a few complete sentences. Notice how we add `です` at the end to keep things polite.

```jp
野[や]菜[さい]を食[た]べなくてもいいです。
```
*You don't have to eat the vegetables.*

```jp
新[あたら]しい本[ほん]を買[か]わなくてもいいです。
```
*You don't have to buy a new book.*

```jp
明日[あした]は学[がっ]校[こう]に行[い]かなくてもいいです。
```
*I don't have to go to school tomorrow.*

## Asking for permission to skip

Because `なくてもいい` literally means "is it okay if I don't?", you can easily turn it into a question to ask if something is optional. Just add the question particle `か` at the end.

```jp
この新[しん]聞[ぶん]を読[よ]まなくてもいいですか。
```
*Do I not have to read this newspaper? (Is it okay if I don't read this newspaper?)*

## Casual speech

Like most patterns ending in `いいです`, dropping the `です` makes the sentence casual. You will hear this constantly among friends and family.

```jp
今日[きょう]は急[いそ]がなくてもいい。
```
*You don't have to hurry today.*

> If you want to sound even softer when talking to a friend, you can add the particle `よ` to the end (`なくてもいいよ`). It makes it sound like a helpful tip rather than a cold fact.

## Must, must not, or don't have to?

When speaking English, we often mix up "must not" and "don't have to." In Japanese, it is crucial to keep these concepts completely separate.

If you want to say someone absolutely *must* do something, use `なければならない`. If they are free to skip it, use `なくてもいい`.

```jp
今日[きょう]、学[がっ]校[こう]に行[い]かなければならない。
```
*I must go to school today.*

```jp
明日[あした]、学[がっ]校[こう]に行[い]かなくてもいい。
```
*I don't have to go to school tomorrow.*

Likewise, if you are actively asking someone *not* to do something, use `ないでください` (please don't). Use `なくてもいい` only when you are giving them the freedom to choose.

```jp
その水[みず]を飲[の]まないでください。
```
*Please don't drink that water.*

```jp
その水[みず]を飲[の]まなくてもいいです。
```
*You don't have to drink that water.*

Once you are comfortable talking about what you have to do (and what you can skip), we will introduce `たい` — how to talk about what you actually *want* to do!
caution_notes: Do not confuse なくてもいい (don't have to) with なければならない (must).
Do not confuse なくてもいい (it's okay if you don't) with ないでください (please don't).
なくてもいい literally translates to 'is it okay even if I don't?', so it gives the listener permission to skip an action.

items.explanation_markdown:
You are at a friend's house. They point to an empty box and ask if you finished the sweets. You want to say "I ate it." If you say 食[た]べました, you will sound like you are giving a formal report to your boss. You need the casual past tense.

This is where the た形[かたち] (ta-form) comes in. It is the plain, casual equivalent of ました. But here is the best news you will hear all day: if you survived learning the て-form (the connective form), you already know exactly how to make the た-form.

## How it works

The rule is completely identical to the て-form. You just take the て-form of any verb and swap the final て for **た**. If the te-form ends in で, you swap it for **だ**. That is the entire rule.

```jp
食[た]べる → 食[た]べて → 食[た]べた
飲[の]む → 飲[の]んで → 飲[の]んだ
買[か]う → 買[か]って → 買[か]った
行[い]く → 行[い]って → 行[い]った
```
*Eat becomes ate.*
*Drink becomes drank.*
*Buy becomes bought.*
*Go becomes went.*

Let's look at how this sounds in a normal conversation when you are talking to a friend about what you did recently.

```jp
昨日[きのう]友[とも]達[だち]と昼[ひる]ご飯[はん]を食[た]べた。
先[せん]週[しゅう]海[うみ]に行[い]った。
```
*Yesterday, I ate lunch with a friend.*
*Last week, I went to the sea.*

## Rules and exceptions

Because this is the plain form, it is strictly for casual speech. You use this with your friends, your family, or people younger than you.

> Do not use the plain た-form alone at the end of a sentence with a teacher, a boss, or a stranger. It strips away all the politeness and will sound overly familiar. Stick to ました for those situations.

Also, keep in mind that this is only for affirmative past actions ("I did"). The casual negative past ("I didn't do") is a completely different pattern that builds on the ない-form instead.

## Contrast: ました vs た

Both of these patterns tell the listener that an action is finished and in the past. The only difference is your relationship with the listener.

Notice how the exact same meaning changes its outfit depending on who you are talking to. If you are reporting to your teacher, you use ました. If you are chatting with a friend, you drop down to た.

```jp
今日[きょう]学[がっ]校[こう]で先[せん]生[せい]に会[あ]いました。
今日[きょう]学[がっ]校[こう]で友[とも]達[だち]に会[あ]った。
```
*Today I met my teacher at school.*
*Today I met my friend at school.*

You also already know the て-form, which looks incredibly similar and shares the exact same conjugation rules. Remember that て connects ideas, while た finishes a thought in the past. You will often see them working together in the same sentence.

```jp
手[て]紙[がみ]を書[か]いて、寝[ね]た。
```
*I wrote a letter, and went to sleep.*

Mastering the た-form unlocks a massive chunk of everyday, natural Japanese conversation. You will soon see that it isn't just for verbs, either — hold onto this concept, because we will soon see how adjectives have their own past tense rules to say things like "it *was* big". For now, get comfortable swapping your て for a た.
caution_notes: Do not use the plain た-form alone at the end of a sentence with a teacher, a boss, or a stranger, as it will sound too blunt and familiar.

example_sentences.furigana: 寿[す]司[し]を食[た]べたことがあります。

example_sentences.english: I have never seen that movie.

items.explanation_markdown:
You're at a party and someone mentions they just got back from Japan. You want to say "Oh, I've been to Japan too!" — not "I'm going," not "I went yesterday," but the bigger thing: *this is part of my life experience.* Japanese has a dedicated shape for exactly that, and it's built from parts you already own.

Here's the move:

```jp
私[わたし]は日本[にほん]に行[い]ったことがあります。
```

*I have been to Japan.*

That last chunk, ことがあります, is the whole trick. Literally it's saying "the fact of having gone exists" — and once you hear it that way, it stops feeling like a weird idiom and starts feeling logical.

## How it works

You take a verb, put it in its plain past form (the た-form, the casual "did" version), and then bolt on ことがある.

The recipe is always the same:

```jp
食[た]べる → 食[た]べた → 食[た]べたことがある
```

*eat → ate → have eaten (before)*

Let's break down that tail. こと is a nominalizer — a little word that turns a whole verb phrase into a *thing* you can talk about. So 食[た]べた ("ate") becomes 食[た]べたこと ("the experience of having eaten"). Then が marks it as the subject, and ある means "exists." Put together: "the experience of having eaten exists." That's your "I have eaten before."

So the two halves you're managing are the た-form on the left and the fixed ことがある on the right. If your た-form is right, you're done.

```jp
私[わたし]はあの映[えい]画[が]を見[み]たことがあります。
```

*I have seen that movie before.*

```jp
彼[かれ]はお酒[さけ]を飲[の]んだことがあります。
```

*He has drunk alcohol before.*

Notice the polite ending lives all the way at the end: あります for polite, ある for plain. The verb in front stays in casual past no matter how polite you're being — that's normal, and it trips people up the first week. The politeness of the whole sentence is decided by that final ある / あります, not by the た-form.

To ask about experience, just add か, same as any polite question:

```jp
日本[にほん]の料[りょう]理[り]を食[た]べたことがありますか。
```

*Have you ever eaten Japanese food?*

## Rules and exceptions

The big one: this pattern is about *life experience*, not about "one specific time in the recent past." If you did something yesterday, you use plain past (食[た]べた), not this. Save ことがある for "at some point in my life, this has happened."

> Don't use たことがある for things you literally just did or do routinely. "I ate breakfast this morning" is 朝[あさ]ご飯[はん]を食[た]べました, not 食[た]べたことがあります — the experience frame would sound like you're marveling that breakfast has ever occurred in your life.

To say you *haven't* ever done something, you make the ある negative — turn あります into ありません (or ある into ない in plain speech). The verb in front stays exactly the same.

```jp
私[わたし]はまだこの魚[さかな]を食[た]べたことがありません。
```

*I have never eaten this fish yet.*

A common wrong guess is to negate the verb instead of ある — learners write things like `食べないことがあります`, which means something totally different ("there are times I don't eat"). Keep the verb positive and past; move the negation to the very end.

> The negative goes on ある, never on the front verb. 食[た]べたことがありません = "have never eaten." `食べなかったことがある` is a real but rare and confusing shape — as a beginner, don't reach for it.

## Casual speech

In relaxed conversation, two things happen. First, the polite tail drops to plain: あります becomes ある, ありません becomes ない. Second — and this is the one you'll hear constantly — the が simply gets dropped.

```jp
私[わたし]は日本[にほん]に行[い]ったことがある。
```

*I've been to Japan.*

Drop the が and you get the everyday spoken version:

```jp
私[わたし]は日本[にほん]に行[い]ったことある。
```

*I've been to Japan. (casual)*

Both are fine in casual speech; the が-less one just sounds more like talking than writing. For the negative, ない does the same job: 見[み]たことない means "never seen it." When you're writing or being polite, keep the が and use あります.

## Contrast

The closest thing you already know is plain ている — the ongoing-state pattern (Verb-て + いる). It's worth lining these up because both can touch the past, but they point in opposite directions.

ている tells you about a *current* state or an action in progress right now:

```jp
彼[かれ]は今[いま]ご飯[はん]を食[た]べています。
```

*He is eating a meal right now.*

たことがある tells you about a *past experience* that colors the present:

```jp
彼[かれ]はこの料[りょう]理[り]を食[た]べたことがあります。
```

*He has eaten this dish before.*

Swap one for the other and the meaning flips completely: 食[た]べています is "eating now," 食[た]べたことがあります is "has eaten at some point in life." One is a live camera, the other is a résumé line.

It's also worth separating this from the plain past you already use. 見[み]た is "saw (a specific time)"; 見[み]たことがある is "have seen (ever)." If a friend asks どの映[えい]画[が]を見[み]た — "which movie did you watch?" — they mean last night. If they ask あの映[えい]画[が]を見[み]たことがある, they mean "in your whole life, ever?"

Hold onto the こと nominalizer here — that trick of turning a verb into a thing shows up again soon, and the た-form muscle you're building will pay off directly when we meet たり〜たりする for listing actions.

Recap: verb in casual past + ことがある = "have done it before." Negate the ある, not the verb, and drop the が when you're being casual.
caution_notes: Use たことがある for life experience, not for something you just did — 'I ate breakfast this morning' is 食べました, not 食べたことがあります.
Negate the ある (ありません / ない), never the front verb; the verb stays in casual past.
In casual speech the polite tail drops to ある/ない and が is often omitted (行ったことある).

items.explanation_markdown:
Imagine you are catching up with a coworker on a Monday morning, and they ask what you did over the weekend. If you try to list out your actions strictly—saying, "I read a book, I watched TV, and I slept"—it can sound a bit like a police interrogation report. You are giving a rigid, step-by-step timeline of your weekend that feels almost too precise.

In real life, we usually want to give a more relaxed summary. You want to say, "Oh, you know, I did things like reading and watching TV." You aren't claiming that those two activities are the *only* things you did, nor are you saying you did them in a specific order. You are just pulling a couple of representative examples out of a hat to give a general vibe of how you spent your day.

To do this in Japanese, you use the `〜たり〜たりする` pattern. It is the absolute best tool for creating a relaxed, non-exhaustive list of actions, and mastering it will instantly make your Japanese sound more natural and less robotic.

## How it works

To build this pattern, you need the plain past tense form of your verb. You already know this form from when we learned how to talk about past experiences with `たことがある` (have done before). Because it always ends in a "ta" sound, teachers often just call it the "た-form".

Take your verb's た-form, and simply attach `り` to the very end.

- `読む` (to read) becomes `読んだ` (read), which becomes `読んだり`.
- `見る` (to watch) becomes `見た` (watched), which becomes `見たり`.
- `買う` (to buy) becomes `買った` (bought), which becomes `買ったり`.

Once you have your verbs ready, you string them together and finish the entire package with the verb `する` (to do).

```jp
週[しゅう]末[まつ]、本[ほん]を読[よ]んだり、テレビを見[み]たりしました。
```
*Over the weekend, I did things like read books and watch TV.*

Think of these `たり` verbs as floating ideas. By themselves, they do not carry any actual tense, and they aren't polite or casual. They are just raw, timeless concepts: "things like reading", "things like watching". 

It is that final `する` at the end of the sentence that acts as the engine. It grounds those floating ideas in time and determines exactly how polite you are being. In the example above, `する` becomes `しました` because the weekend is in the past, and you are speaking politely to your coworker.

If you are talking about a daily habit or something you do regularly, the final verb is just the present tense `します`.

```jp
毎[まい]日[にち]、友[とも]達[だち]と話[はな]したり、お茶[ちゃ]を飲[の]んだりします。
```
*Every day, I do things like talk with friends and drink tea.*

## Rules and exceptions

Because English speakers are used to assigning time to every single verb in a sentence ("Tomorrow I *will* go and I *will* buy"), this pattern holds a very common trap: trying to make the `たり` verbs match the time of the event.

If you are talking about your plans for tomorrow, you might feel a strong urge to use a future or present form for the list. Do not do this! The verbs inside the list are *always* frozen in the past `た` form, even if the action hasn't happened yet. Only the final `する` gets to change to show the future tense.

```jp
明日[あした]、町[まち]へ行[い]ったり、服[ふく]を買[か]ったりします。
```
*Tomorrow, I will do things like go to town and buy clothes.*

Notice how it is still `行ったり` and `買ったり`, even though the sentence is clearly about tomorrow (`明日`). The final `します` does all the heavy lifting to tell the listener this is a future plan. Never try to say something like `行くなり` or `買うたり`—the form is strictly locked to the past tense shape.

> **The phonetic shift:** Just like with the `て` and `た` forms, verbs that end in a voiced, heavy sound in their dictionary form (like `読む` or `遊ぶ`) carry that heaviness over. Because their た-form ends in `だ` instead of `た`, they take `だり` instead of `たり`.

For example, `遊ぶ` (to play) becomes `遊んだ`, which becomes `遊んだり`. `飲む` (to drink) becomes `飲んだ`, which becomes `飲んだり`.

```jp
公[こう]園[えん]で遊[あそ]んだり、水[みず]を飲[の]んだりしました。
```
*I did things like play in the park and drink water.*

Another massive feature of this grammar point: you do not actually have to list two things. You can absolutely use just a single `たり` to soften a statement. When you use it with just one verb, it implies, "I did this... among other things." It acts like a verbal shrug that keeps you from sounding overly declarative.

```jp
昨日[きのう]は、家[いえ]で寝[ね]たりしました。
```
*Yesterday, I did things like sleep at home.*

## Casual speech

When you are speaking casually with close friends or family members, you simply drop the polite `します` or `しました` and use the casual forms of `する`, which are `する` (for present/future) and `した` (for past).

In extremely casual, fast-paced Japanese, people sometimes drop the `する` completely if the context is totally obvious, leaving the sentence hanging on `〜たり`. However, as a learner, you should strongly stick to always including the final `する` or `した`. Leaving it off by accident in a polite conversation sounds abruptly unfinished and a bit rude, so build the muscle memory of attaching `する` every time first.

## Mixing menus and rules

You already know a few powerful rules for giving permission and setting boundaries. Let's look at how beautifully the `たり〜たり` list integrates with the grammar you already know. 

Think about the pattern `てもいい` (it's okay to / you may). If you say `テレビを見てもいいです` (you may watch TV), it is a specific green light for one single action.

But what if you are hosting a guest, and you want to offer them a menu of options? You just take your `たり` list and swap the final `する` engine for `してもいい`.

```jp
私[わたし]の部屋[へや]で、テレビを見[み]たり、本[ほん]を読[よ]んだりしてもいいです。
```
*In my room, you may do things like watch TV or read a book.*

Suddenly, you aren't just granting rigid permission; you are being an accommodating host offering a variety of choices. The list provides the options, and the final `してもいい` grants the permission for all of them at once.

The exact same magic works in reverse with `てはいけない` (must not). A library doesn't just have one single rule; they have a blanket policy of disruptive behaviors to avoid. By changing the final `する` to `してはいけません` (the polite form of must not do), you create a comprehensive ban.

```jp
図[と]書[しょ]館[かん]で話[はな]したり、電[でん]話[わ]を使[つか]ったりしてはいけません。
```
*You must not do things like talk or use the phone in the library.*

And if you want to reassure someone that they have the day off and absolutely no obligations to worry about, you can plug in `なくてもいい` (don't have to).

```jp
明日[あした]、学[がっ]校[こう]へ行[い]ったり、本[ほん]を読[よ]んだりしなくてもいいです。
```
*Tomorrow, you don't have to do things like go to school or read a book.*

The `たり〜たり` pattern turns rigid, singular actions into flexible, representative lists. Because it relies completely on that final `する` to decide the sentence's ultimate meaning, it is incredibly modular. Hold onto this concept of swapping the final engine. When we learn how to express personal desire with `たい` (want to do) later on, you will already know exactly how to say that you want to do things like watch a movie and sleep—you will just swap that hardworking `する` for a `したい`.
caution_notes: The verbs inside the list are always frozen in the past tense (た-form), even if you are talking about future plans.
Never forget to add the final する (or しました, します) at the very end of the sentence to establish the tense and politeness.
Verbs that end in a voiced sound (like 読む or 遊ぶ) take だり instead of たり.
