items.explanation_markdown:
You've had a long week, and your friend asks what you're doing this weekend. You don't just plan to sleep—you actively crave it. To express what you want to do, you need a specific pattern.

## How it works

To build this pattern, take the stem of a verb (the part right before `ます`) and attach `たい`. The verb `寝ます` (sleep) becomes `寝` plus `たい`. Add `です` at the end to keep things polite.

```jp
週[しゅう]末[まつ]は寝[ね]たいです。
私[わたし]は日本[にほん]へ行[い]きたいです。
あの映[えい]画[が]を見[み]たいです。
```
*I want to sleep on the weekend.*
*I want to go to Japan.*
*I want to watch that movie.*

### Shapeshifting like an adjective

The real magic of `たい` is that once you attach it, your verb transforms into an *i-adjective*. It ends in `い`, so it conjugates exactly like descriptive words you already know, such as `高い` (expensive) or `新しい` (new). 

To make it negative, drop the `い` and add `くない`. For the past tense, drop the `い` and add `かった`.

```jp
今日[きょう]は会[かい]社[しゃ]へ行[い]きたくないです。
昨日[きのう]、あの本[ほん]を買[か]いたかったです。
```
*I don't want to go to the office today.*
*Yesterday, I wanted to buy that book.*

## The unwritten rules of desire

> You can only use `たい` to talk about your *own* desires, or to ask someone directly about theirs (like "Do you want to go?"). You cannot use this pattern to state "He wants to go" or "She wants to eat."

There is also a quirk with particles. When you use a verb that normally takes `を` (like drinking water), you will often hear Japanese speakers swap it for `が` when using `たい`.

Because `たい` acts like an adjective, "wanting to drink" becomes a descriptive state rather than a direct action. Both `を` and `が` are perfectly natural here.

```jp
水[みず]が飲[の]みたいです。
```
*I want to drink water.*

## Keeping it casual

Because `たい` behaves exactly like an i-adjective, making it casual is as simple as dropping `です`. In questions, just use a rising intonation instead of adding `か`.

```jp
今[いま]、帰[かえ]りたい。
明日[あした]、会[あ]いたい？
```
*I want to go home now.*
*Do you want to meet tomorrow?*

## When desire meets obligation

Sometimes what you want to do and what you *must* do are entirely different things. You already know `なければならない` for obligations. Notice how these two patterns stack up against each other in real life.

```jp
病[びょう]院[いん]へ行[い]きたくないです。
病[びょう]院[いん]へ行[い]かなければなりません。
```
*I don't want to go to the hospital.*
*I have to go to the hospital.*

We've spent this whole time talking about actions you want to *do*. If you just want a physical *thing*—like money or a new camera—you won't use `たい`. There is a different word for that coming right up.
caution_notes: You can only use たい to express your own desires, or to ask directly about the listener's desires.
Once you attach たい, the verb transforms into an i-adjective and conjugates exactly like one (たくない, たかった).

example_sentences.japanese: 新しい車がほしいです。
example_sentences.furigana: 新[あたら]しい車[くるま]がほしいです。
お金[かね]がほしい。
時[じ]間[かん]がほしいです。

items.explanation_markdown:
You have been walking around town all afternoon in the summer heat. You walk into a convenience store, head straight for the cold drinks, and think: "I want water."

```jp
水[みず]がほしいです。
```
*I want water.*

When you want a physical object—something you can hold, buy, or point to—you use the word ほしい.

## The mechanics of wanting

The structure for expressing what you want is simple: **Noun + が + ほしい**.

Notice the particle が. In English, we say "I want a car", treating the car as the direct object of an action. But in Japanese, ほしい is actually an *i-adjective* (a descriptive word like 大[おお]きい or 新[あたら]しい). You are literally saying "to me, a car is desirable". That is why we usually use が to mark the thing you want, instead of the object particle を.

```jp
新[あたら]しい車[くるま]がほしいです。
```
*I want a new car.*

Because ほしい functions exactly like an adjective, it follows all the normal conjugation rules you already know. To make it negative, drop the い and add くない. To make it past tense, drop the い and add かった.

```jp
古[ふる]い服[ふく]はほしくないです。
```
*I don't want old clothes.*

```jp
去[きょ]年[ねん]、カメラがほしかったです。
```
*Last year, I wanted a camera.*

## Reading minds

There is one major catch with ほしい. Because Japanese is culturally extremely careful about not claiming to know what other people are feeling inside, you can only use ほしい for **your own desires**, or when asking someone directly about theirs.

You can declare "I want a book" or ask your friend "Do you want a book?". But you cannot state as a plain fact that your friend wants a book.

> Saying `彼女は本がほしいです` sounds presumptuous, as if you are reading her mind. Later on, you will learn specific grammar to talk about what other people seem to want, but for now, keep ほしい limited to the first and second person.

## Casual speech

When you are talking with friends or family, you drop the です completely. In real casual speech, people also frequently drop the particle が, leaving just the noun and the adjective.

```jp
お茶[ちゃ]がほしいですか。
```
*Do you want some tea? (Polite)*

```jp
お茶[ちゃ]、ほしい？
```
*Want some tea? (Casual)*

## Things vs. Actions

This one trips everyone up the first week, so don't worry if it takes a moment to click. You already learned how to say you want to *do* something using たい. So when do you use ほしい, and when do you use たい?

It strictly comes down to nouns versus verbs.

If you want a **thing** (a noun), use ほしい. If you want to **do an action** (a verb), use たい. Look at how these two sentences feel different:

```jp
パソコンがほしいです。
```
*I want a computer.*

```jp
パソコンを買[か]いたいです。
```
*I want to buy a computer.*

You can never attach ほしい directly to a verb, and you can never attach たい directly to a noun. They each have their own strict territory.

Once you master asking for what you want, you will eventually want to rank those desires—hold onto this thought for when we meet 一[いち]番[ばん] (the most) to say what you want more than anything else in the world.
caution_notes: You can only use ほしい to state your own desires, not those of a third person like 'he' or 'she'.
Use ほしい for wanting nouns (things) and たい for wanting verbs (actions)—they cannot be swapped.

items.explanation_markdown:
You're making weekend plans and you want to tell a friend what you're up to. You know how to say "I'm going to the cinema" (映[えい]画[が]館[かん]に行[い]く) and you know how to say "I will watch a movie" (映[えい]画[が]を見[み]る). But how do you combine them into a single, natural thought?

You need a way to say you are going *in order to* do something.

## How it works

You already know the particle に can mark a destination or a time. Here, it steps up to mark the **purpose** of your movement.

To build this pattern, take the verb for the action you want to do and chop off the ます. We call this the "verb stem." Then, attach に, and finish with a movement verb like 行[い]く (to go), 来[く]る (to come), or 帰[かえ]る (to return).

- 見[み]る (to watch) becomes 見[み]. Add に行[い]く and you get 見[み]に行[い]く (go to watch).
- 遊[あそ]ぶ (to play/hang out) becomes `遊び`. Add に来[く]る and you get 遊[あそ]びに来[く]る (come to hang out).
- 食[た]べる (to eat) becomes 食[た]べ. Add に帰[かえ]る and you get 食[た]べに帰[かえ]る (return to eat).

Usually, you also want to say *where* you are going. You put the place at the beginning of the sentence.

```jp
映[えい]画[が]館[かん]へ映[えい]画[が]を見[み]に行[い]く。
```
*I'm going to the cinema to watch a movie.*

```jp
友[とも]達[だち]がうちへ遊[あそ]びに来[く]る。
```
*A friend is coming to my house to hang out.*

```jp
毎[まい]日[にち]、学[がっ]校[こう]へ勉[べん]強[きょう]しに行[い]く。
```
*Every day, I go to school to study.*

> You might notice we used the direction particle へ for the destination (映[えい]画[が]館[かん]へ) instead of に. While you *can* say 映[えい]画[が]館[かん]に映[えい]画[が]を見[み]に行[い]く, using に twice in the same sentence feels repetitive. Many Japanese speakers prefer へ for the destination just to keep things sounding clean.

## Rules and exceptions

This pattern is incredibly strict about how it ends. The final verb **must** be a verb of physical movement. You can't use this grammar to say "I stood up to see" or "I sat down to eat." It exists exclusively for going, coming, or returning somewhere.

```jp
妹[いもうと]は毎[まい]晩[ばん]、晩[ばん]ご飯[はん]を食[た]べに帰[かえ]る。
```
*Every night, my younger sister returns home to eat dinner.*

## Dropping it in casual speech

In fast, casual conversation, Japanese speakers often drop the purpose に entirely to save breath, smashing the two verbs straight together. You should stick to the full に行[い]く form for polite speech or any written tests, and only recognize the dropped version when you hear it.

## Stacking with what you know

Because 行[い]く is just a normal verb, you can plug it right into other grammar rules you've already learned, like combining it with a list of activities using たり〜たりする.

```jp
週[しゅう]末[まつ]、友[とも]達[だち]と遊[あそ]びに行[い]く。
```
*This weekend, I'll go hang out with a friend.*

```jp
レストランへおいしいご飯[はん]を食[た]べに行[い]く。
```
*I go to a restaurant to eat delicious food.*

```jp
週[しゅう]末[まつ]は、本[ほん]を買[か]ったり、映[えい]画[が]を見[み]に行[い]ったりする。
```
*On the weekend, I do things like buy books and go watch movies.*

Now you can declare your own plans. But what if you want to invite someone else? "How about going to eat?" You'll need どうですか for that, which is coming up next.
caution_notes: This grammar pattern only works with verbs of physical movement like 行く, 来る, and 帰る at the end.
Using に twice in a sentence for both the destination and the purpose is grammatically fine, but many speakers prefer へ for the destination to avoid repeating it.

example_sentences.english: I brush my teeth before sleeping.

items.explanation_markdown:
Picture this. You just arrived at a friend's house. You can smell something amazing coming from the kitchen. They just finished cooking dinner, and the table is set. You are starving and ready to dig right in. You pull up a chair, but your friend points a stern finger toward the bathroom sink.

You need to wash your hands *before* you eat.

In English, "before" is a very simple word. You just slap it in front of a noun or a verb phrase and move on with your life. But to talk about the sequence of events in Japanese, you have to understand how the language treats time. It helps to think of time as a physical space.

## How it works

To say "before" in Japanese, we use the pattern `前に` (まえに). Let's break this down.

The word `前` translates directly to "front." Think of time as a road you are walking down. The things that haven't happened yet are physically in "front" of you.

Then we have the particle `に`. You already know that `に` is used to pin an action to a specific time on the clock. It works the exact same way here. By combining them, `前に` literally means "at the time in front of" or "at the point just before."

Let's look at how to attach it to the actions you want to take.

### Attaching to verbs

When you are attaching an action to `前に`, you must always use the verb's **dictionary form**. This is the plain, basic form of the verb you look up in the dictionary.

```jp
食[た]べる前[まえ]に手[て]を洗[あら]う。
```
*I wash my hands before eating.*

Why the dictionary form? This is where Japanese logic is incredibly consistent. The dictionary form is technically called the "non-past" or "incomplete" form.

Think about the exact moment you are standing at the sink washing your hands. Has the eating happened yet? No. The eating is still in the future. It is completely incomplete. Because the eating hasn't happened yet relative to washing your hands, it must stay in its basic, un-conjugated state.

### Attaching to nouns

What if you want to use a noun instead of a verb? Maybe you want to say "before class" or "before dinner."

Grammatically speaking, `前` is actually a noun itself. In Japanese, you cannot just smash two nouns together like building blocks. You need a way to link them. This is where your trusty noun-gluing particle `の` comes to the rescue.

The formula is straightforward: Noun + `の` + `前に`.

```jp
授[じゅ]業[ぎょう]の前[まえ]にコーヒーを飲[の]む。
```
*I drink coffee before class.*

```jp
晩[ばん]ご飯[はん]の前[まえ]にテレビを見[み]る。
```
*I watch TV before dinner.*

You can use this structure with almost any "event" noun. It works perfectly for meals, school, work, or any scheduled block of time in your day.

## The past tense trap

Now we arrive at the single biggest trap for English speakers learning this pattern. This one trips almost everyone up the first week, so it is completely normal if it feels a little backwards at first.

What happens if you are telling a story about yesterday? In English, we say "Before I *slept*, I *read* a book." Both verbs are safely conjugated into the past tense.

Let's see how Japanese handles that exact same sentence.

```jp
寝[ね]る前[まえ]に本[ほん]を読[よ]んだ。
```
*I read a book before sleeping.*

Look closely at that first verb. `寝る` (to sleep) is still in the dictionary form! Even though you read the book last night—an action firmly in the past, shown by the past tense `読んだ` at the end of the sentence—the sleeping is not conjugated.

> **Never put the verb before 前[まえ]に in the past tense.** Even if your entire story happened ten years ago, `寝た前に` is always grammatically incorrect and will confuse the person you are talking to.

Why does Japanese do this? It comes back to that relative time logic we talked about earlier.

Japanese grammar doesn't care about the absolute time on the clock right now. It cares about the time *relative to the actions*. At the exact moment you were reading the book last night, the sleeping was still in your future.

The verb at the very end of the sentence acts like a time machine. That final verb (`読んだ`) is the anchor. It pulls the entire sentence into the past. Every other verb in the sentence just relates to that final anchor point. 

## Using it to say "ago"

There is a special, extremely useful shortcut you can take when dealing with exact numbers and time durations.

If you attach `前に` directly to a duration of time—like minutes, hours, or days—it translates to "ago." It literally means "at the time before this duration."

```jp
三[さん]時[じ]間[かん]前[まえ]に来[らい]た。
```
*I came three hours ago.*

Notice what is missing here? There is no `の`. When you use a specific time duration like "three hours" (`三時間`) or "five minutes" (`五分`), you attach it directly to the pattern. You do not say `三時間の前に`.

```jp
五[ご]分[ふん]前[まえ]に起[お]きた。
```
*I woke up five minutes ago.*

This is one of the most common and natural ways to answer the question "When did you get here?" or "When did that happen?"

## Casual speech drops

As you start listening to native speakers, you will notice that casual Japanese is all about efficiency. When speaking casually with friends, people love to drop particles to speed up their sentences.

The `に` in `前に` is a prime target for this. In casual, everyday speech, it is often dropped entirely, leaving just `前`.

```jp
友[とも]達[だち]が来[く]る前[まえ]、部屋[へや]を出[で]る。
```
*Before my friend comes, I'll leave the room.*

This doesn't change the meaning at all. It just lowers the formality and makes the sentence flow a bit faster. You can safely use this shorter version around people you are close with.

## Contrast: Setting the sequence

You already know how to use `てから` to say "after doing" something. You use it to sequence events, like saying "After I wake up, I eat."

`てから` and `前に` live in the exact same grammatical space. They are two tools for the exact same job, but they are mirror images of each other. Knowing when to use which depends entirely on what part of the sequence you want to emphasize.

Let's say you have a movie you want to watch and you also want to get some sleep.

If you want to emphasize the first action, you use `てから`. Remember that `てから` requires the `て`-form of the verb.

```jp
映[えい]画[が]を見[み]てから、寝[ね]る。
```
*After watching the movie, I sleep.*

If you want to emphasize the second action, you use `前に`. And as we just covered extensively, `前に` demands the dictionary form.

```jp
寝[ね]る前[まえ]に、映[えい]画[が]を見[み]る。
```
*Before sleeping, I watch a movie.*

Notice how swapping from `てから` to `前に` means you have to physically flip the order of the actions in your sentence.

With `てから`, the first thing out of your mouth is the first thing you actually do. You watch the movie, then you sleep.

With `前に`, the first thing out of your mouth is the *second* thing you actually do. You mention sleeping first, but watching the movie is what actually happens first in reality.

It takes a little bit of mental gymnastics to flip these around on the fly. Don't worry if you have to pause for a second while speaking to line up your timeline. Everyone goes through that phase!

Mastering `前に` gives you immense control over telling stories and scheduling your day. Just remember the golden rule: lock that first verb in the dictionary form, and let the end of the sentence do all the time traveling for you. 

Hold onto this relative-time logic tightly. It's going to become incredibly important when we learn the exact opposite pattern—`後で` (after)—very soon!
caution_notes: Never use the past tense before 前に; the verb must always stay in the dictionary form, even if the sentence describes a past event.
When attaching a noun to 前に, you must always use the particle の (e.g., 授業の前に).

example_sentences.furigana: 食[た]べた後[あと]で、コーヒーを飲[の]みます。
授[じゅ]業[ぎょう]の後[あと]で、遊[あそ]びます。

items.explanation_markdown:
You're wrapping up at the office, and a friend texts to ask if you want to hang out. You want to tell them you'll call them after work. You already know how to say "work" and "call", but you need the glue to stick them together.

In Japanese, to say "after doing X," you use 後[あと]で. It literally translates to "at the later (time)."

```jp
仕[し]事[ごと]の後[あと]で、電[でん]話[わ]します。
```
*After work, I will call.*

## How it works

If you want to place a noun on the timeline, you just connect it to 後[あと]で with the particle の.

```jp
授[じゅ]業[ぎょう]の後[あと]で、映[えい]画[が]を見[み]ます。
```
*After class, I will watch a movie.*

But when you want to say "after *doing* something," you have to attach a verb. Here is the golden rule: the verb before 後[あと]で must always be in its plain past form (the た-form).

```jp
ご飯[はん]を食[た]べた後[あと]で、お茶[ちゃ]を飲[の]みます。
```
*After eating a meal, I drink tea.*

Why the past tense? Because on your mental timeline, the eating has to be completely finished before the tea drinking can begin. You're saying "in the aftermath of having eaten." Do not use the dictionary form here — saying `食べる後で` is grammatically incorrect.

## Rules and exceptions

The most common trap here is overthinking the tense of your sentence. Remember that the verb before 後[あと]で is *always* locked into the past tense (た-form), even if the whole sentence is talking about your plans for tomorrow.

> The tense of the actual event is controlled entirely by the very last verb in the sentence.

If you did something yesterday, the ending verb is in the past tense. But the verb glued to 後[あと]で stays exactly the same.

```jp
本[ほん]を読[よ]んだ後[あと]で、寝[ね]ました。
```
*After I read a book, I went to sleep.*

## Casual speech

You will very often see this written entirely in hiragana as あとで. Both are perfectly normal, though the kanji is slightly more common in formal writing.

In casual speech, people sometimes drop the で entirely and just say あと. If you're talking to a friend, `食べたあと` (after I eat) sounds a bit more relaxed than `食べた後で`, but keeping the で is the safest habit to build right now.

## Wait, what about てから?

You already know `てから`, which also means "after doing." They feel similar, but they have a slightly different flavor.

`てから` is a tight, direct sequence. It implies "A finishes, and then B happens as the direct next step." `後で` is a looser timeline. It just means B happens at *some point* after A.

There's also a structural difference. You can use nouns directly with `後で` (like `仕事の後で`), but you cannot do that with `てから`.

And what about `前に` (before)? They work as exact opposites, but notice the verb forms. Since "before" means the action hasn't happened yet, `前に` takes the dictionary form. Since "after" means the action is finished, `後で` takes the た-form.

```jp
映[えい]画[が]を見[み]る前[まえ]に、ご飯[はん]を食[た]べます。
```
*Before watching a movie, I will eat a meal.*

```jp
映[えい]画[が]を見[み]た後[あと]で、ご飯[はん]を食[た]べます。
```
*After watching a movie, I will eat a meal.*

Hold onto this sense of a mental timeline. Right now we're looking at things that happen clearly before or after each other. Soon, we'll look at how to describe things happening at the exact same time when we meet `ながら`.
caution_notes: The verb before 後で is always in the past tense (た-form), even if the main event happens in the future.
The tense of the entire sentence is controlled by the final verb, not the verb attached to 後で.

example_sentences.japanese: 子供のとき、よく遊びました。
example_sentences.english: When I was a child, I played a lot.
example_sentences.furigana: 子[こ]供[ども]のとき、よく遊[あそ]びました。

example_sentences.japanese: 暇なとき、本を読みます。
example_sentences.furigana: 暇[ひま]なとき、本[ほん]を読[よ]みます。

example_sentences.japanese: 日本へ行ったとき、写真を撮りました。
example_sentences.english: When I went to Japan, I took photos.
example_sentences.furigana: 日本[にほん]へ行[い]ったとき、写[しゃ]真[しん]を撮[ど]りました。

You are chatting with a new friend and want to share a few stories. Maybe you want to mention that you hated vegetables as a kid, or explain that you always drink iced coffee when it is hot outside. To link a specific situation to an action, you need a way to say "when" or "at the time of".

Enter とき.

## The "Time" trick

The secret to mastering this pattern is simple: とき (sometimes written in kanji as 時[じ]) literally means "time". It is not a magical grammar particle; it is just a regular noun.

Because it behaves like a noun, you connect other words to it using the exact same rules you already know for modifying nouns.

When you want to attach another noun to it, you need the particle の to bridge them together:

```jp
子[こ]供[ども]の時[じ]、野[や]菜[さい]が嫌[きら]いでした。
```
*When I was a child, I hated vegetables.*

```jp
学[がく]生[せい]の時[じ]、毎[まい]日[にち]勉[べん]強[きょう]しました。
```
*When I was a student, I studied every day.*

If you want to use a Na-adjective to describe the time, you leave the な attached, just as you would when describing any other noun:

```jp
暇[ひま]な時[じ]、本[ほん]を読[よ]みます。
```
*When I am free, I read books.*

I-adjectives are the easiest. Because they are designed to attach directly to nouns on their own, you just stick them right in front of とき:

```jp
暑[あつ]い時[じ]、冷[つめ]たい水[みず]を飲[の]みます。
```
*When it is hot, I drink cold water.*

## The Time Travel Trap

You can also attach verbs to とき to say "when I do X". Verbs connect using their plain forms (like the dictionary form `帰る` or the casual past form `帰った`). 

However, this is where English and Japanese disagree, and it trips almost everyone up at first. In English, if you are telling a story about yesterday, you put every verb in the past tense. Japanese does not do this.

In Japanese, the tense of the verb right before とき depends *only* on whether that specific action was finished at that exact moment in the story.

If the first action hasn't finished yet, you use the dictionary form:

```jp
家[いえ]へ帰[かえ]る時[じ]、パンを買[か]いました。
```
*When I was going home (on the way), I bought bread.*

Because you were still in transit and had not arrived home yet, `帰る` stays in the dictionary form. It does not matter that you bought the bread in the past (`買いました`)—relative to buying the bread, the "going home" part was still happening.

If the action was already entirely finished, you use the past (`た`) form:

```jp
家[いえ]へ帰[かえ]った時[じ]、テレビを見[み]ました。
```
*When I went home (after arriving), I watched TV.*

Here, the action of going home was completely finished before the TV watching began, so you use `帰った`.

> Don't let the end of the sentence drag the とき clause into the wrong tense. A good rule of thumb: if you can replace "when" with "on the way to", use the dictionary form. If you can replace it with "after arriving", use the past form.

## Setting the scene vs. Strict sequence

You already know how to use 後[あと]で (after doing) to put events in a timeline.

```jp
ご飯[はん]を食[た]べた後[あと]で、コーヒーを飲[の]みます。
```
*After I eat a meal, I drink coffee.*

This gives you a strict sequence. Step one is completely finished, and then step two begins. とき covers similar ground but is looser—it just sets the scene or the general timeframe for the main event.

```jp
ご飯[はん]を食[た]べる時[じ]、コーヒーを飲[の]みます。
```
*When I eat a meal, I drink coffee.*

Using とき here means the coffee drinking happens as part of the mealtime experience, rather than waiting strictly until the food is gone.

The same difference applies to 前[まえ]に (before doing).

```jp
寝[ね]る前[まえ]に、本[ほん]を読[よ]みます。
```
*Before I sleep, I read a book.*

```jp
寝[ね]る時[じ]、電[でん]気[き]を消[け]します。
```
*When I go to sleep, I turn off the light.*

Using とき simply frames the situation. Hold onto this idea of setting a scene. When you eventually want to talk about doing two specific things simultaneously—like walking exactly *while* drinking coffee—there is a different pattern waiting for you.
caution_notes: Because とき is grammatically a noun, you must use の after another noun and な after a Na-adjective to connect them.
The tense of the verb right before とき depends on whether that specific action was completely finished, not on when the overall story happened.

example_sentences.furigana: 漢[かん]字[じ]を読[よ]むことができます。

You're making weekend plans with a new friend, and they ask if you want to check out a famous sushi restaurant. You hate fish. Or maybe you're at a job interview and need to confidently state your language skills. You need a way to clearly say what you can—and cannot—do.

To talk about your abilities or what is physically possible, you use the pattern **ことができる**.

## How it works

To build this, take any verb in its dictionary form (the basic, present-tense form like 食[た]べる or 行[い]く), and attach **ことができる** (casual) or **ことができます** (polite).

Why does this string of words mean "can"? Let's look at the machinery. You already know that you cannot just stick a noun particle like が directly onto a verb. So, we use こと, a nominalizer—a little word that turns a whole verb phrase into a noun thing. 食[た]べる (to eat) becomes 食[た]べること (the act of eating).

Finally, you add が (the subject marker) and できる (a verb meaning "is possible" or "can be done"). Literally, you are saying "the act of eating is possible."

```jp
彼[かの]女[じょ]は日本[にほん]語[ご]を話[はな]すことができます。
明日[あした]、学[がっ]校[こう]に行[い]くことができます。
```
*She can speak Japanese.*
*I can go to school tomorrow.*

## Rules and exceptions

Making this pattern negative or turning it into a question works exactly the same as any other polite verb. You just change the final できます to できません (cannot) or add か to make できますか (can you?).

```jp
あの鳥[とり]は飛[と]ぶことができません。
ここで本[ほん]を読[よ]むことができますか。
```
*That bird cannot fly.*
*Can I read a book here?*

One structural detail to watch out for is your particles. Even though the whole verb phrase is eventually marked with が, the object of your action usually keeps its original を particle. You say 日本[にほん]語[ご]**を**話[はな]す (speak Japanese), so you keep that exact phrasing right before こと.

## Casual speech

In casual speech with friends or family, you simply drop the polite ます endings. You will use the plain form できる for "can" and できない for "cannot."

```jp
僕[ぼく]は漢[かん]字[じ]を書[か]くことができる。
昨日[きのう]、寝[ね]ることができなかった。
```
*I can write kanji.*
*I could not sleep yesterday.*

## Potential vs. Experience

You recently learned how to talk about your past experiences using たことがある (have done before). Because these two patterns sound so incredibly similar, they trip up almost everyone at first.

The secret to keeping them straight is the verb form that comes immediately before こと.

```jp
魚[さかな]を食[た]べたことがあります。
魚[さかな]を食[た]べることができます。
```
*I have eaten fish before.*
*I can eat fish.*

> Swapping the dictionary form for the past-tense た-form completely changes the meaning from "I am able to" to "I have done it before." Take an extra second to verify your verb tense before you speak!

Now you can clearly explain exactly what you are capable of doing. Hang onto this dictionary form structure—you'll see a very similar shape when we learn how to say what *might* happen using かもしれない soon.
caution_notes: Always use the dictionary form of the verb before ことができる; using the past tense (た-form) changes the meaning to 'have done before'.
Keep the object's original を particle intact before the verb, even though the phrase ends with ができる.

items.explanation_markdown:
You are sitting in a restaurant, and you just finished an incredible meal. Your friend asks how the food was. You want to say "It was delicious!" But wait—how do you make an adjective past tense in Japanese?

In English, adjectives are lazy. We say "is cold," "was cold," or "is not cold." The verb (*is/was*) does all the heavy lifting. In Japanese, however, i-adjectives are independent. They conjugate—meaning they change their own endings—to show time (past or present) and reality (positive or negative).

## How they shape-shift

Every i-adjective ends in the hiragana い. That final い is the hinge. To change the meaning, you simply pop off the い and attach a new ending.

**1. The Negative (It is not): `くない`**
If something isn't a certain way, drop the い and add くない.

```jp
このカメラは高[たか]くないです。
```
*This camera is not expensive.*

**2. The Past (It was): `かった`**
To talk about the past, drop the い and add かった.

```jp
レストランの料[りょう]理[り]はおいしかったです。
```
*The restaurant's food was delicious.*

**3. The Past Negative (It was not): `くなかった`**
This one looks long, but it's just a combination of the first two rules. First you make it negative (`くない`), then you treat that new い like an adjective and make it past tense (`くなかった`).

```jp
その本[ほん]は難[むずか]しくなかったです。
```
*That book was not difficult.*

**4. The Adverb (Doing things adjective-ly): `く`**
Sometimes you want an adjective to describe an action instead of a noun—like saying you woke up *early*, rather than describing an *early* morning. Drop the い and add く to connect it directly to a verb.

```jp
昨日[きのう]は早[はや]く寝[ね]ました。
```
*I slept early yesterday.*

## Politeness and casual speech

You might have noticed the です at the end of some of those examples. When you conjugate an i-adjective, the adjective itself is doing the grammatical work. Adding です to the very end just acts as a politeness bumper. It doesn't change the meaning, it just makes the sentence polite.

If you are talking to a friend, you can drop the です entirely. The adjective carries all the information you need.

```jp
あの映[えい]画[が]はつまらなかった。
```
*That movie was boring.*

## The one big exception

There is one word that trips everyone up the first week, and that is いい (good). 

いい is actually a newer, slightly lazier pronunciation of an older word: 良[よ]い (よい). While we say いい in the present tense, whenever it needs to conjugate, it snaps back to its original よ root.

```jp
今日[きょう]の天[てん]気[き]はよくないです。
```
*Today's weather is not good.*

Never say `いくない` or `いかった`. Always use よくない and よかった.

Mastering these endings gives you incredible freedom to express how you feel about the world around you. Hold onto this concept—it becomes very important when we meet な-adjectives, which live in the same space but behave completely differently.
caution_notes: いい (good) conjugates from its original form 良い (よい), so its negative is よくない and its past is よかった.
i-adjectives conjugate themselves; the です added at the end is only there to make the sentence polite, not to show time.

items.structure: な-adj + な + Noun / + です

example_sentences.furigana: 静[しず]かな部屋[へや]です。
彼[かれ]は親[しん]切[せつ]です。
ここは便[べん]利[り]な町[まち]です。

items.explanation_markdown:
You're showing a friend pictures of a hotel you stayed at. You want to tell them it was a quiet place, but you also need to warn them that the location wasn't very convenient.

To do this, you need the other half of the Japanese adjective system: **na-adjectives** (な形[けい]容[よう]詞[し]).

You already know *i-adjectives* like 高[たか]い (expensive) or 新[あたら]しい (new). Those words are highly independent—they change their own endings to show past or negative tense (like 高[たか]くなかった).

Na-adjectives are completely different. Think of them as noun-like words that are a bit lazy. They don't change their own shapes at all. Instead, they rely on helper words (like the copula です, which functions like *is/am/are*) to do the grammatical heavy lifting.

## Ending a sentence

When a na-adjective is the last piece of information in a sentence, you treat it exactly like a noun. You just attach です (or its past tense でした) right after the dictionary form of the word.

```jp
この町[まち]は静[しず]かです。
```
*This town is quiet.*

```jp
部屋[へや]はきれいでした。
```
*The room was clean.*

> **Wait, isn't きれい an i-adjective?** It ends in an "i" sound, so it's a very common trap! But きれい is actually a na-adjective. There are a handful of these tricksters (like 有[ゆう]名[めい], famous, and 嫌[きら]い, disliked). You just have to memorize them as you meet them.

## Connecting to a noun

Here is where na-adjectives get their name. When you want to put the adjective directly in front of a noun to describe it (like saying "a quiet town" instead of "the town is quiet"), you must use **な** as the glue between them.

```jp
ここは静[しず]かな町[まち]です。
```
*This is a quiet town.*

```jp
有[ゆう]名[めい]な人[ひと]に会[あ]いました。
```
*I met a famous person.*

Without that な, the two words would just crash into each other awkwardly. The な tells the listener, "Hey, the word I just said is describing the noun coming up right now."

## Making it negative

Because na-adjectives act like nouns, you make them negative the exact same way you make a noun negative: by adding ではありません (is not).

```jp
私[わたし]は暇[ひま]ではありません。
```
*I am not free.*

```jp
犬[いぬ]が好[す]きではありません。
```
*I do not like dogs.*

## Casual speech

In real conversation with friends, the stiff ではありません almost always contracts. You'll hear people say じゃない instead. So, 暇[ひま]ではありません shrinks down to 暇[ひま]じゃない (I'm not free).

## The biggest trap: mixing up the two groups

When you're speaking quickly, your brain will try to apply i-adjective rules to na-adjectives. 

If a book isn't new, you know to change the i-adjective 新[あたら]しい to 新[あたら]しくない:

```jp
本[ほん]は新[あたら]しくないです。
```
*The book is not new.*

But if you want to say you don't like something, you absolutely cannot chop off the end and turn 好[す]き into `好きくない`. Because 好[す]き is a na-adjective, it can't conjugate itself. You have to use the noun-style negative.

```jp
魚[さかな]が好[す]きではありません。
```
*I do not like fish.*

Learning which adjective belongs to which group takes a bit of practice, but whenever you learn a new word, pay attention to whether it needs that な glue. Speaking of glue, hold onto the idea of な connecting these words to nouns. Later on, when you want to connect them to verbs (to say you did something "quietly"), you'll swap that な out for a に.
caution_notes: Words ending in an 'i' sound like きれい and 有名 are actually na-adjectives, so they take な before a noun instead of connecting directly.
Never try to conjugate a na-adjective like an i-adjective; forms like 好きくない are incorrect.

items.meaning: make an i-adjective into an adverb

example_sentences.furigana: 早[はや]く起[お]きます。

example_sentences.japanese: 大きく書いてください。
example_sentences.furigana: 大[おお]きく書[か]いてください。
安[やす]く買[か]いました。

items.explanation_markdown:
You've got a big trip tomorrow and need to tell your friend you are waking up early. You know the word for "early" (早[はや]い) and the verb for "wake up" (起[お]きる). But you can't just mash them together as `早い起きます`. That sounds like "early wakes up."

When you want an adjective to describe *how* you do an action—waking up *early*, writing *big*, running *fast*—you need to turn it into an adverb.

## How it works

For い-adjectives, making an adverb is incredibly simple: drop the final `い` and replace it with `く`.

```jp
早[はや]い → 早[はや]く
```
*early → early (as an adverb)*

Now you can attach it directly to your verb to describe how the action happens:

```jp
明日[あした]は早[はや]く起[お]きます。
```
*I will wake up early tomorrow.*

You can use this with almost any い-adjective and verb combination. 

```jp
これを安[やす]く買[か]いました。
彼[かれ]は速[はや]く走[はし]ります。
ノートに大[おお]きく書[か]きました。
```
*I bought this cheaply.*
*He runs fast.*
*I wrote big in the notebook.*

## The one big exception

Just like with every other rule you've learned so far, the adjective いい (good) is the rebel. Before you can change it, it reverts to its older, formal shape 良[よ]い (よい). Drop the `い` and add `く`, and you get よく.

```jp
よく勉[べん]強[きょう]します。
```
*I study often.*

> `よく` is incredibly common, but notice how the translation usually becomes "often" rather than "well" in many situations. If you say よく遊[あそ]びます, it usually means you play a lot, not necessarily that you are highly skilled at playing.

## A mind-blowing connection

Does dropping `い` and adding `く` feel weirdly familiar? It should.

Think about how you make an adjective negative. To say a bag isn't heavy, you change 重[おも]い to `重くない`. What you are actually doing is turning "heavy" into the adverb "heavily" (重[おも]く) and attaching it to the negative word ない (not exist).

You've been using this exact grammar rule since your very first week of adjectives without even knowing it!

## Describing things vs. describing actions

When you learn a new pattern, it's easy to accidentally overuse it. If you catch yourself making mistakes, look at what word you are actually trying to describe.

If you are modifying a noun (a person, place, or thing), keep the regular `い`.
If you are modifying a verb (an action), use `く`.

```jp
これは速[はや]いバスです。
バスは速[はや]く走[はし]ります。
```
*This is a fast bus.*
*The bus runs fast.*

In the first sentence, "fast" describes the bus itself. In the second, "fast" describes the action of running.

Keep this logic in your back pocket. We just learned how to do this with い-adjectives, but soon you'll need to know how to make na-adjectives (like 静[しず]か) do the exact same thing using に.
caution_notes: Adverbs ending in く are used to modify verbs and actions, not nouns.
The adjective いい (good) changes to よく, not いく.

items.meaning: make a na-adjective into an adverb

example_sentences.furigana: 静[しず]かにしてください。
きれいに書[か]きます。
元[げん]気[き]に遊[あそ]びます。

items.explanation_markdown:
Imagine you are sitting in the library trying to study. A few tables over, some people are talking loudly, and you want to describe your own situation in contrast. You want to say, "I am studying quietly."

You already know the word for "quiet" (静[しず]か), and you know the verb for "to study" (勉[べん]強[きょう]する). But how do you glue them together? If you just smash them next to each other and say `静か勉強します`, it sounds broken to a Japanese speaker, roughly like saying "I quiet study" in English. 

We need a way to turn the adjective "quiet" into an adverb—a word that modifies an action instead of a thing. We need the Japanese equivalent of "-ly".

## How it works: The "-ly" of Japanese

To turn a na-adjective into an adverb, you just take its base form and attach に. 

That's the entire rule. You do not use the な that normally accompanies these adjectives. The に particle steps in to connect the descriptive word directly to the verb that follows it.

*   静[しず]か (quiet) → 静[しず]かに (quietly)
*   上手[じょうず] (skillful) → 上手[じょうず]に (skillfully)
*   丁[てい]寧[ねい] (polite / careful) → 丁[てい]寧[ねい]に (politely / carefully)

Let's see this in action to solve our library problem.

```jp
私[わたし]は静[しず]かに勉[べん]強[きょう]します。
```
*I study quietly.*

Notice how perfectly に links the state of being quiet directly to the action of studying. This works for almost any na-adjective you want to use to describe how an action is performed.

```jp
彼[かの]女[じょ]は上手[じょうず]に歌[うた]います。
```
*She sings skillfully.*

When we translate 上手[じょうず]に into English, "skillfully" can sometimes sound a bit stiff. In natural English, you would probably just say "She sings well." But the Japanese literally means she performs the action of singing with skill.

```jp
手[て]紙[がみ]を丁[てい]寧[ねい]に書[か]きます。
```
*I write the letter carefully.*

The word 丁[てい]寧[ねい] is often taught as "polite," like bowing at the right angle or using formal speech. But when applied to physical actions like writing or making something, 丁[てい]寧[ねい]に usually translates closer to "carefully," "neatly," or "meticulously."

## Modifying nouns vs. modifying actions

You already know how to use na-adjectives to describe nouns (things or people). To do that, you use な. For example, `静かな町` means "a quiet town." 

But when you want to describe a verb (an action happening in space and time), that な must flip to a に. Let's put both rules into a single sentence so you can see the gears turning.

```jp
静[しず]かな町[まち]を静[しず]かに歩[ある]きます。
```
*I walk quietly through the quiet town.*

This distinction is an important mental anchor. If you accidentally use な before a verb, or に before a noun, the sentence breaks down. You cannot say `静かな歩きます` (quiet walk-ly) or `静かに町` (quietly town).

## The false friend: きれい

> **Warning:** Remember our old friend きれい (pretty / clean)? It ends in an "i" vowel sound, but it is secretly a na-adjective. 

Because きれい is a na-adjective, it absolutely must follow the に rule to become an adverb. You will hear many beginners try to treat it like an i-adjective and say `きれいく`. This is completely incorrect. To describe doing something cleanly or beautifully, you must say きれいに.

```jp
部屋[へや]をきれいに掃[そう]除[じ]します。
```
*I clean the room beautifully.*

Using きれいに correctly is one of the fastest ways to show a native speaker that you genuinely understand your grammar basics and aren't just guessing based on how a word sounds.

## Contrasting with i-adjectives

You have already learned how to turn i-adjectives into adverbs. To do that, you drop the final い and attach く.

For example, 速[はや]い (fast) becomes 速[はや]く (fast / quickly).

```jp
彼[かれ]は速[はや]く走[はし]ります。
```
*He runs fast.*

Both に and く do the exact same job: they turn adjectives into adverbs so you can paint a clearer picture of an action. Your only job is remembering which type of adjective you are dealing with before you choose your connector.

```jp
子[こ]供[ども]は元[げん]気[き]に遊[あそ]びます。
```
*The child plays energetically.*

Here, 元[げん]気[き] is a na-adjective, so it takes に. When a child plays 元[げん]気[き]に, they aren't just playing "healthily"—they are playing with a ton of energy, running around, and probably making a lot of noise. 

Master the difference between な for describing things and に for describing actions, and your Japanese will instantly sound much more natural. Keep this に pattern in your back pocket, too—you will need it again very soon when we learn how to talk about things "becoming" a certain way!
caution_notes: Use に to connect a na-adjective to a verb, but remember to still use な when connecting it to a noun.
Do not fall for the きれい trap; it is a na-adjective, so it must become きれいに to modify an action, never きれいく.

items.structure: A は B より + adj

example_sentences.japanese: 電車はバスより速いです。
example_sentences.furigana: 電[でん]車[しゃ]はバスより速[はや]いです。

example_sentences.japanese: 今日は昨日より暑いです。
example_sentences.furigana: 今日[きょう]は昨日[きのう]より暑[あつ]いです。

example_sentences.japanese: 犬は猫より大きいです。
example_sentences.furigana: 犬[いぬ]は猫[ねこ]より大[おお]きいです。

items.explanation_markdown:
You're looking at a menu with a friend. You want to eat steak, but they suggest sushi. How do you say "I like meat more than fish"?

When you want to compare two things in Japanese, you don't change the adjective like we do in English (big becomes bigger, cheap becomes cheaper). Instead, you use the pattern より.

```jp
肉[にく]は魚[さかな]より好[す]きです。
```
*I like meat more than fish.*

## How it works

The structure for a basic comparison looks like this: **[Item A] は [Item B] より [Adjective]**.

Think of より as meaning "compared to". So the sentence literally reads as: "As for Item A, compared to Item B, it is [Adjective]."

```jp
タクシーはバスより速[はや]いです。
```
*Taxis are faster than buses.*

```jp
今日[きょう]は昨日[きのう]より暑[あつ]いです。
```
*Today is hotter than yesterday.*

Notice how 暑[あつ]い (hot) and 速[はや]い (fast) didn't change at all? Japanese adjectives don't have a special comparative form. The word より does all the heavy lifting to tell the listener you are making a comparison.

## Flipping the order

In English, "Taxis are faster than buses" and "Compared to buses, taxis are faster" mean the same thing, just with a slightly different emphasis. Japanese does this too. You can easily swap the order of the two items as long as the particles stick to their words.

**[Item B] より [Item A] は [Adjective]** is perfectly natural.

```jp
ひらがなより漢[かん]字[じ]は難[むずか]しいです。
```
*Compared to hiragana, kanji is difficult.*

```jp
あの店[みせ]よりこの店[みせ]は安[やす]いです。
```
*Compared to that shop over there, this shop is cheaper.*

> When you flip the sentence like this, you are throwing a little extra spotlight on the thing you are comparing against. It sounds a bit like, "If we're talking about hiragana... well, kanji is definitely harder."

## Leaving parts out

If you and your friend are already talking about dogs, you don't need to explicitly name them again just to say cats are smaller. If the context is obvious, you can drop the Item A part entirely.

```jp
猫[ねこ]より大[おお]きいです。
```
*It is bigger than a cat.*

```jp
昨日[きのう]より寒[さむ]いです。
```
*It is colder than yesterday.*

## より vs. から

You already know that から means "from" (like starting from a location or a time). Historically, より also meant "from", and in very formal or older written Japanese you might still see it used that way.

Because of this, you might occasionally see letters or messages end with something like 私[わたし]より (From me). But in modern, everyday spoken Japanese, から is what you use for starting points (家[いえ]から学[がっ]校[こう]まで — from home to school). Keep より strictly for comparing things.

Hold onto this concept of making comparisons — soon you'll meet ぐらい, a handy little word that lets you say two things are *about the same*.
caution_notes: Japanese adjectives do not change form when making comparisons (there is no equivalent to adding '-er' in English); the word より does all the work.
Do not use より to mean 'from' a starting point in place or time in everyday speech—stick to から for that.

example_sentences.japanese: この店が一番安いです。
example_sentences.furigana: この店[みせ]が一[いち]番[ばん]安[やす]いです。
夏[なつ]が一[いち]番[ばん]好[す]きです。

example_sentences.japanese: 富士山が一番高いです。
example_sentences.furigana: 富[ふ]士[じ]山[やま]が一[いち]番[ばん]高[たか]いです。

items.explanation_markdown:
You are debating with a friend about the best season to visit Japan, or you are trying to figure out who in your family is the busiest. You do not just want to say someone is busy or a mountain is tall—you want to point out the absolute top of the category. You want to express the *most*, the *best*, or the *number one*.

In Japanese, creating this superlative state is incredibly straightforward. It does not require you to learn a complex new conjugation rule.

## How it works

Unlike English, which alters the adjective itself to change "tall" to "tallest" or adds extra grammatical words like "the most", Japanese leaves the adjective completely untouched. This is a huge relief when you are learning.

Instead, you just use the word 一[いち]番[ばん]. It literally translates to "number one". To use it, you simply drop 一[いち]番[ばん] directly in front of the adjective or the word you want to emphasize.

```jp
ここはおいしいです。
```
*This place is delicious.*

```jp
ここが一[いち]番[ばん]おいしいです。
```
*This place is the most delicious.*

When you declare that something is the best or the tallest, it usually has to be the best *somewhere* or *among* a specific group. To define this category, you use the particle で right after the group noun. 

Think of this で as drawing a boundary line or a circle around the group you are talking about. It tells the listener, "Inside the boundary of Japan" or "Inside the circle of my family."

```jp
富[ふ]士[じ]山[やま]は日本[にほん]で一[いち]番[ばん]高[たか]い山[やま]です。
```
*Mt. Fuji is the highest mountain in Japan.*

```jp
家[か]族[ぞく]で誰[だれ]が一[いち]番[ばん]忙[いそが]しいですか。
```
*Who is the busiest in your family?*

## Pairing with your desires

Because 一[いち]番[ばん] simply means "number one," it is not restricted to just describing facts like the weather or geography. It is highly useful when talking about the things you want the absolute most.

You can easily pair it with grammar patterns you already know, like the たい (want to do) verb ending or 欲[ほ]しい (want a thing).

```jp
明日[あした]何[なに]を一[いち]番[ばん]したいですか。
```
*What do you want to do most tomorrow?*

```jp
今[いま]、カメラが一[いち]番[ばん]欲[ほ]しいです。
```
*I want a camera the most right now.*

## Rules and exceptions

> You can only use 一[いち]番[ばん] when you are choosing from **three or more** options, or a general category.

If you are holding up exactly two shirts in a store and asking "Which one is cheaper?", you cannot use 一[いち]番[ばん]. Japanese treats comparing two things as a balancing act, and uses entirely different grammar for it. Once you have a crowd of three or more items, the balancing act becomes a competition, and 一[いち]番[ばん] is your tool to crown the single winner.

Also, pay attention to where you place the word in your sentence. 一[いち]番[ばん] loves to stick as close as possible to the word it modifies (usually the adjective or the verb). Putting it way too early in the sentence, such as starting with `一番私は…`, sounds highly unnatural and disconnected.

## Casual speech

In casual speech with friends, nothing about the core pattern changes. You drop the polite です or ます as usual. 

However, you will frequently see it written entirely in hiragana (いちばん) in text messages or informal writing. Because kanji can sometimes feel a bit stiff or academic, writing it in hiragana softens the visual impact of the sentence, making it feel friendlier and more conversational.

```jp
ここのご飯[はん]がいちばんおいしい！
```
*The food here is the most delicious!*

## Contrast: Liking vs. Liking the most

Let's look at how adding 一[いち]番[ばん] shifts the focus of a sentence, especially with preference words like 好[す]き (liked/fond of). They might look similar, but the intention is entirely different.

```jp
私[わたし]は肉[にく]が好[す]きです。
```
*I like meat.*

This is a simple fact. You like meat, but you probably like fish and vegetables too. It is an unranked statement.

```jp
私[わたし]は肉[にく]が一[いち]番[ばん]好[す]きです。
```
*I like meat the best.*

Now you have officially ranked it. Out of all the foods in the world, meat takes the absolute top spot for you. Hold onto this concept of ranking your preferences—soon you will learn how to state your own opinions with と思[おも]う (I think that), and pairing it with 一[いち]番[ばん] will let you smoothly declare things like "I think this is the best!"
caution_notes: Do not use 一番 when comparing exactly two things; it is exclusively for choosing the top item from three or more options.
Keep 一番 close to the adjective or verb it modifies; placing it too early in the sentence sounds unnatural.

example_sentences.furigana: お茶[ちゃ]はどうですか。

example_sentences.japanese: 日本の生活はどうですか。
example_sentences.furigana: 日本[にほん]の生[せい]活[かつ]はどうですか。

example_sentences.japanese: この映画はどうでしたか。
example_sentences.furigana: この映[えい]画[が]はどうでしたか。

items.explanation_markdown:
You're trying to set up a time to meet a friend, or you want to hear all about their new job. You need a simple way to suggest an option ("how about...") or ask for an impression ("how is...").

The word you are looking for is どう, which means *how*.

## How it works

To use this pattern, just take a noun, mark it with the topic particle は, and add どうですか. It works perfectly for offering suggestions, like a time or a place to meet.

```jp
明日[あした]はどうですか。
```
*How about tomorrow?*

It also works just as well for asking someone's opinion or impression of something.

```jp
新[あたら]しい仕[し]事[ごと]はどうですか。
```
*How is the new job?*

If you are asking about something that already happened, just change the copula です (the word that works like *is/am/are*) to its past tense form, でした.

```jp
昨日[きのう]の映[えい]画[が]はどうでしたか。
```
*How was yesterday's movie?*

## Rules and exceptions

This pattern is strictly for nouns. You can use it with times, places, and things, but you cannot attach it directly to a verb to say something like "how about we go."

If you want to be more polite—for example, if you are offering a drink to a visitor at your company—there is a formal version of どう. You swap it out for いかが.

```jp
お茶[ちゃ]はいかがですか。
```
*How about some tea?*

> Because いかが is already very polite, you will almost never use it in casual speech or with close friends. Reserve it for guests, teachers, or formal situations.

## Casual speech

When you are talking to friends, you can drop the ですか entirely. Just say どう and raise your intonation at the end to make it a question.

```jp
土[ど]曜[よう]日[ひ]の夜[よる]はどう？
```
*How about Saturday night?*

## Offering things: どう vs がほしい

You already know that you can ask what someone wants using がほしい. But when you are hosting someone, you have to be careful which one you use.

```jp
お茶[ちゃ]がほしいですか。
お茶[ちゃ]はどうですか。
```
*Do you want some tea?*
*How about some tea?*

Asking お茶[ちゃ]がほしいですか can sound a bit too direct, almost like a medical questionnaire or an interrogation. Offering it as a suggestion with どうですか (or いかがですか) is much softer and gives them an easy, polite way to accept or decline.

Next time someone asks for your opinion with どうですか, you'll need a way to answer them. Hold onto that thought—it becomes important when we look at と思[おも]う (I think that) later on.
caution_notes: どうですか attaches directly to nouns, so you cannot use it right after a verb to suggest an action.
When asking for an impression of a past event, remember to change ですか to でしたか.
Offering food or drinks with がほしいですか can sound overly direct; use どうですか or いかがですか instead.

example_sentences.furigana: 明日[あした]は雨[あめ]でしょう。
彼[かれ]は来[く]るでしょう。
難[むずか]しいでしょう。

items.explanation_markdown:
You check your watch. Your friend is thirty minutes late to meet you at the restaurant. You know they missed their train, and they had a lot of work to finish today anyway. Another friend asks if you think they are still showing up. You can't predict the future with absolute certainty, but all the evidence points to one conclusion. How do you say they probably aren't coming?

Whenever you need to make an educated guess, express a probability, or just soften a statement so you don't sound like a know-it-all, you will reach for だろう.

It is the easiest way to add a layer of "probably" or "I suspect" to your sentences in Japanese. Let's break down exactly how to use it.

## Attaching to verbs and adjectives

だろう acts like a caboose that you attach to the end of a train. The train, in this case, is the plain form of a word—the casual, dictionary shape of the word, rather than the polite polite forms you might be used to.

When you want to make a guess about an action, just take the plain form of the verb and add だろう.

```jp
彼[かれ]は帰[かえ]るだろう。
```
*He will probably return home.*

You can also use this to guess that an action won't happen. Just use the negative plain form of the verb.

```jp
今日[きょう]は彼[かの]女[じょ]は来[らい]ないだろう。
```
*She probably won't come today.*

This same logic applies directly to i-adjectives. If you are guessing that something is expensive, hot, or difficult, you just leave the adjective in its natural state and tack だろう on the end. Imagine you are looking at a fancy department store from the outside. You haven't looked at the price tags, but you can guess.

```jp
あの店[みせ]の服[ふく]は高[たか]いだろう。
```
*The clothes at that shop are probably expensive.*

## The noun and na-adjective trap

Because だろう is the designated word for guessing, it naturally works with nouns and na-adjectives too. But there is one major pitfall here that trips up almost everyone in their first week of using it.

When you speak casually in Japanese, you usually attach the plain copula だ (the casual version of です, the word that works like *is/am/are*) to nouns and na-adjectives to say that something "is."

You might be very tempted to leave that だ attached and simply add だろう on top of it. Do not do this. Stacking them into `雨だだろう` is a grammatical traffic jam.

Why? Because だろう is actually just a modified, guessing version of だ itself. It already has that fundamental "to be" energy baked directly into its DNA. If you put another だ right before it, you are essentially stuttering the verb.

Instead, you must drop any だ and attach だろう directly to the bare noun or na-adjective.

```jp
明日[あした]は雨[あめ]だろう。
```
*Tomorrow will probably be rain.*

```jp
あの図[と]書[しょ]館[かん]は静[しず]かだろう。
```
*That library is probably quiet.*

## Fact versus probability

Let's look at the space this new pattern occupies compared to the grammar you already know. Until now, you've relied heavily on です to describe things. 

When you use です, you are stating something as a concrete, objective fact. You are telling your listener that you are certain of the information.

```jp
この本[ほん]は面[おも]白[しろ]いです。
```
*This book is interesting.*

Using です here implies you have already read the book, or you know for an absolute fact that it is a universally great read. But what if you haven't read it yet? What if you are just looking at the cover, and you want to recommend it based on a guess?

Using です would feel a bit too strong. You need to soften your statement.

```jp
この本[ほん]は面[おも]白[しろ]いだろう。
```
*This book is probably interesting.*

Swapping です for だろう immediately signals to your listener that this is your prediction. It leaves room for you to be wrong, which is an incredibly important social tool in Japanese conversation. People generally prefer to avoid stating things too aggressively, and making educated guesses is a great way to soften your speech.

## When things are probably not true

We mentioned earlier that you can use the negative plain form of verbs. You can do the exact same thing with nouns and adjectives by using their negative plain forms.

You already know that the negative of です is ではありません, and its plain equivalent is じゃない. To say something is *probably not* true, just attach だろう to that negative plain form.

```jp
彼[かれ]は医[い]者[しゃ]じゃないだろう。
```
*He is probably not a doctor.*

## Guessing locations and existence

You can also use this pattern with verbs of existence, like いる (for living things) and ある (for objects), to guess where something is right now.

Imagine you are looking for your cat, but you can't find her in the living room. It's a cold day, so you make a logical guess about her location without knowing for sure.

```jp
猫[ねこ]はベッドにいるだろう。
```
*The cat is probably on the bed.*

> A quick note on talking to others: In casual conversations, asking someone a direct question about themselves using this pattern (like "Will you probably go?") sounds unnatural, as people don't usually need to guess their own plans. Also, directing だろう at another person can carry a slightly masculine or blunt nuance. However, everyone—regardless of gender—uses it when they are thinking out loud or muttering a pure internal guess to themselves.

Hold onto this guessing mechanic. Right now, the pattern we've learned is perfect for casual speech with your friends or musing to yourself. But eventually, you'll need to make these same guesses in polite situations, like talking to a teacher or a boss. When we step up the politeness later on, this exact same pattern will upgrade to its polite twin: でしょう.
caution_notes: Never attach the casual copula だ directly before だろう; attach it directly to the bare noun or na-adjective instead.

items.structure: Plain form + かもしれない

example_sentences.japanese: 明日は雪かもしれません。
example_sentences.furigana: 明日[あした]は雪[ゆき]かもしれません。

example_sentences.japanese: 彼は忙しいかもしれない。
example_sentences.furigana: 彼[かれ]は忙[いそが]しいかもしれない。

example_sentences.japanese: 遅れるかもしれません。
example_sentences.furigana: 遅[おく]れるかもしれません。

items.explanation_markdown:
You look at the dark sky. The weather is getting worse, and you want to warn your friend that tomorrow's plans are looking a bit uncertain. How do you tell them "it might rain" when you aren't a meteorologist?

```jp
明日[あした]は雨[あめ]かもしれません。
```
*It might rain tomorrow.*

Enter かもしれない, your go-to pattern for expressing a guess or possibility. When you aren't one hundred percent sure about something, this pattern softens your statement from a hard fact to a "maybe." The pattern literally builds on the idea that the truth "cannot be known" for sure.

## How it works

Building this pattern is mostly a matter of taking the plain form of a word—the dictionary version without the polite *masu* or *desu* endings—and attaching かもしれない.

If you want to be polite to the person you are talking to, you swap the ending to its formal version: かもしれません.

```jp
彼[かれ]は明日[あした]来[く]るかもしれません。
```
*He might come tomorrow.*

```jp
この映[えい]画[が]はつまらないかもしれない。
```
*This movie might be boring.*

## The "da" exception

There is exactly one sharp edge to watch out for. When you use a noun or a Na-adjective, you do not use the plain copula だ (the casual word for *is/am/are*). You just attach かもしれない directly to the bare word.

> Do not say `雨だかもしれない`. Drop the だ entirely: 雨[あめ]かもしれない.

```jp
ここは病[びょう]院[いん]かもしれない。
```
*This place might be a hospital.*

```jp
先[せん]生[せい]は暇[ひま]かもしれません。
```
*The teacher might be free.*

## Casual speech

In real, everyday conversations with friends, かもしれない is a bit of a mouthful. People almost always chop it down to just かも.

```jp
あれは犬[いぬ]かも。
```
*That over there might be a dog.*

It works exactly the same way as the full version, just shorter. You will hear this constantly in casual Japanese.

## Possibility vs. Ability

You already know ことができる for talking about what is possible. It helps to see how these two patterns live in different spaces.

```jp
明日[あした]、彼[かれ]は来[く]ることができます。
```
*Tomorrow, he is able to come.*

```jp
明日[あした]、彼[かれ]は来[く]るかもしれません。
```
*Tomorrow, he might come.*

Use ことができる when you are talking about ability or physical capability (he has the time and the means to show up). Use かもしれない when you are making a prediction about what will actually happen (you are guessing about his actions).

Get comfortable with leaving things a little uncertain here. Soon, you'll learn と思[おも]う (I think that), which will give you another great way to express your own thoughts without stating them as absolute facts.
caution_notes: Do not use the copula だ before かもしれない; attach it directly to the bare noun or Na-adjective.

example_sentences.japanese: 明日は晴れると思います。
example_sentences.english: I think it will be sunny tomorrow.
example_sentences.furigana: 明日[あした]は晴[は]れると思[おも]います。

example_sentences.japanese: この本はいいと思います。
example_sentences.english: I think this book is good.
example_sentences.furigana: この本[ほん]はいいと思[おも]います。
彼[かれ]は来[らい]ないと思[おも]う。

items.explanation_markdown:
You are walking out of a cinema with a friend. They turn to you and ask what you thought of the film. You want to say "It was interesting," but stating it as a universal fact feels a little too heavy. You want to soften it to "*I think* it was interesting."

To express your opinion or make a prediction, Japanese uses the verb 思[おも]う (to think) paired with the quoting particle と. It literally works like "I think quote: [my thought]."

```jp
あの映[えい]画[が]は面[おも]白[しろ]いと思[おも]います。
```
*I think that movie is interesting.*

## How it works

You take a complete, casual sentence (the "plain form") and attach と思[おも]う. If you want to be polite to the person you are talking to, you make the final verb polite: と思[おも]います. But the thought *inside* the quote always stays casual.

```jp
彼[かれ]は今日[きょう]来[らい]ないと思[おも]います。
```
*I think he will not come today.*

There is one major trap here. If your thought ends in an i-adjective or a verb, you just attach と思[おも]う directly. But if it ends in a noun or a na-adjective, you have a missing piece.

In casual Japanese, nouns and na-adjectives need the casual "is" word だ to form a complete sentence. If you forget to include だ before と思[おも]う, the sentence falls apart.

```jp
この店[みせ]は静[しず]かだと思[おも]います。
```
*I think this shop is quiet.*

```jp
明日[あした]は雨[あめ]だと思[おも]います。
```
*I think it will rain tomorrow.*

## Rules and exceptions

The biggest mistake beginners make is making the inside of the quote polite. The quote must always be plain form. Never say `行きますと思います` — it sounds like "I think: I will politely go." Always use the plain form inside, and save the politeness for the very end of the sentence.

> **Mind reading is not allowed:** You can only use と思[おも]う for your *own* thoughts. If you want to say "He thinks," you need a different grammar pattern. Japanese grammar strictly separates what you feel from what you guess others are feeling.

When you want to ask someone else's opinion, you just ask them what they think.

```jp
これ、どう思[おも]いますか。
```
*What do you think about this?*

## Casual speech

When you are talking to friends, you drop the polite ます and just end the sentence with 思[おも]う. Everything inside the quote stays exactly the same.

```jp
この本[ほん]は面[おも]白[しろ]いと思[おも]う。
```
*I think this book is interesting.*

## Contrast

You already know かもしれない for guessing "might" or "maybe." The difference between the two is confidence and intent.

```jp
明日[あした]は雪[ゆき]かもしれない。
```
*It might snow tomorrow.*

```jp
明日[あした]は雪[ゆき]だと思[おも]います。
```
*I think it will snow tomorrow.*

かもしれない means you are tossing a coin; there is a chance it happens, but you aren't sure. と思[おも]う means you have formed an actual opinion or prediction that you stand behind.

Hold onto this quoting particle と. It works exactly the same way when we learn how to talk about things "called" or "named" a certain way using という later on.
caution_notes: Always use the casual plain form inside the quote before と思う, never polite forms like ます or です.
When expressing an opinion about a noun or na-adjective, you must include the casual 'is' word だ right before と思う.
You can only use と思う to express your own thoughts or ask the listener for theirs, never to state what a third person is thinking.

example_sentences.furigana: 田中[たなか]という人[ひと]です。

example_sentences.japanese: これは何という花ですか。
example_sentences.furigana: これは何[なに]という花[はな]ですか。
「猫[ねこ]」という映[えい]画[が]を見[み]ました。

items.explanation_markdown:
You are making weekend plans in a new town, and a friend recommends a great local spot. They do not just say "go to the coffee shop"—they tell you to visit a specific place called "Spring." In English, we handle this by just capitalizing the name or pausing slightly before it. We say, "I went to a coffee shop called Spring." But in Japanese, you need a reliable mechanical way to link a very specific proper noun (the name) to a broad category (the type of place or thing), ensuring the listener knows exactly what you are talking about. You cannot just stack two nouns against each other and hope they stick.

```jp
春[はる]という喫[きっ]茶[さ]店[みせ]に行[い]きました。
```
*I went to a coffee shop called Spring.*

This pattern acts as a bridge. It tells the listener, "Hey, I am about to give you a specific name, and here is the general category that name belongs to." It is an incredibly powerful tool for self-learners, because it allows you to talk about anything in the world even if you only know its title.

## How it works

The structure here is entirely logical once you look at its two moving parts. You take the specific name or quote you want to share, attach という, and then follow it up immediately with the broad category noun.

```jp
白[しろ]という犬[いぬ]がいます。
```
*I have a dog named White.*

This phrase breaks down into two fundamental pieces you are likely starting to recognize. The first half is the quoting particle と. Think of this particle as a pair of invisible quotation marks holding the exact name in place. The second half is the verb 言[い]う, which simply means "to say."

When you glue them together into という, the literal translation of the phrase is something much closer to "is said to be." So, a purely literal reading of our example sentence above would be "a dog that is said to be White." Over time, this phrasing smoothed out in natural speech into a simple grammatical tool that just means "called" or "named."

You always place the specific quote or name on the left of という, and the broad category noun on the right. In Japanese grammar, descriptive information always comes *before* the thing it describes. English puts the category first ("a dog named White"), but Japanese always puts the specific description first ("White-named dog").

## Rules and exceptions

This pattern gives you a massive amount of freedom, but it has one extremely strict requirement regarding what goes on the right side of the bridge.

> The right side of this pattern must always, without exception, be a noun. You are permanently attaching a specific name or quote to a "thing" (a book, a song, a person, a dog). You cannot use this pattern to modify an adjective or a verb.

You can also use this pattern dynamically to ask about names you do not know. When you combine the question word 何[なに] (what) with this grammar point, you get the phrase 何[なに]という. This is by far the most natural way to ask what something is called in Japanese.

```jp
これは何[なに]という花[はな]ですか。
```
*What is this flower called?*

Asking it this way is much clearer than just pointing and asking "what is this?" because it signals that you understand what the object is broadly (a flower), but you want to know its exact title or species.

You might be wondering if you can use this pattern for abstract concepts, or if it only applies to concrete names. The answer is yes, absolutely. The left side does not have to be a simple name—it can be an entire clause (a mini-sentence with its own verb) acting as a direct quote of information.

```jp
明日[あした]海[うみ]に行[い]くという約[やく]束[そく]があります。
```
*I have a promise to go to the sea tomorrow.*

Here, the "name" being quoted is the entire descriptive phrase "we are going to the sea tomorrow." The noun being modified is the abstract concept of a "promise." You are literally saying "the promise called 'we are going to the sea tomorrow'." Because Japanese does not use relative pronouns like "that" or "which" in the same way English does, this pattern is exactly how you link full descriptions to abstract nouns like promises, stories, or news.

## Casual speech

When you are hanging out with friends or chatting in a relaxed environment, taking the time and breath to clearly articulate the full という can feel slightly stiff or overly formal. In real, everyday conversation, native speakers almost always crush these sounds together.

```jp
時[じ]間[かん]っていう映[えい]画[が]を見[み]ました。
```
*I watched a movie called Time.*

The casual version is っていう. It functions exactly the same way, but the tongue relaxes, dropping the formal quoting particle and replacing it with a sharp, compressed pause. You will hear this constantly in casual Japanese, especially when talking about pop culture, movies, or music with your peers. Keep in mind that you should stick to the full という when speaking to a teacher, a boss, or someone you just met, but actively listening for this casual compression will dramatically improve your ability to understand native speech.

## Contrast

You already know how to use と思[おも]う to talk about your internal opinions and thoughts. Because both of these patterns rely on the exact same quoting particle と, they live in the same mental space. However, they perform very different jobs for your listener, and swapping them changes the reality of your sentence.

When you use と思[おも]う, you are taking a quote and connecting it directly to a verb—your own internal, subjective action of thinking. You are explaining your personal perspective to the world.

When you use という, you are taking a quote and connecting it to a noun in the real world. You are establishing an objective fact about what something is actually named or called, regardless of your personal feelings.

```jp
これは青[あお]という本[ほん]だと思[おも]います。
```
*I think this is a book called Blue.*

In this example, you can see both patterns working together in perfect harmony. First, という links the specific title "Blue" objectively to the noun "book." Then, the entire idea is wrapped up with と思[おも]う to explain that this whole scenario is just what you personally believe. 

Being able to define what things are called gives you incredible leverage to talk about new topics, even if your vocabulary is still growing. Keep an eye on how this bridging superpower works—it will come in handy again when we learn how to give direct advice with ほうがいい later on.
caution_notes: The right side of という must always be a noun, because you are permanently linking a specific name or quotation to a broader category.
Stick to the full という in formal or polite situations, as the compressed っていう form is strictly for casual speech among friends.

items.structure: Verb stem / adj stem + すぎる

example_sentences.furigana: 食[た]べすぎました。
この服[ふく]は高[たか]すぎます。
昨日[きのう]は飲[の]みすぎた。

items.explanation_markdown:
You are at a shop looking at a nice bag. You check the price tag, and it has way too many zeros. You need a way to express that it crosses the line from just "expensive" to "too expensive."

When an action or a state goes beyond a reasonable limit, Japanese uses the helper verb すぎる. It attaches right to the end of your existing verbs and adjectives to mean "too much" or "excessively."

## How it works

To use すぎる, you need the stem of your word. For verbs, this is the stem (the base part you normally attach ます to).

```jp
彼[かれ]は働[はたら]きすぎる。
```
*He works too much.*

```jp
昨日[きのう]、パンを食[た]べすぎた。
```
*Yesterday, I ate too much bread.*

For adjectives ending in い, simply drop the final い and attach your new ending. The whole package now behaves just like a regular verb.

```jp
このかばんは高[たか]すぎる。
```
*This bag is too expensive.*

```jp
部屋[へや]が寒[さむ]すぎます。
```
*The room is too cold.*

## Rules and exceptions

Because すぎる translates to "too much," it inherently carries a negative feeling. You are saying a boundary was crossed. In English, you might say "this cake is too good!" as a compliment. In Japanese, traditionally, attaching this to a positive word implies a problem.

> If you say someone is 親[しん]切[せつ]すぎる (too kind), it might sound like they are overbearing or naive, rather than it being a pure compliment.

Because すぎる acts just like a regular verb that ends in る, you can conjugate it into polite speech or the past tense. Notice how we used すぎます for politeness and すぎた for the past tense in the examples above.

## Contrast: The most vs. too much

It is easy to mix up saying something has the highest degree of a trait versus saying it has too much of it. If you want to say something is the absolute peak of a category, you already know to use 一[いち]番[ばん].

```jp
あの店[みせ]が一[いち]番[ばん]高[たか]いです。
```
*That shop is the most expensive.*

But being the most expensive doesn't necessarily mean it is unreasonable. If you want to express that the price is out of bounds, you swap in our new pattern.

```jp
あの店[みせ]は高[たか]すぎます。
```
*That shop is too expensive.*

Hold onto this concept of attaching patterns to verb stems. You will see a similar structural shift when we meet ほうがいい (had better) to give strong advice later on.
caution_notes: Because すぎる implies an excess that crosses a reasonable boundary, using it with positive traits can sound like a complaint rather than a compliment.

items.structure: Verb-た / Verb-ない + ほうがいい

example_sentences.japanese: 早く寝たほうがいいです。
example_sentences.furigana: 早[はや]く寝[ね]たほうがいいです。

example_sentences.japanese: 薬を飲んだほうがいい。
example_sentences.furigana: 薬[くすり]を飲[の]んだほうがいい。

example_sentences.japanese: 行かないほうがいいです。
example_sentences.furigana: 行[い]かないほうがいいです。

items.explanation_markdown:
You're at a friend's place and they've been coughing all evening. You want to say, gently, "you should go to the hospital." Not a command, not "you must" — just solid, caring advice. That's exactly the job of ほうがいい.

The pattern means something like *had better* or *should*. You attach it to a verb and you're handing someone a recommendation: this choice is the better one. Here's the hospital line.

```jp
病[びょう]院[いん]に行[い]ったほうがいいですよ。
```

*You should go to the hospital.*

Notice the verb is 行[い]った — the past form — even though nothing has happened yet. That surprises everyone at first. Hold that thought; it's the whole trick of this pattern.

## How it works

There are two shapes, depending on whether you're recommending *doing* something or *not doing* it.

For "you should do X", take the plain past form of the verb (the た-form) and add ほうがいい.

```jp
薬[くすり]を飲[の]んだほうがいいです。
今日[きょう]は休[やす]んだほうがいいですよ。
```

*You should take medicine.*
*You should rest today.*

Why the past form for future advice? Think of ほう as "the ~ side / the ~ option" (it's the same 方[ほう] you'll meet in comparisons). You're literally saying "the *having-taken-medicine* side is good" — you picture the action as already done and judge that outcome as the better one. The past form freezes the action into a completed picture you can weigh.

For "you should *not* do X", use the plain negative — the ない-form — and add ほうがいい. This one stays present, no past trickery.

```jp
そのお酒[さけ]を飲[の]まないほうがいいです。
今日[きょう]は泳[およ]がないほうがいいですよ。
```

*You'd better not drink that alcohol.*
*You'd better not swim today.*

So the split is clean: **positive advice → past (た) + ほうがいい**, **negative advice → ない + ほうがいい**. That asymmetry looks odd but it's fixed and reliable.

You can make the whole thing more polite by keeping です on the end (ほうがいいです), or leave it off for plain speech (ほうがいい). And you can soften it further by tacking よ on the end, which makes it feel like a friendly heads-up rather than a verdict.

## Rules and exceptions

The biggest trap is reaching for the plain *present* form on the positive side. 行[い]くほうがいい isn't the natural advice pattern — for a specific recommendation to a specific person, you want 行[い]ったほうがいい.

> For concrete, in-the-moment advice ("you should go *now*"), use the past form: 行[い]ったほうがいい. The present form 行[い]くほうがいい drifts toward general comparison ("going is the better option, in general") and sounds weaker as personal advice.

The negative side has no such split — it's always ない, never past.

```jp
たくさん食[た]べないほうがいいですよ。
```

*You'd better not eat a lot.*

One more thing about tone: ほうがいい is genuinely stronger than a bare suggestion. When you say 休[やす]んだほうがいい, you're implying there's a real downside to *not* resting. For a lighter "how about resting?" you'd reach for something else entirely (you already know どうですか for that). Save ほうがいい for when you mean it.

## Casual speech

Drop the です and you're already casual: 飲[の]んだほうがいい. In fast speech people often shorten ほう to ほ and swallow the が, so ほうがいい can come out sounding like *ほうがいい* run together — you'll hear it, you don't need to produce it. The safe casual form is simply the plain one with よ:

```jp
早[はや]く寝[ね]たほうがいいよ。
```

*You'd better go to sleep early.*

That よ is doing a lot of work — it turns a flat statement into "hey, just so you know." Very common when you're looking out for a friend.

## Contrast

The closest thing you already know is かもしれない, *might / maybe*. They feel related but do opposite jobs. かもしれない reports a possibility; ほうがいい pushes a choice.

```jp
明日[あした]は雨[あめ]かもしれません。
傘[かさ]を持[も]ったほうがいいですよ。
```

*It might rain tomorrow.*
*You'd better take an umbrella.*

See how the first sentence just floats a possibility, and the second one leans in with a recommendation because of it. Swap them and it breaks: you can't advise with かもしれない, and ほうがいい can't merely speculate.

It also brushes up against と思[おも]う, *I think that*. と思[おも]う is your private opinion; ほうがいい is a recommendation aimed at the listener. "この本[ほん]はいいと思[おも]う" says what *you* feel; "この本[ほん]を読[よ]んだほうがいい" tells the other person what to *do*. Same warmth, different direction.

## Closing

Recap: past (た) form for "you should," ない form for "you'd better not," both capped with ほうがいい — and add です or よ to set the tone. The past-tense-for-future-advice quirk is the one to burn in.
